A precise determination of the B^0_s meson's lifetime is crucial for identifying possible non-SM processes, such as the b->s gamma decay at the tree level or the tree-level bbsb vertex. We employ the end point rule to analyze three-body decays of the B^0_s meson at the factorization scale. By applying the "lattice" method to eliminate long-distance contributions, we can subtract semi-leptonic decays from two fully determined semi-leptonic decay rates to derive a quantity denoted as \Delta\tau. By combining \Delta\tau with the B^0_s meson mass, we can obtain a value for the decay rate. At tree level, we calculate the B^0_s meson decay rate to be 4.65±0.11 GeV^5, assuming a f_B^0_s value of 239 MeV. We compare our results to previous model-based predictions and lattice determinations. Furthermore, we discuss the influence of power corrections on the absolute value of the B^0_s meson decay rate.

This research examines the optimization of switch-time in the chance-constrained problem of a continuous-time system, which belongs to a specific class and can be mapped to a quasi-variational inequality. We provide value function estimates, demonstrate the existence of a smooth solution for the mapped problem, and establish the map's continuity properties. Furthermore, we show the presence of a convergence sequence of controlled trajectories that satisfy the discretized constraint, both globally and locally.

Our analysis of dipole anisotropy in cosmic ray directions has been conducted using data from 1.6 EeV to 1.2 EeE, encompassing 31 million events. By separating the dipole amplitude into power law segments across this energy range, we identified a notable "knee" structure in the anisotropy that does not mirror the established "knee" in the cosmic ray energy spectrum. Specifically, the amplitude of the dipole increases with energy for cosmic rays above 4 EeV.

The dependence of the mean transverse momentum (〈$p_T$〉) and collisions (s) on the centrality of collisions is directly linked to the variation in net baryon number variation. This relationship is used to eliminate the influence of 〈$p_T$〉 and s variations when analyzing net-baryon number cumulatives, as demonstrated in previous studies at RHIC and LHC. This approach is now applied to analyze the cumulatives (up to order 6) for net-baryon number, net-charge, and net-charge in 20 $Au+Au$ collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=200$ GeV. The findings indicate that lower order cumulatives (up to 4) are non-zero for net-baryon number but absent in the other categories. Moreover, a non-zero 5th and 6th order cumulative is observed in net-baryon number, whereas no such patterns exist in net-charge or charge. These observations are consistent with previous findings from more central collisions and proton-lead collisions.

In this study, we reformulate noncommutative quantum mechanics based on a specific relationship between noncommuting coordinates, based on the operators of momentum that commutes with each other. We demonstrate the equivalence of this approach to the first formulation proposed by Seiberg and Shwarz under a change of basis. We also establish the link to the deformed Schrödinger equation based on the cubic exponential triple. Finally, we present the method for calculating noncommutative expectation values in a straightforward manner.

The primary objective of this research is to develop an effective method for predicting the abundance of tumor infiltrating lymphocytes in digitized cancer tissue samples. According to various lineages, tumor infiltrating lymphocytes are essential for understanding the immune system's influence on the progression of cancer and the efficacy of immunotherapy treatments. Although using histopathology to estimate tumor infiltrating lymphocytes is common, this approach can be inconsistent and varies in reliability based on the level of detail examined. To address this challenge, we have devised a novel deep learning framework that leverages visual and contextual information from digitized tissue sections to generate more accurate estimations. Specifically, we employed a recurrent neural network to analyze the distribution of histological regions, which were automatically generated by segmenting the tissue sections. The attention mechanism was incorporated into this framework to enhance its ability to focus on the most relevant pieces of information when making these estimations. To validate our framework, we analyzed 1200 breast cancer tissue sections and successfully demonstrated its effectiveness in estimating tumor infiltrating lymphocytes. Furthermore, we found that our framework's predictions correlated positively with the actual results and helped doctors identify patients with higher levels of tumor infiltrating lymphocytes more accurately.

This paper proposes a modified joint equalization and decoding scheme for optical communications over wavelength-division multiplexing systems affected by burst errors. Due to the correlated nature of these errors, traditional square Euclidean metric (SEM) used in maximum likelihood sequence estimation (MLSE) is not effective, leading to increased memory requirements and decreased decoder performance. To address these limitations, a novel metric called corrected SEM (CSEM) is introduced and a modified algorithm, C-WDFE-MLSE, is developed to efficiently equalize and decode signals with significantly lower frame error rates. Simulation results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over conventional equalization and decoding techniques, particularly in high multiplexing scenarios with limited encoder memory. To further evaluate the proposed method, a theoretical analysis of the maximum likelihood (ML) decoding distance is conducted and finds strong alignment with simulated data, providing valuable insights into the method's performance.

Neural network architectures that are meticulously designed by humans are by nature limited in their creative potential and do not fully explore the possible design space. Moreover, the intricate process of creating such models often poses challenges. In this study, we introduce a innovative and self-sufficient optimization algorithm for a specific class of architectures known as Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs). Our algorithm efficiently adjusts a key parameter in TCNs called dilation factors, ensuring a uniform growth in both model size and inference latency. By integrating this algorithm into the open-source TC-Gen framework, we allow users to define a range for model size and latency, and automatically find the optimal dilation factors that yield a TCN with the best performance while staying within those constraints. Our method has been successfully tested on multiple benchmark datasets, yielding impressive improvements of up to 7.4% in accuracy over existing variants of the HUBERT architecture while incurring only 2.4% increased computational cost. Furthermore, our model can achieve 95.4% word error rate with 17x faster inference latency compared to the hugging-face implementation of HUBERT.

This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the key properties of finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras, focusing on dimensions, bases, nilpotency, solvability, lower central series, and derived series. A specific formula for the dimension of Zinbiel algebras is derived, and it's demonstrated that every finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra exhibits nilpotent behavior. Additionally, this study obtains the precise values for the nilpotency and solvability indices of three-dimensional solvable Zinbiel algebras.

According to real-time thermodynamics, the initial irregularities in energy density directly impact the final particle distributions in high-energy collisions. Specifically, particle fluctuations provide a quantitative measure of inhomogeneous quark-gluon plasma formation. Furthermore, particle correlations can be used to determine the local viscosity to entropy density ratio and its fluctuations. Notably, this study finds that the quark-gluon plasma's r3 charge distribution exhibits a distinct separation from its momentum distribution. Additionally, it identifies a direct correlation between the two. The article also investigates the relationship between them in central and peripheral collisions and finds that central collisions exhibit stronger deviations from ideal hydrodynamics. On the other hand, in peripheral collisions, increasing centralities within each particle type display similar patterns. The article further explores centralities within each particle type and displays similar patterns. Additionally, it finds that in peripheral collisions, centralities within each particle type and displays similar patterns.

We build upon our previous work to provide computationally feasible methods for determining precise, canonical formulas from abstract specifications in modal logic. These formulas are derived from ALBA algorithms, adapting inductive formulas to produce a first order correspondent that is computationally efficient and based on an antitone computation component ALBA2.

Query answering using first-order logic under four-valued semantics is demonstrated to be achievable through the reinterpretation of database states as partial interpretations. This approach enables coherent interpretation of truth values like true, false, both, and neither. Our consistent query answering framework extends this by assigning false values to queries answered from damaged databases, and we show that certain classes of first-order formulas can be efficiently answered by augmenting their classes of model-based partial interpretations with additional, freely specifiable classes. This formulation allows for a unified treatment of various criteria for database repair, and we apply it to examine the complexity of first-order consistent query answering under different semi-naive and bi-naive repair definitions.

We introduce a novel time series modeling approach using a time-inhomogeneous Poisson process, which can effectively capture complex nonlinear patterns and sudden shifts inherent in financial data. This approach enables researchers to develop linear state-space models based on external variables that influence the mean of a time series, as well as its associated deviations. Our empirical analysis and a comparison with a standard modeling technique, along with a real-world dataset during the COVID-19 pandemic, demonstrate the superior performance and flexibility of our proposed model in handling even extreme events and periods of market turmoil.

To make robot manipulations more versatile and adaptable, contact-rich Descriptors are essential. However, creating detailed 3D Descriptors for complex objects can be time-consuming and often unnecessary, as precise geometry isn't always required for successful manipulations. This research introduces Neural Descriptor Fields (NDF), a contact-specific network that NDF can learn from a small amount of demonstration data. By focusing on a task-specific objective function, NDF efficiently represents object states for rigid manipulations involving pinpoint contacts with complex shapes. The proposed model allows robots to generalize from a single 2D projection and thousands of training data points are unnecessary. NDF's performance can be improved with a small amount of extra demonstration data. A physical experiment shows that NDF can succeed with as little as one demonstration by learning from synthetic data.

The SiD Detector is a comprehensive simulation of the final central detector that will accompany the upgraded PiXie/Beam Dump at SLAC's Linac Coherent Light Source. Its calorimeter system consists of extended coverage compared to the BFactory SiD Prototype, featuring improved performance in jet energy resolution in the transverse plane at higher energy levels (above 200 GeV) in the forward regions. Additionally, it includes upgraded muon detection systems in the SiD Muon System.

We have utilized data from the APOGEE-2 to analyze six A-giant stars within the globular cluster Tononzintla 2, located in the Galactic bulge. These six stars have been individually deblended to accurately measure their metallicity and elemental abundances. Findings from our study show that Tononzintla 2 has a total metallicity of $+0.16\pm0.06$ dex and a very small spread in elemental abundances of $0.12$ dex for iron, along with moderate spreads in other elements like $-0.14$ to $+0.14$ for carbon. To ensure accuracy, we compared our results with those from the APOGEE data stream, which indicated a slightly higher metallicity of $+0.24$ but a similar spread in iron. Tononzintla 2 appears to be an unusual high-metallicity globular cluster with a homogeneous composition that sets it apart from other similar clusters. It also has a unique chemical composition that does not fit the typical patterns seen in other similar clusters, especially when examining the [Mg/Fe] and [Al/Al] values. These unusual chemical properties may be attributed to different formation processes involving massive intermediate-age populations within the cluster.

Researchers in verification and security frequently depend on the reliability of software components, but this dependence can propagate as they rely on more components. We investigated the structure of dependencies in formal proof collections to determine if they form a circular pattern or mirror the self-reinforcing nature of networks found in nature. Using Inductive Database (Idris) as a case study, we analyzed its dependency network and found that node connections follow a scale-free pattern, while node levels display a self-similar structure. This indicates that users should carefully consider the credibility of more fundamental nodes in these networks.

The structure of QCD in three dimensions can be reorganized as a power series in the inverse of the color number, with a critical point determining the radius of its convergence. For N=4, the value of $|z_c|$ increases by approximately 50% from its N=2 value of 0.4995, while showing little dependence on the beta function.

We investigate the connection between the Tetration-Approximation-Policy (TAP) free energy and the convergence of the (approximate) message passing algorithm for a specific problem, $\text{Z}_2$-synchronization. To address this $\text{Z}_2$-synchronization challenge, we modify the TAP formulation by applying a particular correction to its entropic term and compute the corresponding variational approximation. Subsequently, we analyze the persistent current and compute the exact average free energy per node in the infinite system. This modified free energy appears to correlate with the basin of attraction of the message passing algorithm. To further support this hypothesis, we compare the free energy with and without the correction for a specific problem, the Ising spin glass, and observe a notable difference in outcome. This comparison reveals that the standard TAP free energy may be a suitable criterion for assessing a system's equilibrium properties, rather than its initial state.

Generalized Sheet Transition Conditions or Effects have been widely employed in advanced metasurface design, enabling significant signal modifications when interacted with electromagnetic waves. Despite this, a complete theoretical GSTC formulation for interacting with lossy media has not yet been achieved. This paper addresses this gap by deriving a novel GSTC formulation tailored for GSTC-interaction with lossy media. A specific application, involving a tailored anisotropic absorption layer designed to convert circularly polarized waves into linearly polarized ones with enhanced efficiency, demonstrates the practical utility of this new GSTC formulation. Full-wave simulation results validate the concept, showcasing a 40% reduction in required medium thickness while attaining nearly complete conversion efficiency.

In this work, we investigate various aspects of a well-known technique employed to establish local orbital linearization and resonance elimination theories for nonholonomic systems near singular points. By examining the method of blowing up, we demonstrate its inefficiency in obtaining simple orbital linearization results in close proximity to the origin. Furthermore, we develop an alternative approach to the traditional method and prove two supplementary conclusions regarding orbital linearization. Finally, we compare the methods of proving local orbital linearization, including a variant achieved through our new strategy.

We utilize deep learning to create an electron restriction operator based on a generative model, which can derive potential functions accurately capturing the complex correlations among electrons in their spatial distribution. Building upon this operator, a novel algorithm is developed to solve the time-independent Schrödinger equation, taking advantage of the operator's electron correlation-generating capability. Calculations on hydrogen-like helium show comparable accuracy to previous methods at similar computational costs, while studies on beryllium hydride and water molecules also demonstrate the method's reliable performance.

We have detected a massive structure, referred to as the Giant Arc, within the Cosmic Microwave Background anisotropy map. This finding supports the Kashlinsky effect theory which suggests that mappers can observe signals from the Bulk Flow of galaxies affecting the CMAP at the edge of the visible universe. The size of the Giant Arc, at roughly 1.5 times the horizon radius, is notably larger than similar features and significantly bigger than the previously reported Sloan Great Wall, indicating a strong correlation with the largest galaxy distribution we know of. Our statistical analysis using the Minkowski functionals and an analogous test for cluster redshifts show strong evidence, with 99.73% and 99.6% confidence levels respectively, confirming that the Giant Arc is not a random fluctuation. However, more studies with similar scales are necessary to further verify this discovery. If these results hold true, it would mean that the influence of galaxy distributions can be seen all the way to the farthest reaches of the visible universe, raising questions about standard cosmological theories, particularly the assumption that we can ignore super-horizon scale effects. Also, it would suggest that the current record for the largest wall of stars might not be as isolated as previously thought.

A new understanding of how wide-area photography can accurately measure changes in atmospheric clarity has been demonstrated previously. Under certain conditions, the equipment used in this type of photography can be skipped altogether. We used an unusual setup to further prove this method's reliability without the need for precise calibration. Observing the lunar eclipse on 2015 April 4 from the La Palma Observatory, we employed a wide-area camera to study how particles in the atmosphere affected light passing through them. By analyzing video frames, we measured the clarity of the atmosphere independently of the equipment's sensitivity. Our findings showed a significant decrease in light during the total phase of the eclipse, but little change before and after. This study used a non-standard camera setup to study particle movement in the atmosphere, and our results suggest that wide-area photography can accurately measure these particles under favorable conditions.

In complex environments, estimating the pose of objects in motion is a complex task. To address this challenge, we introduce a new learning-based method called PRoGPoseNet. This approach leverages a novel technique known as projection grouping, which is inspired by the concept of cyclic symmetry. By applying this technique, our method can effectively distinguish between the foreground object and the background in a scene. We have incorporated a simple yet effective projection grouping network into PRoGPoseNet to refine the estimation of object pose. To further enhance performance, we have designed a projection grouping module (PGM) that is capable of utilizing multiple depth maps generated from different camera angles. By integrating this PGM, PRoGPoseNet can optimize the object pose in a coarse-to-fine manner. We have conducted comprehensive experiments on challenging object pose estimation benchmarks, and the results show a significant improvement in estimation accuracy. Additionally, PRoGPoseNet has demonstrated superior performance on the COSE benchmark by outperforming existing methods.

In this theoretical paper we propose that certain Peridynamic kernel structures
are inherently incompatible with accurate prediction of fracture formation.
Our argument is that peridynamic kernels which do not adhere to a rotation
invariant will result in spurious prediction of cracks in all directions along
with the grain of any applied stress. We support this claim by demonstrating
this issue through a range of examples which include well established
peridynamic kernel forms, as well as variations used in peridynamic stress
tests. Furthermore we show how the directionality present in peridynamic
simulations can be linked to kernel structure and how this can be modified to
avoid unnecessary cracks. Finally we suggest alternative peridynamic kernel
forms that may aid in this aim.

A new Graphical Lasso framework is proposed, which integrates latent variables to build upon and enhance G.Lasso for robust precision estimation in the presence of hidden variables influencing the observed variables.

To evaluate and predict biomolecular properties with molecular dynamics, simulations are frequently complemented by a set of discrete states modeled using a Markov model. However, for systems requiring extensive simulations, applying coarse-graining to reduce computational cost through the removal of degrees of freedom can introduce inaccuracies due to the introduction of fictitious forces. In this study, we investigate this issue by examining simulations of the alanine dipeptide system under various potentials and addressing this problem through four solutions using numerical methods. Our findings show that these methods mitigate the distortion introduced by restricted simulations, yielding accurate free energy landscapes and ensuring correct equilibrium distributions. Additionally, we assess the efficiency of these methods, revealing that they can be cost-effective compared to all-atom simulations. Furthermore, these results can be extrapolated to systems investigated with restricted simulations during applications of the QMC-REST method.

A new strategy for modeling binary black holes in a matter-filled environment has been introduced, based on type B initial conditions. In this approach, the binary black holes are assumed to be point masses surrounded by a smoothly distributed gaseous medium, which may be in motion, subject to an external potential. The approach begins with solving the linearized equations of motion for a small binary moving through a symmetric, externally perturbed medium, before deriving nonlinear gravitational waveforms. The method is applied to various scenarios, including binaries at minimal separation in symmetry-perturbed environments, and the results show that the binary's orbital motion leads to significant matter disturbances, ultimately shaping the gravitational waveform's amplitude and phase.

This study analyzes the exponential decay of energy in a star-shaped metric graph
equipped with a dynamic equation that combines the sum of Laplacians and elasticity.
We map each edge to an interval and assign a elasticity parameter and a unique star
connection condition at each endpoint. When elasticity is uniform and elasticity
values on the graph's edges approach infinity, we prove the system's exponential
stability. However, we show that elasticity along the graph's branches does not
guarantee stable decay, but adding elasticity along the main edge results in stable
decay instead of polynomial decay. A key factor here is elasticity along the main
edge acting as a damper for the elasticity along the branches. When there is no
elasticity on the graph's slopes, we have a previous result showing only polynomial
decay and we improve this to exponential decay. Systems without elasticity on the
graph's slopes are common and often lead to better stability.

This study examines the acoustic characteristics of Stycast 1090SI, a two-part epoxy used as an alternative to PMMA. As a modeling material, Stycast 1090SI offers certain advantages over PMMA despite its poorer acoustic properties. With a central frequency of 1.15MHz and an amplitude transmission of 30%, the acoustic features of Stycast 1090SI led to a modification of experimental conditions and results. This observation's implications were determined to be minimal, mainly due to the material's accurate representation of a dense, lossy medium's complex impedance, which is relevant in cases where incidents and reflections have comparable magnitudes.

The study examines how intermediate layers in a four-layer network model affect the relationship between layers and explains the inter-layer connections through projection matrices.
These matrices are developed based on a generalized bond percolation model that accounts for multiple layers and their unique characteristics.
By computing node centrality within this framework, the research reveals the distinct impact of betweenness on the computation of node importance and identifies the conditions under which a node is considered essential for betweenness.
Additionally, for a specific type of multilayer network where each layer consists of a complete graph, betweenness scores are computed and compared for nodes in different layers.
The results indicate that nodes in core layers typically possess higher betweenness scores than those on the periphery.

A novel approach to correcting color distortion in images is introduced, first
pinpointing inhomogeneities in a camera's point spread function (PSF) across
different color wavelengths. This method models the PSF using a series of
Hermite polynomials and acquires calibration images using a neutral density
filter to ensure uniform exposure. The resulting calibration data is used to
create a corrective lookup table (LUT) that adjusts raw images based on color
channel. Compared to traditional methods like cubic convolution interpolation,
this color-aware correction yields more accurate color representation in
images.

The structure of the Dirac equation is determined within the R-Minkowski spacetime, which is a subset of the de Sitter spacetime. A direct relationship between the two is established through conformal transformation. Leveraging this connection, we derive a spectral representation of the Dirac operator in de Sitter spacetime by applying the transformation to the spectral sequence of the R-Minkowski spacetime.

We provide an in-depth introduction to probabilistic graph models focused on time-dependent events, covering Causal Diagrams, Event-Calculus Augmented Bayesian Network Models (EABNMs), Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs), and Semi-Markov Networks (SMNs). Causal diagrams and Event-calculus augmented Bayesian network models are our original contributions to the field. To facilitate the use of these frameworks, Causal Dynamics Toolkit (cdt) is a Python-based package that we have developed.

This research analyzes the possibility of oil seal failure caused by cavity resonance in a journal bearing due to the buildup of pressure inside a defined area. High-speed video footage of water vapor from an intentional cavity in a modified surface seal was captured at various rotation speeds of the inner ring. An acoustic sensor also recorded sound waves to correlate them with video observations. Inside the cavity's pressure was monitored using a real-time oil pressure transducer. The findings show that as rotation speed increases, the reduced pressure causes the seal to retract, closing the cavity. A sudden release of pressure results in an expanding cavity and may lead to seal failure. The observed findings were also supported by the sound data. A theoretical model of the cavity's dynamics was used to explain the observed behaviors.

Using string-field theory, we explore the relationship between the Witten gravity model and the spectrum of charged states, which is linked to the generalized witten effect and the charge gap. By analyzing the spectrum of charged states in string theory, we establish a direct correlation with the CEC of the massless scalar field and confirm that this charge gap corresponds to the production of charged states, thus verifying the consistency of the CEC in quantum gravity.

Mobile applications are frequently modified post-release, sometimes to introduce malicious changes. To address this issue, a framework called OctopOS for Android is presented, enabling app developers to securely modify their applications in response to detected threats. Additionally, the concept of a Trust Zone for the Android environment is incorporated into OctopOS, allowing for the secure modification of apps and user notification of the alteration process. Furthermore, the feasibility and practical applicability of OctopOS are verified through the demonstration of several case studies, showcasing its capability to protect applications from malicious activity while maintaining the intended functionality for end-users.

We examine the FPG algorithm applied to solving MDP problems with unknown dynamics under a finite horizon of $H$ and stochastic noise. This algorithm is capable of finding an $\epsilon$-optimal policy within $ \tilde{O}(\sqrt{dH^2/\epsilon^2})$ samples in an setting where up to $k$ episodes can be arbitrarily corrupted. This is despite being the first policy learning algorithm to achieve such performance when $k \geq H$. Additionally, this is also the very first gradient-based method to gain optimal scaling with respect to the dimensionality of the state and action when robustness is considered. Notably, our findings do not rely on any boundedness assumptions of the action dimensionality or the reward function.

A solution to the original paradox of the "Quantum Magic Square" is presented, which posits that observers' knowledge of measurement basis alignment influences the outcome's possibility. Considerations from Heisenberg's uncertainty principle and the element of choice are also posited to play a pivotal role in determining this outcome.

First hand experiments on cubanite revealed that the mineral remains intact when exposed to water vapor up to 523 K and exhibits a rare temperature-dependent magnetic transition from ferromagnetic to paramagnetic states. To investigate these temperature-dependent magnetic properties of cubanite, we performed full-relativistic linearized augmented plane wave (RLM) calculations and found them to be in line with experimental observations. Our analysis of the electronic band structure of cubanite provides an explanation for its resistance to degradation at high temperatures and its magnetic transition. Moreover, our results reveal the origin of the unusual ferromagnetic ordering in cubanite and demonstrate how the electronic configuration contributes to this magnetic behavior.

By combining a quantum dot and an acoustic cavity, a new approach emerges for creating qubits with long coherence times.  Rabi oscillations, which are crucial for quantum operations, can be accomplished using a single radio frequency laser that interacts with an electron spin via the acoustic wave.  Our theoretical analysis shows that as the quantum dot-acoustic cavity coupling strength increases, the rate of Rabi oscillations also rises, particularly when the quantum dot energy level aligns with the frequency of the driving laser.  However, a significant discrepancy arises when the quantum dot is off-resonance, with the error rate of Larmor precession increasing as the quantum dot laser frequency deviation grows.  To address this challenge, we propose using a radio frequency modulator to adjust the quantum dot laser driving frequency dynamically.  This method allows the system to operate in both quantum dot resonant and non-resonant conditions, leading to stable qubit state transformations.  Notably, by fine-tuning the quantum dot laser driving frequency, the influence of Rabi oscillations can be minimized even when there is a substantial difference in frequency between the quantum dot and the laser.  Our method has demonstrated the ability to achieve a Rabi oscillation error rate below 1% and a quantum dot non-resonance error rate under 0.1%.

A generalized Hamiltonian for the herringbone lattice was examined through numerical simulations to determine its ability to replicate the observed electronic band structure of CuIn$_2$S$_4$. By introducing different types of on-site energies and hopping integrals, various lattice configurations were analyzed. We demonstrated that any modification to the Hamiltonian's symmetry could be balanced by a corresponding change in the lattice's space group symmetry. Specifically, we were able to achieve a replica of the material's band structure by adjusting the Hamiltonian to match the tetragonal space group symmetry.

We discuss the characteristics of single-photon catalyzed coherent states, which can be produced at output ports of beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. In particular, we calculate the success probabilities for their generation and analyze how these probabilities differ in the case of using beam splitters and parametric amplifiers. We define single-photon catalyzed coherent states as a result of detecting two photons at both output ports with annihilation operators, but we also explore alternative definitions, such as with a combination of ordinary and creation operators, and calculate the corresponding success probabilities for these definitions. We also discuss the relationship between the definitions and provide expressions for the success probabilities in the weak coherent state limit. In all cases, we find that the success probabilities for generating the desired state can be significantly different depending on the production method, and in some cases, the probabilities can be equal up to a catalytic factor. We provide expressions for the success probabilities in terms of the mean photon numbers and discuss their behavior in the weak coherent state limit.
The provided summary translates the complex tensor coefficients of the Weyl tensor into simple, form-bearing expressions within the context of the Newman-Penrose formalism.

A new method has been developed for representing a polymer's configuration invariance through its constituent monomers. This approach, based on a set of rotation and translation operators, utilizes eigenvalues and eigenoperators of the polynomial to invariantly describe the polymer's geometry. Notably, this description results in a significantly more compact configuration space, as the number of parameters required to describe the polymer is reduced from O(N^d) to O(N), where N is the number of beads in the polymer and, d is the dimensionality of the space. This method offers a polymer configuration encoding that not only maintains rotational and translational invariance but also facilitates variational optimization, as it involves dividing the dimension of the polymer configuration space by a factor of N^(d-2).

A single ventilator can effectively breathe for multiple patients in a confined space, such as an ambulance or military vehicle, by using magnetic couplers to transmit air pressure. Traditionally this setup only worked if the patients had the same lung volume requirements. To overcome this limitation, a new dual-channel ventilation system has been developed that allows each patient to receive their own unique tidal volume from a single source. The innovative system utilizes a combination of mathematical equations and feedback mechanisms to simultaneously ventilate two patients with differing respiratory volume requirements. Computer simulations using a lung model demonstrated the efficacy of the new system in achieving accurate ventilation for both patients.

A widespread and fatal condition known as esophageal cancer often goes undetected due to the extensive use of Endoscopic Ultrasound necessitating manual operation. Fully automatic segmentation of esophageal tumors using deep learning has been hampered by a lack of adequately labeled data. To overcome this limitation, we investigated two approaches: training two smaller Unet networks to combine their outputs and selecting the most suitable dataset to train a single Dense Unet. For method 1, we explored three strategies including fixed output selection, unet2's output modification based on a region of interest determined by unet1, and a voting system for regions not covered by either network. For method 2, we experimented with two attention mechanisms to enhance unet2's focus on relevant areas. Evaluating these methods at the Medical Image Understanding and August 2021 challenges, we developed and presented our best results in the esophageal tumor segmentation and endoscopic polyp segmentation tracks. Unfortunately, due to confidentiality agreements, we cannot openly discuss our performance but were pleased to see our unet2+attention approach achieving strong results, particularly in the challenging track of segmenting esophageal tumors.

A new framework for real-time formation evaluation has been introduced, utilizing probabilistic machine learning techniques. This framework can be applied to real-time reservoir history matching and subsequent automatic evaluation of reservoir properties. To achieve this, a novel approach called Low-fidelity surrogates for Metal-Embedded Random trees (ME-RML) has been developed, replacing the previously used Low-fidelity surrogates for Maximum-A Posteriori estimations (MAP). This new approach not only yields a random tree that reflects the entire history of production data but also evaluates the uncertainty in a computationally efficient manner. A key advantage of the proposed framework is its ability to provide real-time history matching and property evaluation, providing an up-to-date result for each new flow rate measurement without the need for extensive re-computation. As a proof of concept, a single oil well with constant bottom-hole pressure was simulated, evaluating a range of parameters such as skin factor, well-block flow rate, and various pressures. Notably, a new method called LM-EnRML has been developed, enabling formation evaluation using Least Squares updates for Mean values, which provides an efficient alternative to traditional inference techniques. Results show that LM-EnRML and low-fidelity surrogates for posterior distributions can accurately estimate most parameters and provide realistic uncertainty assessments, often matching the results of rigorous re-simulation-based inference methods. Furthermore, LM-EnRML and low-fidelity surrogates for posterior distributions have demonstrated the ability to accurately estimate most parameters

Our research focuses on improving named entity recognition (NER) by utilizing external corpus-level information to identify entity types. By representing information from Wikipedia pages as inputs for NER systems, we achieved better results compared to standard methods. However, leveraging pre-trained BERT models for NER yielded disappointing results in our experiments. Surprisingly, our research indicates that NER is not a local task and benefits significantly from considering broader contextual information. Based on these findings, we propose a novel low-rank adaptation framework that adapts BERT representations at a low rank using extra information and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple NER datasets.

We have developed an analytical method to track the rationality of bitangents in a quartic curve as its tropicalization structure evolves. By leveraging linear models of bitangent lines, we are able to identify specific bitangents within each edge of the curve's tropicalization. We can then determine rational bitangents within interior edges and boundary rays by applying standard techniques from the study of real curves and broken lines respectively. A key innovation in our work is the development of a method to transform bitangents rational in boundary edges into bitangents rational in interior edges, even when transforming between edges with different twist orientations forces tangencies to collide and split along the bitangents' delta-notches.

In this research, a new algorithm is proposed for locating users inside a building using signal strength data, based on a model that accounts for signal propagation effects. The algorithm minimizes localization error by comparing measured data with simulated scenarios, identifying clusters with the closest match. These matches are used to create a 3D grid structure for accurate user positioning. Our proposed algorithm outperforms traditional methods by nearly 2 meters in accuracy, outdoing ideal simulation results by about 2.5 meters, and even achieving an 8.11-meter improvement over standard RFS models in some cases.

Natural language research has the potential to transform multiple industries in society such as education, legal services, and politics by improving multilingual accessibility and efficiency. This research should be conducted with an understanding of its societal impact and by considering a wide range of real-world languages, including those that are underrepresented in current studies. Building on these principles, we developed TioGuaruini, a new low-resource Brazilian Indigenous language for which we created open datasets and resources including corpora, treebanks, and grammatical analyses. These resources are now available for further research and are designed to support the preservation and revitalization of TioGuaruini, an endangered language with very few remaining speakers. We also established ethical guidelines for working with this community and language which should be followed during research and development processes.

A significant number of individuals world-wide are affected by visual impairments, necessitating the development of high-quality image descriptions that are reliable and accurate. Currently, many existing image description systems fail to meet these standards due to the lack of established metrics and guidelines for assessing their performance. This study introduces a comprehensive framework for evaluating image description systems consisting of three key elements: a set of universal best practices for assessing these systems, a dataset of human-written descriptions to benchmark their accuracy, and a specialized evaluation tool designed to assess both the factual correctness and style of image descriptions across a range of languages. FrameEval provides a structured approach for evaluating image description systems and can be applied to a variety of contexts, including different models, settings, and domains.

This study investigates local field and spin-orbit considerations in TaO materials energy loss, accounting for timing between timescales of photon interaction and electron motion. We incorporate these factors into a time-dependent TaO model and analyze the results, showing that neglecting local field and spin-orbit effects leads to inaccurate model predictions. Furthermore, our research reveals strong 5f electron contribution to energy loss at higher energies and that spin-orbit effects manifest as Ta oxide core screening asymmetry between 5f channels.

A crucial obstacle to understanding the online dissemination of misinformation lies in pinpointing its origins. This research explores various aspects of false information propagation, including its diverse nature, a observed pattern known as 'The Big Sort', and potential solutions such as graph anonymization. Observing the spread of misinformation in geographically isolated areas reveals that users tend to cluster into distinct segments based on preferred topics, a behavior that's amplified compared to overall user patterns, and that's difficult to mask through anonymization techniques.

A key objective in developing machine learning applications is to make them
accessible to a wider audience by making them function on low-resource devices
like smartphones and tablets. However, achieving this objective often clashes
with another critical aim in research: to train models on extensive datasets for
improved performance. This paper proposes two distinct strategies to overcome
this challenge by enabling a model to learn from a small dataset on a resource-
constrained device from a large, extensive dataset without a network connection.
These strategies have been tested on a variety of devices, including a smartphone,
a laptop, and a server, across different tasks such as image classification,
natural language processing, and audio processing. The experiments demonstrate
that both strategies yield satisfactory performance under all tested conditions.

Understanding how language is used in teaching is crucial, as it represents a significant form of social communication. However, everyday instructional interactions vary greatly, making it difficult to assess the semantic content of the speech involved. To address this challenge, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the semantic content of instructions given during a teaching task. We employed a multidimensional approach to examine the data, varying our assessments across different dimensions. By leveraging multiple annotation methods, we were able to map the distribution of demonstration types, instructions, speech acts, and error types. Notably, our study revealed a diverse range of semantic concepts being taught by our participants, spanning over 400 unique terms. We also found that certain types of errors were prevalent among the instructions, with a high percentage of concepts being represented by flawed speech. Additionally, we discovered that two distinct clusters of speech acts were involved, with one being highly frequent but containing a significant number of errors. From a variety of teaching strategies employed by the participants, we identified several effective methods that could be learned from. These findings have significant implications for the development of instructional agents and could inform future research in this area.

A key challenge in quantum field theory on spacetimes with symmetry is finding an ansatz that precisely matches the system's true evolution. For SU(N) matrix models, J. Balog, Z. Csáki, and E. Gorbar previously proposed a concept, based on Euler-Arnold equations, that would simplify the search. Through a rigorous examination, we demonstrate that this proposal can be viewed as an an approximation strategy, where the system's Lagrangian is expressed in terms of Euler angles, and only certain integrals of motion are employed. Consequently, the method transforms the high-dimensional, non-linear equation of motion into a minimized problem, based on the gradient being represented by a specific set of factors. This framework allows us to analyze the Balog-Csáki-Gorbar matrix model and a generalised version with potential, and in both cases, we find that an exact ansatz corresponds to a stationary configuration of the revised Euler-Arnold equation.

Conversational systems are increasingly being adopted in customer service, yet a significant issue persists in effectively testing them with automated testing frameworks. The current tests often fail to address the complexities of real-world conversations, impacting both accuracy and practical usage. The existing testing frameworks often lack adaptability and efficiency, struggles that we aim to resolve. We've developed a novel, efficient and user-friendly testing framework, a key component of which is a formalized specification for understanding the temporal dynamics of conversational systems. This efficient and scalable solution is designed to be used both individually and in collaboration with other test tools. We've demonstrated its capabilities by successfully testing the conversational skills of an existing system, showcasing its effectiveness, efficiency and scalability in a practical scenario.

Researchers are using wide-field surveys to locate small solar system objects before they approach closer to the Earth. Such programs take advantage of the gravity of these objects to deflect their paths, increasing the likelihood of a collision with the Earth. To effective such programs, it is crucial to understand the limitations of current search techniques which are constrained by how far they can search over a certain distance from the Earth. Using the existing star catalogs to estimate the effectiveness of current programs and to identify improvements that could be made to the catalogs to extend the reach of such programs. The results show that with the existing catalog, the gravitational pull of an unknown object similar to the Earth can only be felt over 60% of the sky within 1 Astronomical Unit, while with a next-generation catalog, such as the one proposed for the LSST, the gravitational effect can be felt over 90% of the sky within the same distance. Extensive simulations using the existing catalog and star fields to emulate the future catalog and to test the performance of such programs in both scenarios, demonstrating a potential ten-fold increase in sensitivity with the future catalog.

This work explores the potential of a cross-lingual memory retriever to access a wider range of sentence pairs for BMT tasks, beyond the limitations of a bilingual memory bank. By incorporating a cross-lingual retrieval mechanism, the model can generate contextually relevant source language contexts, enhancing its performance. This approach contrasts with a fixed-bilingual memory bank by a dynamic retrieval process that can leverage multiple source language queries. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, a simple cross-lingual memory bank was constructed using approximately 30 million sentence pairs from Wikipedia in 209 languages. When employing this large memory bank, the model's performance degrades due to increased noise. Thus, novel filter techniques were developed to generate high-quality context samples. These techniques include hard negative mining, a technique to eliminate sample duplicates and enhance relevance, and a technique to generate relevant contexts by combining unigrams and bigrams, as well as a technique to filter irrelevant contexts based on a second retriever. This approach resulted in enhanced performance across seven BMT pairs, outperforming a monolingual encoder by at least 1.5 points. Furthermore, the model's design allows for easy adaptation to existing monolingual memory banks, such as those used in parallel corpus-free BMT and domain-adapted BMT. This approach can be applied to a wide range of BMT tasks, such as parallel corpus-free BMT and domain-adapted BMT.

The Planck satellite's data has confirmed the existence of "Hawking points" - a variation of temperature across the sky that might be a remnant of the universe's early development. Using the parameter $f_2$ from the CMB temperature map, we calculated its power spectrum and found no supporting evidence for low-variance circles in the CMB after accounting for foregrounds. Our analysis revealed that while 8-degree-scale anomalies are present at 1$\sigma$ confidence level, smaller-scale anomalies match the random expectations based on the $\Lambda$CDM model. Notably, different processing methods for the data produced distinct results for the circle variance distribution and the auto-spectral power of the B-mode at large angular scales. Furthermore, our findings indicated that foreground contamination affects the Hawking points parameters within 5%. Contamination from the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect and the intrinsic the ALP inflaton model also were evaluated and found to differ significantly in their predictions, which could be tested with future CMB experiments like CMB-S4. Circle-based templates did not have better signal-to-noise ratios than the best-fit Halos in the CMB map. If the ALP model is correct, we expect to find circles with temperature differences of more than 6$\mu$K with 90% probability and this could be tested with the upcoming data from CMB-S4.
