The strength of Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions can be modified by adjusting the lattice structure, which is possible due to varying spin-orbit coupling strengths among different materials. This was achieved by creating a double perovskite compound that combines two types of transition metals with high and low spin-orbit coupling strengths. Specifically, researchers synthesized HoMnIr$_{0.5}$Pd$_{0.5}$ and discovered that reducing the Ir content in this compound resulted in a corresponding decrease in DM interactions. Furthermore, they observed that at sufficiently weak DM interactions, the spin and lattice can reorient, allowing for the stable coexistence of chiral and collinear phases. This coexistence was also found in HoMnIr$_{0.5}$Pd$_{0.5}$ and may offer a route to manipulate the boundary between these phases through the control of DM interactions.

This study explores the suitability of employing a simplified "effective" WIMP velocity distribution, detached from the broader halo WIMP velocities, in resolving apparent inconsistencies between dark matter findings. Utilizing the refined eight-point Lagrangian method, we obtained more precise incident WIMP velocities and identified significant discrepancies with the expected velocities reported in recent studies such as Finkberg, 2017, and WIMPsearch, 2017. Furthermore, we found that incorporating the incident halo WIMP velocities alone is insufficient to account for the observed transverse velocity dispersion of the Solacicentric solar system within the Local Standard of Rest, in contrast to some previous conclusions. Consequently, we propose that employing semi-isotropic N-body simulations to generate realistic WIMP velocity distribution functions (VPFs) should be a priority, as demonstrated with the Heilman-Wilson-Vogel (HVV) function of choice.

Public sector professionals rely heavily on Internet searches to perform their duties, making it essential to obtain accurate and unbiased search results. Unfortunately, inherent flaws in these results can lead to flawed conclusions and inefficient work. Although existing methods for detecting bias in search results have shown effectiveness, they fail to consider the background and expertise required of public sector professionals. To bridge this gap, we developed a novel approach that leverages expert knowledge to identify and learn from subjective preferences in search engine rankings. This approach employs support vector devices and reinforcement learning to model expert opinions. When applied to real-world data, our model outperformed traditional methods and provided a significant improvement of 13.5% in reducing bias in search results for a typical user query. Additionally, our approach can easily be adapted to enhance search results for other professional groups.

Consider the potential of a TeV-scale muon collider for research into CDM, for example through $MM$ and $MM$ annihilation at high energy, and $\gamma\gamma}$ collisions at moderate energy. It could also investigate $\gamma M$ fusion at high energy for CDM research and standard model studies, and particle production at moderate energy through $pp$ collisions. Complementary research could be offered by displaying cosmic muons and neutrinos and accelerating neutrino and antineutrino beams for standard model and beyond research. With all these capabilities, a TeV-scale muon collider could effectively explore a broad spectrum of beyond standard model and dark matter-related possibilities, including those beyond the reach of the LHC.

A new approach called rCASPR has been developed to enhance low-contrast imaging by building on the principles of CASPR. Unlike its predecessor, rCASPR utilizes randomly oriented beam shears and offers improved point spread functions through modulation of the sampling pattern. This technique is designed to be robust against various distortions, including varying indices, parabolic distortions, and even when the number of sampled beams exceeds the number of spatial dimensions. Additionally, a convolution-based method has been created for real-time image reconstruction without the need for inverse fast Fourier transforms. When tested with experimental data, rCASPR demonstrated better performance than both CASPR and linear sampling, showing greater contrast and less distortion in images. A physical real-time reconstruction method has also been developed that enhances the speed of image processing.

This paper introduces a novel concept known as Higher-Order Control Contractive Barrier Functions (ICCBFs) building on existing ICCBFs.  The ICCBF criteria are adaptable to both linear and nonlinear systems, making them highly versatile.  We demonstrate that ICCBFs can be considered a adaptable version of Higher Order Control Barrier Functions (CO-CBFs), which is suitable for both linear and nonlinear systems.  Moreover, under specific conditions, our model reduces to both CO-CBFs and ICCBFs for systems with fixed relative degrees.  To address the issue of determining relative degree in nonlinear systems, additional concepts such as weakly coherent subspaces and strong normal forms are developed.  Finally, safe controllers based on the ICCBF criterion can be designed for linear systems.

CF-closed sets are defined in CF-approximation spaces built from continuous domains, which serve as a CF-closed counterpart to open sets in traditional topological spaces.  Researchers have established key characteristics of CF-closed sets and determined their precise behavior within continuous domain spaces.  Additionally, the notion of CF-normals has been introduced into continuous domain spaces, and it's found that CF-normal spaces correspond to partially ordered sets whose down-sets form a continuous domain.  Another contribution is the introduction of CF-clast and CF-dense sets, which are crucial in determining the CF-separation properties of spaces.  Lastly, authors explore the relationship between CF-closed sets and CF-contiguous sets to identify conditions under which the union of two CF-closed sets forms a CF-closed set.

We've developed an innovative exact algorithm for computing paired-permutation p-values, contrasting relationships between paired data values. This method is highly effective for moderate and small sample sizes, significantly surpassing the performance of Monte Carlo methods in these scenarios. Notably, even for large samples, our algorithm excels over the conventional normal approximation. Furthermore, we have adapted our algorithm to compute paired-t p-values exactly, and this extension along with empirical comparisons of our method for both paired-permutation and paired-t tests is provided.

A significant shift occurred in 1983 with the breakdown of shipping cartels, resulting in a sudden change in the relationship between prices and quantities in the global market. To study the long-term effects of this event, we utilized a comprehensive annual dataset of real freight rates and ship quantities from 1972 to 2014, which was compiled from various sources including world price indexes, the World Bank, and our own calculations. Empirical analyses, including difference-in-averages and regression discontinuity methods, confirmed our initial findings. The breakdown of shipping cartels not only lowered world freight rates by approximately 15 percent but also had a lasting effect on rates for about 10 years. Notably, this change had a more profound impact on rates than on the quantities shipped, which also exhibited a difference of about 10 percent and influenced rates for a much longer duration than expected, likely due to increased entry into the industry and a resulting decline in world supply.

We show that every loom space can be divided into a geometric structure known as an $N$-cube complex. If a loom space has a specific property called aspherical characteristics, it can be broken down further into a specific type of complex structure called a 3-dimensional binary link complex.

Deep learning models for node classification in graph-structured data rely heavily on a graph neural network (GNN). While effective, the classification accuracy of GNNs can be hindered by noisy labels commonly found in real-world labeled datasets. To address this issue, we present a novel pseudo-labeling method, designed with graph structure in mind, to generate high-quality labels for noisy data. Our method, Pseudo-Labeling with Graph Structure (PLGS), focuses on leveraging the inherent graph structure, as node features often exceed quality expectations. By creating reliable pseudo-labels through an iterative process, PLGS produces robust labels that can be used to train more accurate GNN models. Our extensive experiments across both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of PLGS over current state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the algorithm's hyperparameters and offer guidance on its practical applications.

Style of surgery arguments have a significant impact on research into geometries linked to singular compact area minimizers. This work offers general criteria for conducting C^2 surgery on a broad range of geometries, aiming to provide a more comprehensive framework. The proposed approach is then applied to specific cases, including the 2nd Varifold Ricci Flow in high dimensions and the Endharmonics Flow in dimensions 3 and above.

A novel type of excitation, consisting of a counterflow of counterwinding vortices within a narrow core region, is predicted to exist in counterflowing type-II superconductors with a thick lamellar lambda phase. This excitation, described as a thick flux line or superflux, is also expected to have a higher entropy than a moving flux line due to the presence of opposite vortices in its center. Our numerical modeling of the time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau equations confirms the predicted properties of the superflux's structure and dynamics, including its entropy and resistance to motion. Additionally, we identify regions of enhanced and reduced voltage across the superflux's core, which may be observable using scanning SQUID microscopy. The superflux's resistance to motion is also found to cause a unique voltage profile at the trailing edge of the superflux. Its existence could have significant implications for understanding the motion of magnetic flux lines in superconducting devices, particularly in Josephson junction racetrack memory devices.

This paper explores a novel approach for efficient communication between an energy aggregator and the numerous system users it represents, as well as between the aggregator and the energy market. We focus on a scenario where the aggregator makes decisions in a distributed system without direct knowledge of the individual users' needs or their immediate responses to its requests. Instead, it relies on a maximum entropy feedback (MEF) system that utilizes historical average data (arm means) for this purpose. We establish a theoretical framework using distributed bandit models to analyze this situation and prove that a specific algorithm can achieve a desired level of performance regret. We also examine an energy market application, where we demonstrate how MEF enables the aggregator to effectively coordinate with the users and optimize its operations, taking into account their individual energy consumption patterns and preferences. Numerical simulations support our findings and validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

This paper presents a novel deep learning approach that integrates machine learning indicators into a convolutional neural network for stock movement prediction.

We refine a concept known as a random price game and employ this framework to anticipate stock movements.

Our proposed method leverages technical analysis data, including indicators and historical prices within our refined model, which demonstrates superior performance compared to alternative forecasting approaches.

Our results indicate that our proposed method can effectively predict the S&P 500 index and other stocks with minimal prediction errors.

Furthermore, our model achieves a high accuracy rate of 63.36% in predicting stock trends, which is significantly better than the 50% accuracy expected in a random price game.

Our findings are supported by real-world experiments conducted on historical stock data spanning over two decades.

Type Ia supernovae can originate from white dwarf mergers, which can create heavy elements like manganese through the r-process. However, model predictions of MW production for Type Ia events significantly exceed observations of the solar system. To investigate this discrepancy, we examined the impact of MW from Type Ia supernovae with varying delay time distributions and from the MW-rich double-degenerate channel. Our research indicates that even with White Dwarfs made entirely of oxygen-neon-magnesium, only a 10% O Ia event rate is necessary to account for the observed MW contribution to the solar system, which is well within current estimates of the O Ia event rate in the Milky Way. Furthermore, our results suggest minimal additional O Ia event rate requirements for other heavy elements such as hafnium, ruthenium, and barium, essentially meeting their observed solar system abundances with the baseline O Ia event rate, while some elements like barium can also be satisfied by double white dwarf mergers with limited contribution of Type Ia supernovae. Including MW from the O Ia double-degenerate channel also enables better independent event rate constraints with "intrinsic" elements like barium, reducing previous upper limits on the O Ia event rate.

To address the limited sensitivity of Higgs signal strengths to Beyond-Standard Model (BSM) phenomena, it's essential to explore BSM interactions in other processes. Double Higgs boson production offers an alternative approach, focusing on effective couplings of the Higgs boson in the Standard Model Extension (HEffective). We analyze this production using both Monte Carlo simulations and an analytical Effective Field Theory (EFT) approach, comparing our results with more elaborate calculations. Our study demonstrates that for HEffective, the relationship between the Lorentz structure of the coefficient $c_i$ in the 0-helicity amplitude and $c_i'$ in the SM Extension, the square of the coefficient $c_i'$ in the positive helicity amplitude is not preserved. Consequently, in Higgs data analysis, constraints on HEffective coefficients cannot be directly translated from their CSMET counterparts. Additionally, we evaluate the impact of our analytical findings on the feasibility of distinguishing between HEffective and SMSMEI theories using experimental data, and our comparison with Monte Carlo simulations validates the reliability of these theoretical predictions.

We introduce a novel parametrization termed "pre-non-relativistic" that serves as an alternative to the traditional pre-post-Newtonian gauge in general relativity. This new choice of gauge allows for the seamless extension to higher orders of non-relativistic expansion within analytical approximations. By doing so, it facilitates the straightforward derivation of a pre-non-relativistic $O(c^{-8})$ metric, which in turn can be further expanded into its $c^{-8}$ post-Newtonian and $c^{-8}$ post-post-Newtonian components. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we illustrate how this parametrization enables the simultaneous preservation of weak-field and strong-field regimes in the analytical expansion. Our formulation is complemented by comparable graphs that illustrate its relationship to other standard parametrizations, and the detailed $O(c^{-8})$ metric is provided in the appendix for reference.

We revisit the deconstruction method for Cvetic-Heckman-Louise (CHL) anti-de Sitter spacetimes to illustrate the efficacy of avoiding full solution retrieval when computing specific bulk properties. By decoupling the Einstein equations and solving only the necessary variables, we demonstrate how computing the complexification of the Chern-Simner term and the variational boundary energy does not require the complete spacetime metric. For a class of CHL spacetimes parameterized by $n$, we show that the computed properties depend linearly on $n$, a result confirmed by a example involving CHL AdS black holes. Our approach is further generalized to other spacetimes, such as Chern-Simons-Maxwell-AdS and CHL dS, and dynamic spacetimes.

We investigated how a rapidly driven cylindrical intruder, rotated at a constant rate, affects the drag it experiences as it moves through loose granular material. We measured the drag forces acting perpendicular and parallel to the intruder's axis of rotation in both shallow and deep beds of sand. Our observations revealed an unusual speed dependence of the drag in shallower areas, which could be attributed to changes in the intruder's effective driving rate as the driving force was balanced by changes in the angular velocity. We also discovered that the drag in deeper areas of the bed exhibits a different speed dependence, which we believe results from changes in the intruder's motion and a decrease in the overall drag it experiences due to the balance of forces. Our study provides valuable insights into the complex relationship between the intruder's motion and the drag it experiences as it moves through granular material.

This study leverages the low-resolution IFU data of the IFU42 survey to examine a distance of 18 Mpc, aiming to examine the relationship between ionised gas deformations and neutral gas distributions in starburst disk galaxies. We combined data on neutral gas kinematics and ionised gas properties with a sample of 18 interacting and deforming gas galaxies. Our analysis showed that these galaxies have significant ionised gas deformations and significant gas outflows. We found that a significant mass loss occurs due to these outflows - about 25 percent of the gas consumed over a Hubble time, indicating that ionised gas deformations can reveal massive gas outflows in starburst disk galaxies. We also found evidence of correlated gas consumption and neutral gas consumption in these systems. Furthermore, we found no correlation between gas deformations and neutral gas consumption, suggesting that observing ionised gas spectra can assist in understanding the full gas consumption in feeding supermassive black holes during the consumption of neutral gas.

Finding optimal configurations for complex systems involves navigating expansive search spaces, typically using localized evaluation methods. Auto-Configuration and similar algorithms improve efficiency by leveraging an iterative, hierarchical approach. Recent advances in neural architecture search using Auto-NC have introduced innovative search methods, resulting in significant improvements over traditional techniques and notable successes on standard benchmarks. However, these methods rely on assuming a hierarchical search space, which isn't always applicable and can introduce complications due to negative transfer. To address these issues, **BoAnon** introduces a novel, neuro-evolutionary algorithm that combines global exploration with localized assessment. By building and refining diverse populations of search agents, BoAnon achieves state-of-the-art efficiency compared to Auto-NC and other state-of-the-art methods. It also demonstrates robust performance on a broader range of benchmarks. Source code for BoAnon is openly available at https://github.com/boai-lab/BoAnon.

Our analysis of 20% most central Au+Au collisions at 20 GeV reveals that the 3D Lattice Equation of State (EOS) derived from combining measured $v_3$ and $v_2$ from various particle types aligns perfectly with the initial findings based on $v_2$ and $v_3$ from protons alone. This outcome supports the reliability of CEC's application of systematics to flow coefficients across different particle types. Notably, the dependence on transverse momentum ($p_T$) for $v_3$ from various particle types follows the same pattern as $v_2}$, a crucial prediction of hydrodynamics that validates the use of chemical freeze-off to determine particle yields in central collisions. Furthermore, incorporating multi-particle flow into 0+90% most central collisions demonstrates a partial decoupling between $v_2$ and $v_3$ at low $p_T$, offering fresh insights into the relative coalescence of particle types at low transverse momenta.

Our research team at University of Warsaw has developed a novel quality assessment system for extensive RDF datasets called DistQualityAssessment. This system is based on sampling and utilizes kernel density estimation to estimate data quality metrics. To address performance issues, we have created an enhanced implementation of KDE using multiple kernels in parallel, specifically tailored for calculating distinct counts. The new approach includes new quality estimation formulas, a new kind of data duplication, and a set of related experiments.

We develop uniform convergence theory for independent increment processes and applications to parametric models, also covering Gaussian processes and spectrally positive processes. Our findings extend to processes with independent increments, ensuring consistent behavior, while noting that results for certain processes require reworking due to lack of pathwise bounds, as seen with fractional Brownian motion. Our framework provides a foundation for statistical inference using maximum likelihood estimates, specifically showing that certain score functions yield consistent and asymptotically normal estimators, while others do not, while also providing broader implications.

A widely spread theory proposes that shock waves generated by accretion onto the black hole in the galaxy's center ionize gas and initiate star formation through a feedback mechanism. However, our analysis of shock-ionization properties does not support this view. Instead, we propose that visco-resistive magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) processes, which incorporate the interaction between ionized and neutral gas components, are necessary to effectively convey ionized energy to the surrounding neutral gas. As for the alternative model, we argue that star formation should be triggered by thermal compression within the dense, cold, neutral gas located at the center of an H-I region, rather than by the ionized and warm gas at the region's periphery. These non-stellar components can significantly alter a galaxy's properties, creating broad spectral lines that mimic those from broad-line region gas and creating additional, ionized regions around the galaxy's center. This has notable implications for identifying and studying a galaxy's central black hole.

IoT applications are increasingly common, but they often suffer from security issues due to bugs, so it's essential to prioritize their reliability and safety through rigorous testing. Existing automated testing methods can aid in identifying vulnerabilities, but they struggle with the complexity and diversity of IoT applications, especially when testing multi-device applications. To address this challenge, we developed Frisbee, a comprehensive framework for creating and testing IoT test suites that span across multiple devices. Frisbee consists of three key components: an IoT learning module that analyzes protocols and applications to build a graphical state machine; an distributed genetic algorithm that generates a testing plan by learning from this state machine; and an IoT analysis module that uses patterns from crashes and logs to identify potential security vulnerabilities. By demonstrating Frisbee's capabilities with three cases, we showed that it can efficiently test IoT applications across multiple devices and uncover previously unknown security vulnerabilities, some of which have been verified and rewarded with bug bounties.

Recent discoveries of rare $B$ meson decays, such as the mode $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$, have revealed a rare decay process with notably low branching ratio and S-wave structure. This has given new insight into scalar and pseudoscalar contributions from the $b \to s \ell^+\ell^-$ transition, which in turn have constrained the corresponding form factors. Building on this foundation, this work examines the absolute decay rate and structure of the $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decay process, and makes a first theoretical estimate of the absolute decay rate and a $\mu^+\mu^-$ pair invariant mass distribution for the $B^0$ meson decay.

A neural network can create realistic driving scenes from raw image data, but this process is limited by what it can learn from available examples. To overcome this challenge, we developed a flexible generative model called SceneGen. It combines a latent variable image-to-image translator with a custom database of 3D object information. This enhanced model learned from the 2D images and 3D object data it generated, by maximizing its likelihood, using the UNET network. SceneGen was built using over 5000 hours of vehicle trajectory data and environment information from the Tuansha dataset. It was designed to efficiently generate scenes with specific characteristics by allowing easy control of the driving conditions, by a small encoder network called TrajCond. It was evaluated by several metrics, by a series of tests. It passed all of them, by a series of tests. It produced accurate predictions of object locations and sizes, by a series of tests.
