This study explores how LATE (Learning And Teaching Effect) varies across different student groups during a remote learning study. By analyzing online learning platform data, it reveals significant disparities in learning habits and performance between under-represented minority students and non-under-represented groups. Specifically, non-under-represented students showed higher software module engagement, participated in more webinars, and spent more time on the learning platform. Additionally, there were differences in module engagement between pre-pandemic and pandemic periods for non-under-represented students, whereas no such differences were observed for under-represented minority students. To explore the causes of these discrepancies, the learning platform was modified to offer a more personalized and engaging experience. It also shows that reducing disparities in performance is feasible by providing a more tailored platform experience, resulting in increased engagement and a 0.35-day decrease in the LATE.

Research on spin-three Ward identities in two-dimensional Toda conformal field theories (TCFT) is conducted using large-$c$ limits in the path integral formulation. We demonstrate that these Ward identities correspond to the higher-spin symmetry by showing the time independence of certain three-point correlation functions of current operators. Furthermore, we derive finite-$c$ sum rules based on this symmetry, which can be applied to analyze the alpha primas ($\alpha'$) of BPS states in TCFT.

Recent research has established that the class of uniform lattice groups within a specific family of geometric objects, such as negatively curved spaces, Cayley graphs of certain transformation groups and solvable varieties, share the property of being biautomatic. This paper expands this study by generalizing to a more complex form, higher curvature graphs, demonstrating that these objects also exhibit the biautomatic property.

This study investigates near-extremal and extremal black holes at the threshold of chaos in scattering with a scalar field. For both types of black holes we observe divergent final states; however their natures differ significantly. Notably, the scattering process can result in non-singular final states for extremal black holes. For instance, when a near-extremal Reissner-Nordstr\"om black hole is scattered with a charged scalar field and satisfies $q_\phi\leq1$, we obtain a well-behaved final state. Furthermore, we find that more complicated final states can be achieved by tuning the scattering parameters of near-extremal black holes, including those that were previously unattainable with standard scattering methods. These findings suggest that near-extremal and extremal black holes behave in a fundamentally distinct way compared to their non-extremal counterparts at the point of chaos.

In his 1984 work, Robert Vaught introduced the concept of anti-classicality into model theory. Here, we redefine the axiom of anti-classicality to state that the presence of at least one non-classical set is guaranteed, based on a clear distinction between types of sets. This revised definition allows us to demonstrate that first-order logic combined with the new axiom is equivalent to the logical system of first-order logic plus the ultrafilter lemma in terms of provability. Furthermore, we show that this concept does not contradict classical set theories like ZFC or systems based on natural numbers.

Using high-resolution ECoG data to train an advanced deep learning model enables a remarkable 25% improvement in accuracy compared to traditional EEG methods when predicting a person's ability to walk on their toes or heels.

Computing entropy measures of complex distributions is a common challenge as their exact calculation often requires evaluating their marginal probabilities which are not directly available. This problem has been further exacerbated with the emergence of diffusion models that define their own complex likelihood functions based on intractable integrals. In this paper, we introduce a novel entropy estimation method using the Fisher trick that bypasses the need for explicit probability evaluations. This new approach builds on our previously developed entropy-estimator-fir and demonstrates comparable performance to other leading methods using only a single training run. This result signifies that diffusion models can be trained with significantly reduced training runs while still achieving robust and reliable entropy estimates. With this method, we were able to obtain improved training runs for diffusion models with comparable training runs to those using other leading methods. This result demonstrates that diffusion models can be trained with significantly reduced training runs while still producing reliable entropy estimates even when applied to private data. This approach is simple to implement and provides a robust and efficient solution to computing entropy measures of complex distributions that were not directly evaluatable.

Given a right-angled Artin group acting on a tree, we consider the underlying graph $\Gamma$ and a subgraph \ $\Gamma_0$ of it. If this subgraph is capable of dividing the entire right-angled Artin group into two distinct parts, we can characterize its specific subgroups that arise from this division.

Dynamic graph classification is a critical classification task that involves graph structures that undergo changes. Existing solutions are primarily based on extracting fixed features from a sequence of graph sequences. Building on this, we introduce DECENNT, a novel approach that combines continuous graph attention networks and ensemble learning for sequential graph representation. Unlike traditional methods using mean pooling that use fluc-tuating features, DECENNT uses RNN to capture the sequential dependencies in graph data. We employ ensemble learning to enhance its performance. Our method offers multiple innovative contributions: introducing continuous GATs to capture dynamic graph representations, exploring the effectiveness of graph representation learning techniques, and exploring the potential of ensemble learning. We validate DECENNT's efficiency and accuracy on three benchmark datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Steinchachs mean field operator has produced great results in various fields such as evolutionary analysis, phylogeny reconstruction, and chemical reaction modeling due to its ability to provide accurate approximations of complex stochastic processes and simple exact expressions. Despite these benefits, applying this method to stochastic processes that occur in time has been limited by the lack of stochastic models that accurately reflect the intricate relationships between the configurations of their corresponding transition probabilities. Our model overcomes this challenge by introducing an infinite number of taxa represented as points on the real line and studying their evolutionary histories through the migration and branching of segments between non-negative integers and infinity. Our findings reveal that the system adheres to the principles of a non-homogeneous Brownian motion with dynamic variance and linear drift, resulting in a transition probability distribution that follows the Rayleigh type and allows for a more comprehensive analysis of tree-building methods such as maximum likelihood.

A new category of smart devices called LifeCam has been proposed which
distinguish themselves from inanimate objects through a unique movement pattern.
These cams' locations form a specific pattern that resembles a Koole-Vermes
process when viewed over time. We have developed a statistical testing method
to effectively differentiate the movement pattern of LoCa (locations of cams)
from NaLoc (locations of inanimate objects). Our approach uses a hidden Markov
model-based distance measure and determines significance levels through p-values.

Building upon a previous study, we extend the Nested Neumann algorithm for risk-averse robust control by incorporating inception depth at both outer and inner levels. The resulting algorithm forms a combination of nested fixed point and power iteration cycles. The depth variables for this algorithm are denoted as $D_1$ (outer) and $D_2$ (inner). The nested fixed point algorithm's convergence rate is determined by the product of $\rho_1 = 1/D_1(D_1+1)$ and $\rho_2 = 1/D_2(D_2+1)$. Specifically, increasing inception depth at either level reduces $\rho_1\cdot \rho_2$, which in turn accelerates the convergence rate of the algorithm. To handle higher dimensional problems, we also integrate Monte Carlo estimation into the algorithm. Theoretical convergence rates for this Monte Carlo variant are also established.

Building on previous research into the eigenchannels of symmetric waveplates and periodic multilayers, a comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to analyze this concept for any symmetric optical resonator. Due to the symmetry present in such structures, the eigenchannels can be categorized into two types: symmetric and antisymmetric types. This category not only applies to the phase relationship between channel pairs but also defines distinct intensity patterns. It has been demonstrated that the category of an eigenchannel remains consistent with its constituent phase components, and thus can be predicted based on the properties of the scattering matrix. This framework has been validated through theoretical calculations and experimental analysis of light trapped in a ring resonator divided into two parts, which exhibits varying degrees of symmetry.

Anderson insulators exhibit a rich set of topological properties that can be difficult to measure. A practical approach to identifying these characteristics involves observing the topological currents carried by excited states and detecting the Anderson topological marker in X-ray absorption spectra. To test this concept, we used an experimentally achievable quantum system of rubidium atoms in a lattice to demonstrate the detection of the topological marker in an X-ray analog spectrum via an intra-electronic transition. Our simulation results show distinct differences between the indicator's appearance in two distinct decay patterns of a specific excited state, thereby verifying the feasibility of utilizing Anderson insulators for studying complex dynamics in many-body systems.

Computing invariants for curves at a specific point can be done using various geometric methods, despite their differences. This observation being supported by various invariants' behavior suggests a conclusion. To test this, we propose a set of invariants for genus-one curves that share this trait. Additionally, we examine the j-linearized biextensions of such curves, defining key properties including a cyclic pattern and a specific pattern related to the curve's torsion points. We also discuss alternative approaches to deriving these invariants, such as using the Eichler-Shimura class or specific cycle maps. Finally, we establish a connection between these invariants and a cycle on a modular variety, which becomes rational after a certain transformation.

Our research quantifies the impact of complex phases on the impact of squark loops in the production of the three CP odd Higgs bosons, specifically in $gg \to \eta_a$, $gg \to \eta_b$, and $gg \to \eta_c$ processes. We employ the effective field theory approach, taking into consideration the phase-dependent contributions from both linear and loop terms of the relevant BSM particles. Our findings demonstrate that the size of the complex phase significantly influences the squark effects, particularly when loop and linear terms have opposite interference patterns and are sensitive to the mass difference between the Higgs penguins. Research also indicates that the interference between the loop and linear terms will have a more substantial influence on the process as the BSM particle mass decreases. We further conduct a detailed analysis of the process $gg \to \eta_d \to b\bar b \gamma$, involving four separate contributions to the Higgs decay amplitude in the differential photon energy distribution. This distribution can distinguish between four components with distinct signatures, allowing for potential differentiation of the Higgs boson's nature.

Network time series models that incorporate parameters with non-negative constraints are developed for scenarios where networks represent connections or flows between entities. We establish the consistency and local asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator for these models. To address the question of testing overidentifying restrictions in parameters' inverse boundaries, we develop a consistent alternative to the Wald test and compare it with an interior test. Since these tests may lack the same asymptotic power as in models that do not have boundary issues, we modify them to ensure the same performance in such cases. Additionally, we provide a non-asymptotic bound to aid in making rejection decisions close to the boundary of the parameter space. Through simulations and real-world data analysis, we show that our proposed network autoregressive model can effectively capture complex dependencies and that our test is efficient and operational for moderate-sized datasets. Furthermore, our test demonstrates an improvement in power over its interior counterpart.

When solving optimization problems, evaluating a differentiable function $f$ is often necessary, which can be done using the chain rule, however, this approach can be computationally expensive. Given that most problems have a specific structure, we propose that problem structure can be exploited to significantly speed up computations during the backward pass. We demonstrate this concept by applying it to optimal control problems, presenting an efficient algorithm for computing gradients of $f$ that utilizes control vectorization and results in comparable or superior performance to traditional methods. Moreover, our method enables implicit numerical integration schemes, such as the trapezoidal rule, to compute gradients of $f$ with high accuracy and significantly reduced runtime and memory requirements.

Single stress fibers behave mechanically like composite materials with unique properties of extensibility and elasticity. A simplified model captures this complexity by integrating two viscous components and elastic elements. However, removing the contractile component of the model causes stress fiber rupture, underscoring their functional importance. Although contractility can vary, it typically remains constant and is crucial for maintaining the integrity of stress fibers. This finding highlights single stress fibers as a distinct mechanical system that requires further study.

The blockchain technology underpinning Bitcoin has significant advantages yet also faces challenges due to its vulnerability to abuse. Although the decentralized nature of the network is a major advantage, it also makes security challenges more complex. To address this issue, we propose leveraging the visible and recurring patterns of temporal transaction graphs. By examining and modeling the recurring behavior of transactions over time, we aim to uncover hidden and intricate patterns that are not apparent through privacy-preserving measures. A key contribution of this study is a novel approach called CyclicTemporalTransactionGraphAnalysis which exploits recurring behavior to surface hidden patterns. This approach is notable for not requiring access to unobtrusive data. Our experiments on real-world transaction graphs reveal that our method can effectively identify newly emerged and intricate suspicious patterns, such as those employed by the MyDarkMarket. Specifically, we demonstrate the ability to automatically generate rules that accurately classify a high percentage of marked transactions in real-world malware datasets. Moreover, our analysis highlights the discovery of previously unreported suspicious patterns. Additionally, we present a cyclic transaction graph behavior model capable of efficiently representing and predicting complex transaction patterns with high precision. This model is also computationally efficient in terms of both storage and processing time.

Quantum fault tolerance relies on the ability to decode stabilized measurements effectively, enabling the correction of errors caused by noisy quantum gate operations. We propose a novel approach using machine learning, specifically reinforcement learning, to develop optimal decoders for small-scale quantum codes. Our method aims to create immediate corrective quantum gate sequences and demonstrates their benefit on the repetition code and the $R(9,7)$ code under various types of noisy channels. For potentially large quantum codes, our approach can be enhanced by integrating a tailored likelihood function, enabling efficient learning of maximum likelihood decoders. We demonstrate its efficiency on the $R(9,7)$ code and various quasi-cyclic LDPC codes, including those used in recent experiments.

Precise measurements of short duration can be advanced through monitoring the behavior of quantum systems near a transition point between two quasi-stable states. When a quantum system is observed through photon emissions, both states can be directly detected. We suggest utilizing a specific type of quantum system - a quantum Rabi model with an extra frequency - where a quantum jump can produce multiple photons at varying frequencies. By optimizing a specific quantum circuit, our approach offers two key improvements over traditional strategies. Firstly, it allows for simultaneous estimation of multiple parameters through efficient data collection. Secondly, it achieves high precision near a 1:2 resonance ratio without the need to model jump probabilities accurately. As a demonstration, we show that a quantum computing platform could realize this approach using existing parameters. Moreover, this scheme has potential applications in advancing quantum metrology for systems that emit chains of states.

Using PHENIX data from $200$ $GeV$ Au+Au collisions, we measured the $p_T$ spectra and nuclear modification factors of hadrons and observed baryon-meson duality for hadrons. Nonperturbative quark distributions inside the proton were used to calculate predictions for hadron spectra and nuclear modification factors in Au+Au collisions by the pQCD approach, considering a parton energy loss mechanism. Our pQCD predictions with parton energy loss are in excellent agreement with measured data for all hadrons. Analysis shows a $20\% - $ $30\%$ increase in the nuclear modification factor for hadrons originating from quarks with a decreasing $x$ in the range $x \lesssim 0.05$, leading to up to a $30\%$ enhancement in the nuclear modification factor for $\pi^+/$$p^+$ as the momentum fraction of the quark decreases. This observed increase could be attributed to the rising flux of partons at lower $x$ values in nuclear protons.

This study builds upon the ideas presented in A. R. Shashank's paper from 2021 concerning $f_n$ from number theory journal. Building upon this foundation, the author expands on upper bounds provided in the original paper, offering more refined estimates. Additionally, specific numerical upper bounds are derived for various values of $m$ from the number theory journal.

The global scale of high-performance computing (HPC) systems is accompanied by significant delays and data transfers, making real-time interactions and large data transfers uncomfortable and cumbersome. Cloud providers are compelled to allocate separate computer instances for each client to prevent data transfer latency, but this approach is both inefficient and costly. A new approach that sees a single large machine shared among multiple clients via network protocol translation could reduce latency, improve resource allocation efficiency, and provide a foundation for a novel cloud computing experience. This approach, which prioritizes the efficiency of the underlying infrastructure while providing seamless network access, could provide a framework for a user-friendly interface that accounts for network latency and reallocation efficiency, thus enabling a more effective and intuitive experience for both users and applications.

In this work, we analyze the standard setting of contextual linear bandits with an inner dimension of one, focusing on a probability distribution that represents knowledge about a underlying relationship. We first derive a general formula for the expected utility after one sample, based on an assumed form of utility after each new data point. This derived context distribution knowledge is then used to evaluate specific algorithms in a way that is specific to each algorithm. These algorithm-determined context updates result in a sampling strategy that is adaptable to various context distribution management techniques. Due to this flexibility, we can provide performance guarantees for the online and offline settings of contextual linear bandits that are also applicable to recently proposed solutions, offering a more efficient use of bits in our methods than current results and a total regret that is not as high as previous outcomes of a context-truncating algorithm. Additionally, we derive a specific context distribution that yields a non-stochastic setting with a total regret that matches the optimal performance guarantee previously established. This context distribution can be computed efficiently in a polynomial time.

The adoption of Scrum methodologies by startups has been growing, yet there are few studies combining research on remote projects, startup development, and Scrum applications. This gap is filled by a survey of 144 participants, where we investigate the benefits and drawbacks of working remotely on project performance using Mediation Analysis. The findings indicate that remote work enhances the effectiveness of Scrum adoption, but does not directly improve project performance. Additionally, we investigate whether collaborating in a shared physical space can produce similar outcomes to remote work, based on data from 170 students developing a product in a co-working area.

This paper explores efficient function value estimates for policy learning using a small subset of testing samples, which provides a novel perspective on the traditional view that requires large testing datasets. Our neural network-based method, based on conditional expectation, supplies a conditional probability distribution for reward and state transitions given action and state. This conditionally based approach yields a efficient function value estimate that is bounded by small sampling noise. The performance of our method is compared to traditional test-based methods through synthetic tasks, revealing that small testing samples can produce efficient function value estimates. These results offer a new perspective that from a noise-reduction perspective, small testing samples can enhance function value estimation, Bounding the error of our method suggests that our findings can offer a new viewpoint that from noise reduction perspective small testing samples can improve value function estimates.

Our study offers a novel approach to linking the quantum potential and elliptic flow through a hadron RMT based on the Wilson/Cray supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. We found that the hadron transverse momentum distributions, particularly in collisions with low $|y|$, follow universal curves when normalized by exponential factors related to local chemical potential and local flow rapidity at particle mass $m$. Normalizing these universal curves by the chemical potential and flow rapidity at the particle's mass results in a curve that shifts with $1/m^2$. Notably, this $1/m^2$ behavior is connected to the average inverse mass used to relate local flow rapidity to $K_\perp$. However, this relationship breaks down at large $|y|$, likely due to baryon number conservation. Additionally, we found that hadron distributions can be described as local thermal equilibria with a small variation in temperature across the freeze-out surface. Yet, we found that distributions do not fit a single temperature when normalized by elliptic flow, indicating that hadron distributions cannot be uniquely related to temperature and particle density at all points in a collision.

This research paper introduces the Quaternion Linear Canonical Stockwell Transform (QLCST), presenting key inequalities including the uncertainty principle, Hausdorff-Young inequality, and a quaternion version of the Hardy inequality. The formulation of the QLCST is derived from the LCST formulation in the real domain. The establishment of the quaternion basis follows a systematic approach, drawing on methods used in the development of the SLCT transform. Proof of the uncertainty principle for the QLCST is provided, along with a corresponding uncertainty principle for the LCST. The inequality known as the Hausdorff-Young inequality for the QLCST is demonstrated. Additionally, a version of the Hardy inequality is derived for the QLCST.

In large-scale wireless networks, a fundamental challenge lies in managing power allocation to mitigate interference. Due to limited power information available at base stations, a common approach is decentralized power control using local information alone. This paper investigates a specific strategy called binary power control and demonstrates that for certain network topologies, such as full-duplex star and tree networks, it achieves high spectral efficiency with just one bit of coordination between base stations. Moreover, a theoretical upper limit is set for binary power control's performance across all possible graph structures. Notably, as network size expands, this limit becomes sufficiently small to suggest that a more straightforward approach than full optimal power control may be highly effective. Additionally, a case is examined where base stations operate in a time-slotted manner and can function in either transmit or receive mode per stage, again comparing the performance of a simple strategy to optimal power control.

A multiple-time-step integration method (MTSA) has been developed and applied to a simulation of a flow containing particles and a one-way coupled system. In MTSA, different time steps are used for calculating particle trajectories and fluid dynamics, with the former employing a larger time step than the latter. If necessary, this can be optimized so that the total simulation time equals the product of the particle time step and the number of intermediate calculations per step. Compared to standard methods using the same small time step, MTSA significantly reduces computational cost and, consequently, accelerates simulation time. A variant of the algorithm features a modified body force calculation between intermediate steps and on each new time step. Performance measurements using a standard HPC system demonstrate that MTSA achieves a substantial reduction in computational time, with improved efficiency as the number of particles increases. Furthermore, results for accuracy and computational time indicate that MTSA produces outcomes nearly identical to standard methods while offering marked improvements in speed.

This note builds on a previous result from the arXiv, which confirmed the equation 7^n = a^n + b^n + |a^n - b^n| for  n = 9 had 5 solutions.  To expand on this finding, I present five additional examples with n = 9,  n = 27,  n = 28,  n = 36 and  n = 504.

A novel closed-loop control method for a robotic hopper moving on compliant ground has been developed. By modeling ground compliance as a spring, the approach determines spring displacement feedback controls needed to track a desired trajectory. This method accounts for compliance estimation errors and velocity measurement noise through a trajectory planner that generates a feasible reference trajectory. The method's effectiveness was tested using a physical robotic hopper with ground compliance and coasts, and results showed successful synchronization with a moving target despite ground and robot imperfections.

Using a novel approach based on light-front holography, this study delves into the charge radii of mesons, particularly focusing on the limitations of traditional definitions, such as the classical Rutherford one. Charge current density and position density are examined to provide a more accurate assessment of charge distribution. Our calculations exhibit charge patterns that align closely with experimental data and the predictions of the lattice QCD, representing the first application of the light-front holographic model to charge distribution on the full light front. Specifically, our results for charge distribution exhibit an oscillatory behavior that was previously unobserved in other models, especially for axial vector mesons. Furthermore, the associated charge radii are determined for various mesons and the results are compared to the values obtained from the potential model, the lattice QCD, and the available experimental data.

A new model has been developed to explain the behavior of a droplet undergoing significant shape changes, which has major implications for transferring heat and mass in the surrounding environment. This multi-scale model combines multiple approaches to assess complex dynamics within the droplet and its surroundings, which can also influence chemical reactions. To analyze this, several key aspects were studied, including rapid movements of the droplet, thermal and mass fluctuations, and both linear and nonlinear vibrations of the droplet. This new model provides a detailed mathematical framework consisting of numerous equations and boundary conditions that describe the dynamics, vibrations, and transfer of heat and mass both inside the droplet and in its surroundings.

Recent advances in Natural Language Processing using representation learning have outperformed traditional methods in various tasks. However, these advanced models struggle significantly with tasks involving negation, such as inferring the truth value of a negated statement from a positive one. This study examines recent state-of-the-art models' ability to handle negation in natural language inference, revealing that they perform poorly and yield unexpected results like inconsistent error patterns and above-mechanical error rates. In contrast, trained humans on the same data perform near-random accuracy but at least match SOTA models' ability to infer negation. We further provide a framework for analyzing NLI models under the influence of negation and offer design principles for improving their performance when encountering negated statements.

Recently, graph-based methods have gained popularity in organizing and representing knowledge, providing a comprehensive view of complex information networks. A model like HDTM, or a similar framework, can then be used to automatically extract latent structures from these networks, highlighting their hierarchical relationships. Unlike standard techniques that focus on node properties, HDTM can also capture the interactions between nodes and the overall network's local and global characteristics. By-purposely HDTM optimizes a closed-form objective function, which ensures mathematical consistency while considering these various aspects. As HDTM is the first model to handle network dynamics and hierarchies simultaneously, it represents a significant step forward in statistical modeling. In comparison to traditional methods, HDTM can simultaneously consider the interactions between nodes and the overall network structure, while also highlighting the hierarchical relationships. As for HDTM's capabilities, our results show that it can provide more accurate cluster formations, at par with state-of-the-art algorithms, while also considering network connections. Additionally, HDTM can reveal complex topics within the network, along with their hierarchical relationships, while also extracting local and global characteristics. By HDTM's design, we can also extract network-based subtopics, along with their hierarchical relationships, while also highlighting local and global characteristics. As for the benefits of HDTM, our results show that it can provide more accurate cluster formations, at par with state-of-the-art algorithms, while also considering network connections. A quantum annealing gap is frequently understood as crucial, yet the exact role
it plays remains unclear. We offer a general definition of the gap with various
quantitative measures, including the adiabatic time threshold $\tau_{\rm QAP}$ for
quantum annealing and energy overlap following quantum annealing. We show that
this definition can identify significant gaps in models where the annealing gap is
flat, presents multiple gaps smaller than another, or even lacks a minimum. We
also generalise the concept to include models with non-monotonic gap behavior. We
show that for a set of spin glass models, using our definition can identify optimal
quantum annealing protocols that outperform those tailored to annealing gap structure.

This study differs from conventional alignment approaches by considering a an infix string that results from inserting characters into a reference string. We apply this infix concept to trace computer processes, which leads to distinct infix and postfix alignments. We demonstrate that these new alignments offer a more accurate representation of processes and provide better practical outcomes. Furthermore, our findings reveal the superiority of using infix and postfix alignments in comparing programs with similar inputs over the traditional method.

First principles calculations were conducted to examine the effects of on-site and crystal field potentials on the electronic structure of nickelates. A simplified tight-binding model was developed to analyze the modifications to band structures, with implications for magnetic and superconducting properties. Our study reveals that in planar configurations, a high-energy splitting occurs within the d orbitals of filled electrons, which can be incorporated into isotropic phonon couplings to enable a robust mechanism for a charge-dependent crystal field superconductivity. Calculations demonstrate that this mechanism can produce a critical temperature exceeding 300K in nanodisks of La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$.

We examine the non-periodic, cutoff-adjacent and non-cutoff Boltzmann equations in all spatial dimensions and derive separate decay rates for low and high frequency components of solution decays. By combining these rates, we obtain an optimal decay time-scale for the medium frequency components.

Determining the speed of terrestrial vehicles has numerous applications across many industries, which is why accurate wind data is essential. This study starts by examining the probability distributions of wave slopes as influenced by wind speed. It also investigates the asymmetry of these distributions, specifically in relation to the Gaussianity parameter. Speed calculations from our method are compared with camera measurements at varying wind speeds, which in turn is examined against the distributions of wave slopes. Speed errors are studied in relation to the Gaussianity parameter of these distributions, which is in essence is influenced by wind speed. This relationship is compared with sensor readings in the case of calm weather. Our model proposes a connection between the break point and the saturation value of this parameter, which is used to formulate a simplified equation. This model is then incorporated into existing empirical formulas to produce a new theoretical approach to wave propagation that is speed and weather-condition dependent.

A new framework for resilient software product configuration has been proposed,
which leverages a graph of software components and their relationships to
encode software transformations via singular value decomposition. By utilizing
this framework, the proposed method enables efficient learning of software
transformations and their reverse operations, as well as encoding novel
software changes. The proposed framework also facilitates efficient storage of
software transformations by compressing encoding matrices. A protocol for
secure software transformation encoding has been proposed, which utilizes a
distributed key management system to prevent unauthorized reverse engineering.
This protocol is resilient to both honest and malicious key holders. The
framework's and protocol's principles have been demonstrated using a practical
example based on Kubernetes.

Social media sites, such as Twitter, play a key role in spreading news and opinions quickly during crises, providing vital insights into the public's behavior and emotional state. To take full advantage of the vast amounts of data available from Twitter, effective methods must be used to process it. One such method involves applying Natural Language Processing techniques to assess the emotional state and opinions of users based on their tweets. In this study, we used a unique, visually presented dataset consisting of 84,580 tweets related to COVID-19 to refine existing NLP models by measuring how well they could determine the emotional state and opinions of users from their tweets. Our results were surprising as our simple baseline model outperformed more complex models on this specific dataset. Furthermore, we found that this type of data is not representative of all user behavior and Twitter users in general.

In the case of cuprate superconductors like La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_{4}$ and YBa$_{2}$CuO$_{4}$, our study of the high-frequency dielectric constants $\epsilon_{\perp}$ and $\epsilon_{\parallel}$ reveals substantial disparities between intralayer and interlayer interactions. Specifically, the intralayer couplings are orders of magnitude larger than their interlayer counterparts. Within a two-dimensional model incorporating long-range Coulomb interactions screened by vacuum, we estimate the critical carrier densities in cuprates to be on the order of 10$^{21}$ m$^{-2}$. These densities, however, far exceed $\epsilon_{\parallel}$ and $\epsilon_{\perp}$ to such an extent that vacuum screening appears irrelevant to superconductivity in cuprates. Consequently, our findings imply that long-range Coulomb interactions heavily influence the critical carrier densities and can potentially reframe our comprehension of the mechanism behind superconductivity in cuprates.

Another major discovery at the LHC, along with earlier findings from the LCFS, has shown that deconfinement has a transition temperature of approximately $155$ MeV. This has significant implications for quark stars, particularly those with temperatures much greater than this value. Using analytic equations of state, we found that deconfinement reduces the star's density, from $10^{15}$ to $10^{14}$ g/cm$^3$, and causes the star's central temperature to be orders of magnitude higher than its surface temperature, potentially reaching $10^{12}$ K even with relatively low surface temperatures of $10^{11}$ K. This has a profound effect on the star's cooling process and neutrino emission mechanisms, with direct Urca becoming less dominant and cocentric neeutrino emission increasing by several orders of magnitude, with fluxes as high as $10^{33}$ erg/cm$^2$/s. These effects may be observable with more sensitive future detectors and have a significant impact on the interpretation of quark star data.

We examine two related problems concerning unordered trees: the Tail Mapping problem and the Anti Tail Mapping problem. Specifically, we discover that computing a maximum-weight Tail Mapping between two unordered trees is NP-complete, and a maximum-weight Tail Mapping of an unordered tree onto itself can also be computed in polynomial time. On the other hand, we prove that finding a maximum-weight Anti Tail Mapping between two unordered trees is possible in polynomial time, and also determine the difficulty of related problems with start and end constraints. These findings build on previous research by D. Klein (2003) and R. Cole et al. (2010). Additionally, an algorithm for calculating a maximum-weight Tail Mapping of an unordered tree onto itself has been provided.

We have studied the metrological application of a new state, which we call the'compass state', on two levels. First, we investigated the number variance and coherence of number states in the thermodynamic limit, and found that the compass state exhibits good coherence and number variance behavior. It exhibits sub-Poissonian number variance for a wide range of parameters and displays periodic oscillations with an amplitude that decreases as $1/N$ in the large $N$ limit. The compass state also shares similarities with the Schrödinger cat state in its number variance behavior. The compass state exhibits sub-Poissonian number variance for a broad range of parameters and displays periodic oscillations that decrease as $1/N$ in the large $N$ limit. It also exhibits similar number variance behavior to the Schrödinger cat state and can be used to estimate the damping parameter more accurately. The compass state exhibits sub-Poissonian number variance for a broad range of parameters and displays periodic oscillations that decrease as $1/N$ in the large $N$ limit. It also shares similar number variance behavior to the Schrödinger cat state and can be used to estimate the damping parameter more accurately.

A new cooling efficiency model has been integrated into a three-zone disk model for first-generation protoplanetary disks, and the effects of including the cooling efficiency and particle coupling on gas dynamics were examined. In a gas-only model, a high temperature exceeding 100K was observed in the outer region due to limited cooling efficiency, and this issue is resolved with particle coupling by reducing the temperature to around 30K. In a multi-zone gas-solid model, the temperature falls to over 10K in the mid-plane due to reduced radiative leakage. In all single-zone gas models, an accumulation of heat forms due to insufficient cooling in the central region, and this issue does not arise in the multi-zone model as the mid-plane region effectively radiates the incoming radiation. The inclusion of particle coupling and single-zone models demonstrate the importance of these factors in driving thermal accumulation, and this effect of heat buildup may need to be considered in interpretations of observations using spectral lines.

We offer a fresh proof of Perelman's key observation: given a function harmonic on a gradient shrinking Ricci soliton that decays exponentially, it must be smooth polynomial in terms of dimension. This condition can now be replaced with faster decay conditions in our proof, making exponential decay one possible alternative.

Implementing dynamic backdoors in various classification settings has long been associated with complex models requiring extensive inputs and outputs from both clean and poisoned samples. A simpler and more adaptable approach is necessary for a wider range of applications. We present an innovative method called Dynamic Backdoor Attack (DBA) that creates its own output layer and can be easily integrated into existing neural networks. Unlike previous methods that relied on a fixed backdoor trigger, DBA learns and adapts to new threats in real-time. It demonstrates remarkable effectiveness and stability across different data sets and neural network architectures. Moreover, DBA can successfully execute backdoors in challenging settings such as the open-world scenario and the never-seen-before case, where new classes are not considered during the initial malicious phase.

The MACHO variable parallax observed six years ago can now be explained without relying on echelons or binary systems in the three high-precision MACHO variables: HVE, TGS, and IEE. When projected onto the celestial equator, the MACHO variable parallax pattern becomes a prominent elliptical shape. In contrast, the notable bustard-like distortion seen in the MACHO data at first glance seems unrelated to any features of the Sun's apparent path across the sky. A mathematical conversion from ecliptic coordinates to a suitable coordinate system reveals the bustard form as a direct result of this projection process and confirms its consistency with the expected parallax effect. It's also important to note that the bustard form becomes even clearer when analyzing the differential parallax between two stars at different distances from Earth. Additionally, similar bustard forms can be seen in the Hubble Space Telescope data due to their similar observational methods. In a statistical analysis of over half a million stars within the MACHO region, using variable and constant parallaxes resulted in comparable goodness-of-fit values.

This research expands upon key algebraic algorithm AlBuRe's findings in nonlinear dynamics model reduction. Three novel related algorithms are introduced, addressing and solving additional problems while significantly enhancing the efficiency and applicability of AlBuRe. Firstly, modifying AlBuRe's computation from O(n^3) to a faster n * ahr(n^2) complexity for model rank calculation. Secondly, addressing stability across model computation even when nonlinear system equations are non-Lipschitz and exhibiting Zeno behavior. Thirdly, utilizing multiple computer processors to reduce computation time.

We investigate a stationary, self-repelling binary Bose-Einstein condensate composed of two one-dimensional optical traps. By balancing non-linear and non-linear coupling effects, we find solutions that transition between two types of self-localized states. Varying the interaction strengths, we observe that solitons can possess both positive and negative effective masses. In a counter-intuitive scenario, opposite interaction forces actually lead to the formation of negative mass solitons. Our analysis also reveals potential traps for both positive and negative mass solitons. Furthermore, we show that solitons can coexist with each other, as well as with their own mirror images. These findings provide a foundation for future experimental explorations.

This work investigates the potential of homomorphic parallel computation on layered evaluations, starting with fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) and integer homomorphic encryption (IHE). Traditional homomorphic computation at each layer requires decoding, but our approach introduces a novel coding method that enables simultaneous execution of multiple layers of a network without (IHE) or with minimal decoding steps (FHE). Our method significantly reduces communication overhead by around 4 times compared to the current state-of-the-art for secure machine learning (ML) inference. Moreover, our method achieves efficient secure training by introducing a new gradient aggregation technique that preserves security while allowing for effective learning.

Using data from HI4PI, researchers discovered numerous previously unidentified HI clouds in the direction of the Milky Way's nearby spiral galaxies. Further analysis using 21 cm line intensity maps and 3D velocity information allowed for the examination of these clouds' physical properties. As a result, they found the clouds to be relatively close, low-density structures moving at speeds consistent with those expected within the Local Group, and often larger than previously identified HI clouds in similar regions of sky. Notably, some of the clouds show signs of being associated with the spiral arms of M31 and may be related to the outer halo of the galaxy. Additionally, the study emphasizes the importance of thorough HI surveys in identifying potential targets for future observations with next-generation radio telescopes.

Our approach to Incorporating Knowledge (IK) for question answering is driven by semantics and designates IK as an iterative knowledge insertion process.
  A semantic framework is established to establish a connection between questions and knowledge, enabling both automatic and targeted use of knowledge.
  To find the best matching knowledge, retrieval components are employed for both questions and knowledge, ensuring their designs align with their interaction.
  A systematic evaluation is developed to assess the impact of IK on question answering performance and knowledge components' effectiveness, consisting of three key assessments: the impact of IK integration, the effect of IK on question answering performance, and the impact of IK on performance relative to knowledge components.
  As a demonstration, a semantic-driven IQ framework and associated IQ components are introduced and used to incorporate external knowledge base for open-domain question answering.
  A comprehensive assessment was conducted to evaluate the impact of IQ on question answering performance and knowledge components' effectiveness, with results showing that IQ and associated components are design-effective and performance-effective, with additional analysis revealing that the resulting IQ components are cost-effective.

Full electronic structure calculations for large numbers of atoms present a significant challenge in spectroscopy-related fields. While many small molecular ions with unknown or difficult-to-measure spectra can be effectively studied using conventional methods, those involving a significant number of electrons beyond the oxygen core require innovative approaches to overcome limitations imposed by existing techniques. As a result, a new strategy has been successfully applied to investigate a previously understudied molecular ion species. In this case, the SmO++ molecule posed a unique problem that could not be solved with standard methods. Therefore, a combination of specialized algorithms has been applied to model its entire spectrum. First, a method has been developed to drastically reduce smOO++'s effective electronic structure size. Then, a combination of high-accuracy approaches has been used to construct a complete full-valence spectral model. While this new strategy focuses on SmO++, it has broad implications for a variety of other molecular ions with numerous electrons, effectively expanding the feasible scope of such studies.

We've developed an algorithm with a clear, finite execution path that can break down specific formal power series and polynomials over a formal disk into sums of square components. The algorithm's prerequisites are straightforward: the underlying ring's underlying field must provide a finite number of elements that can be expressed as the sum of two elements squared. Though there's currently no established method to extend this to rings underlying fields of three or more elements, the explicit steps provided can still be utilized in these scenarios.

By linking fast timing data from X-ray satellites with optical light curves,
we establish a method to determine the intrinsic correlation lag between
neutron stars' X-ray and optical emissions. This technique can be applied
astronomically to locate fast-moving objects among interstellar clouds or to
detect and track cloud disturbances around pulsars. In our study, we leverage
this approach to reveal a 5.6-second lag with 0.05-second precision between the
objects' X-ray and optical emissions, indicating a possible cloud of electrons or
ionized particles rotating around the neutron star at roughly 6.6 interstellar
parsecs away. Additionally, we demonstrate a correlation between the period
derivative of the cloud and the objects' orbital motion around the pulsar, and
discuss the implications of this relationship.

Developing accurate and reliable machine learning models for predicting molecular properties is a major challenge in computer-aided pharmacology. These models process structured biological data and convert molecular structures into numerical values through various methods. We evaluated 150 pre-trained models across 17 different machine learning tasks, focusing on predicting molecular properties and molecular similarity. We open-accessed our results to encourage researchers to establish a benchmark for molecular machine learning. Our analysis offers two main insights: (a) there is a significant discrepancy between reported and reproducible performance gains, and existing reports lack thoroughness in detailing experimental procedures and results; and (b) current models do not outperform traditional random forest approaches in predicting molecular similarity and certain biological properties. We also examined how different molecular representation methods and task fine-tuning techniques impact model performance. To encourage future research, we created a comprehensive data set containing results from standard evaluations that is available to all researchers on CMLE.org.

A novel communication-efficient stochastic learning algorithm has been introduced.
It combines a random walk that shifts a random direction at set intervals with
iterative gradient descent. This algorithm is shown can achieve an optimal convergence
rate in various strongly convex settings. It is also proposed that a communication-
efficient learning algorithm can derive from this algorithm by employing a sparse
representation of the model in a distributed setting. This proposed approach is
experimentally demonstrated to improve both the convergence rate and accuracy of
the model for the learning tasks.

Our research into wave turbulence driven by inertial oscillations confirms the $k^{-4}$ spectrum, a initial finding by Galtier in 2003. We employed a weak turbulence model to analyze a range of flows and verify this spectrum. Through numerical computation of a closed four-wave interaction model in 3D rotating convection convection cells at high rotation rates, we found that the turbulence's properties could be explained by a four-wave interaction process. This includes the development of an anisotropic turbulent length scale and an anisotropic turbulent energy spectrum ($E_\perp \propto k_\perp^{-2}$). However, at lower rotation rates, the turbulence no longer conforms to the predictions of four-wave interaction and may involve a more complex three-wave interaction process.

This study examines how access to mental health treatment and incarceration influence the probability of individuals committing violent crimes, property-related offenses, and public safety violations, as well as how these effects vary in terms of treating their underlying mental illness. Empirical data comes from almost 9 million court cases in Chicago between 1993 and 2004, taking into consideration a significant policy shift that reduced public mental health treatment costs. Our findings indicate that mental health treatment and incarceration have comparable impacts on reducing reoffending rates, with those receiving treatment exhibiting lower reoffending rates than those subjected to incarceration alone. Moreover, increased mental health treatment leads to lower reoffending rates in line with its potential to adequately address underlying mental illness, primarily affecting individuals with violent tendencies and on the marginal inclination to commit crimes. This study holds considerable significance in presenting a large-scale urban setting where court rulings dictate both insurance coverage for mental health treatment and whether mental illness qualifies for reduced sentencing through the insanity defense.

A novel approach to preventing over-segmentation in medical images through interpolation-based mixing has been proposed. This approach can be integrated into semi-supervised learning models by combining a few marked images with a large collection of unlabeled images. The idea of interpolation-based mixing is guided by the decision boundary hypothesis, which postulates that class decisions in a decision boundary region within the feature space are most susceptible to error. Consequently, data points situated in this region should be assigned to the class with the opposite label of their actual values. A key advantage of this approach is that it utilizes prior knowledge about label distribution in the training data. Furthermore, a metric for quantifying the confidence of a network's feature is also proposed. This approach has been successfully applied to the segmentation of prostate and brain tumors and demonstrated a significant improvement in performance by at least 5% on average in terms of Dice Score.

The upgrade for the Large Hadron Collider's detector, set to be completed by 2029, will significantly boost the processing capacity of the forward physics experiments system from 400 Teraflops to 16 Petaflops. To achieve this enhancement, the project involves expanding the existing system's computing modules and associated high-speed data links in the service voids of the detector's central tunnel. This paper outlines our approach to modeling this future system, known as upgradeFEX, which will involve adding multiple computing and data transfer modules to existing LHC detector infrastructure. Our current prototype simulations demonstrate the system's ability to handle complex tasks at its enhanced processing speed, with results generated in a fraction of a second now taking several days to run.

Recent advancements in 3D reconstruction have been primarily driven by optimization-based neural rendering techniques that efficiently bridge computer graphics and computer vision. Despite their success, most existing frameworks are limited to simple and single-object scenes due to memory costs associated with representing full scene geometry. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a new approach called Articulated Neural Rendering, a memory-efficient method capable of rendering complex and articulated subjects with high precision. By utilizing hierarchical meshes for subject representation, we develop a technique that reuses shared pose-dependent diffuse components and angularly varying normal maps, enabling efficient modeling of subjects with long sequences of reconfigurable parts. As a result, our framework achieves a compact parameterization that significantly reduces memory costs, enabling real-time rendering of high-resolution and multi-part subjects, including a human model with over 10000 triangles. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by formulating our optimization problem in a coherent way and utilizing hierarchical light transport for physically accurate radiance estimation. We also introduce the ar5 dataset, a comprehensive dataset of high-precision dragon data and sequences captured with an optical arm, designed to specifically test and validate our framework.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have been utilized in various tasks related to quantifying local atomic configurations in materials. Despite their effectiveness, existing GNN approaches suffer from limited interpretability, preventing them from providing atomic-level insights. To address this issue, we developed a new GNN framework based on the $\mathbf{M} \ \mathbf{E} \ \mathbf{R} \ \mathbf{E} \ \mathbf{G} \ \mathbf{R} \ \mathbf{E}$ gain theory, which not only provides a robust solution for property prediction but also enables a comprehensive examination of local electronic structures through the embedding produced by GNN. Notably, this framework can be applied universally to any material without being constrained by specific crystal symmetries. To demonstrate the versatility of $\mathbf{M} \ \mathbf{E} \ \mathbf{R} \ \mathbf{E} \ \mathbf{G} \ \mathbf{R} \ \mathbf{E}$, we applied it to two challenging tasks: identifying bond angles and local coordination numbers from local environments, and analyzing local distortions in perovskite structures. The article examines the conditions under which weak convergence occurs in a family of probability measures defined by parameters, and discusses the implications for estimating functions of parameters.

Despite significant advancements in deep learning-based knowledge tracing methods, there's a lingering concern that they may be overfitting to specific datasets. This study aims to evaluate the robustness of these models across varied settings and addresses the generalization gap caused by the lack of knowledge tracing data for comprehensive evaluation. A novel framework, Virtual Virtual Generalization (V2Gen), is introduced to assess a model's ability to perform on unseen datasets. Easier and more controlled evaluation scenarios are also established. Experimental results reveal the limited adaptability of current knowledge tracing models and show that V2Gen and the new evaluation settings outperform baseline models, often by substantial margins. This study highlights the necessity of revisiting the assumptions underlying knowledge tracing and emphasizes the potential of deep learning in this field when its assumptions hold and when models can truly adapt to new data.

This study determines conditions under which second-order elliptic differential operators are surjective on a smooth function space, yielding a negative outcome for general cases and a positive result for certain degenerate cases.

The veriT proof format has significantly advanced since its original version presented at the PxTP workshop in 2010, with improvements continually made ever since. At the 2020 PxTP workshop, we introduced several key features commonly used in internal proofs and client integration but were previously absent from the format specification. These key components have now been formally added to the document.

In the context of federated learning, we present an alternative method that
effectively combines the advantages of FedAvg for enhanced scalability and
FedCM for guaranteed data privacy. The FedBuff algorithm, derived from FedAvg,
integrates the concept of FedCM's buffer while enhancing its efficiency through
reduced memory usage and improved performance. Our analysis reveals that FedBuff
achieves a similar convergence rate to FedCM but with significantly lower memory
requirements, making it suitable for practical deployment on devices with limited
memory capabilities.

Research into transfer learning for speech recognition has focused primarily on languages with similar similarities. To broaden this field, this study examines deep neural network models for recognizing speech in dissimilar languages, specifically English and Polish. By doing so, we examine two approaches - matching the speaker features or aligning the model's output layer - to enhance performance. Our results show that the deep neural network model successfully demonstrates transfer learning capabilities across English-Polish recognition. Furthermore, we found that aligning the model's output layer yields better outcomes than matching features between the two languages. By comparing our findings with recent studies on English-German and English-French recognition models, we uncover that performance in speech recognition is maximized on more dissimilar language pairs by utilizing intermediate target language pairs during training.

To assess novel node embedding algorithms, it's essential to assess their flexibility, as they often involve many parameters affecting both runtime and outcomes. Furthermore, testing these algorithms on diverse sets of inputs is crucial to ensure their performance consistency. A new tool, runae.io, has been created to facilitate this evaluation by experimenting with a wide range of node embedding algorithms on multiple datasets. The generated visual reports from runae.io aid researchers in comparing the best-performing algorithms based on specific performance metrics, as well as conducting robust statistical analyses of the RUMs (Typical RUs with Minimum and Maximum scores).

We used amplitude analysis to study the $B^+ \to K^+ K^0 \overline{K^0}$ decay and break the energy spectrum into distinct regions. To refine our understanding of the broad scalar resonance $f_0(500)$, we reanalyzed a sample excluding this specific region. We found that removing this region unveiled another resonance, likely corresponding to the $f_0(1500)$, and enhanced the $S$-wave contribution, accounting for more of the observed structure in the spectrum.

New extensions to the Standard Model of particle physics can naturally generate a dark matter component consisting of primordial black holes within the mass range of $10^{10}$ to $10^{15}$ grams. We choose three specific particle physics models that match this criteria and simulate their implications for the abundance and distribution of primordial black holes. Our simulations show that these scenarios are consistent with existing observational constraints and can be validated through a combination of methods: using the UV bands with the James Webb Space Telescope to detect the peak of the accretion luminosity, with a specific focus on a signal of ~2 lum. with the Euclid telescope for a specific model, and also looking for an ~$10^{35}$ Watts of energy output in the X-ray band that could be attributed to a model where primordial black holes constitute all of the dark matter.

Series elastic actuatures (SEAs) utilize a spring to ensure safe human-robot interaction by enabling force measurement at the EA's output. Accurate force measurement is critical, yet challenged by the sensor's inability to directly measure elastic deformation and the sensor's nonlinearity and noise. Developing a linearization algorithm is complicated due to the unknown relationship between force and deformation. While simple scaling methods can produce effective force estimates, they do not account for the algorithm's unknown characteristics, making learning algorithm-based solutions inapplicable for measuring force. We propose an adaptive algorithm that estimates force in real-time by combining the scaling algorithm with learning components that compensate for its non-idealities. We derive convergence conditions and compare our algorithm favorably to unprocessed data in experiments using a series elastic robot.

As self-assembling systems enlarge in size, comprehending how they retain functionality poses a significant challenge. While an expanding environment tends to diminish the impact of random fluctuations, the re-aggregation of particles counteracts this by restoring interactions between particles. We investigate this competition using a dual model consisting of random environment expansion and particle re-aggregation, specifically examining how rifts are affected. We discover that the gap between adjacent rifts results from this competition and that the number of rifts that can coexist with a given diameter is directly influenced by the relative rates of re-aggregation and expansion. This balance also dictates that the energy cost of maintaining multiple rifts is lower than closing them, offering an explanation for the observed coexistence of the Golden Gate and San Francisco Bay.

We've developed a method to identify and quantify distinct phases in multicomponent complex scalar field theories. Using a combination of singular value decomposition and machine learning on measured data from a lattice model, we obtained a set of singular values that captured the essential features of a four-component complex scalar field theory in two-dimensional space. These features allowed us to distinguish between multiple phases and quantify the flow from one phase to another as a function of a renormalization-group parameter. Notably, our analysis revealed that some phases were irrelevant due to their features being beyond what our model could capture. We found that our method could accurately reconstruct the singular value landscape and correctly recognize different phases and their boundaries. Additionally, it revealed that the shape of the singular value landscape could serve as a useful tool for phase detection and could provide insights into the underlying flow of a theory from UV to IR.

Underwater navigation using AUVs using traditional methods using pre-set maps has several drawbacks, such as inefficiency and inaccuracy due to inaccurate three-dimensional environment information. To overcome this challenge, we propose a policy evaluation algorithm called SPGP-SARSA that integrates Squared Predictive Filter, Repeatedly Executed Gradient Algorithm, and SARSA to achieve real-time 3D environment construction and policy optimization. Using a simulated underwater environment, we demonstrate the effectiveness of SPGP-SARSA in building precise real-time 3D maps and its suitability for efficient policy learning in complex underwater scenarios. Using real-world data, we also illustrate the algorithm's capability of constructing precise real-time 3D environment information and its suitability for accurate policy learning in actual underwater environments.

We have obtained fresh insights into the relationship between the minimal complexity of sorting networks and their compactness, specifically we found that the minimal arity for sorting networks of depths 1 to 4 are 4, 6, 8 and 10 respectively which shows the earlier discovery by Ahlswede and Koiran that comparing depth and comparison number don't have a linear correlation. We also establish a lower bound of comparisons needed by sorting networks with a comparability graph not containing $P_k$ as an induced subgraph is at least $n\sqrt{n-3/4}-n+4/2$ which improves the existing bound by Benes comparators. In addition we found the precise comparisions needed by 3-deep sorting networks is 6 for 4 elements and 28 for 5 elements which shows the earlier discovery by Rose and Wender 28 is not optimal in 5 elements. We found the main incompleteness of the famous 0-1 principle by giving an example of a non-sorted permutation mask which can be generated from the famous Satcher's sorting network in 3-deep and 6-comparisons. We also discovered two new open problems about sorting networks which can complete the earlier open problems by Benders, S. G. W. Krull and others.

Building upon a previous study, we've developed a range of two-fluid relativistic stellar models using the Kiselev dark energy concept, which involves the endofluid model's multiple endofluids and a dark energy component. By applying a type-1 isobaric equation of state to both fluids, we've obtained seven distinct two-fluid stellar models that can be obtained from seven derived one-fluid stellar models. Similarly, using the type-2 barotropic equation of state for both fluids, we've obtained seven distinct two-fluid stellar models from seven derived one-fluid stellar models. Finally, using the type-3 barotropic equation of state for both fluids, we've obtained seven distinct two-fluid stellar models that can be derived from seven one-fluid stellar models.

In this study, we investigate bar formation in galactic disks with varying density distributions using N-body simulations. We focus on scale lengths in the range of 2-7 Ds(Ds: scale length in the middle) and find that a bar can form in all cases, but its shape changes with scale length. In large scale lengths, the bar is rounded while in small scale lengths, the bar is more pronounced and extends outward as radial spikes. This shows that the density distribution affects the bar's shape and can even lead to distinct morphological features. Our findings also reveal that the bar's formation time is influenced by the density distribution and shows correlations with the central potential and the distribution of angular momentum. This study emphasizes the significance of considering various factors in bar formation research.

Our study investigates how magnetic fields influence the formation of merger remnant galaxies following gas-rich major mergers. Using three-dimensional SPH-MHD simulations, we examined the effects of a horizontal magnetic field on the merger process and remnant galaxy properties. Our results show that magnetic fields significantly impact the formation of accretion disks and the distribution of turbulent gas. Remnant galaxies in magnetized mergers exhibit larger, more irregular, and elongated structures compared to their non-magnetized counterparts. Additionally, we found that the central supermassive black hole's growth is accelerated in magnetized mergers due to increased accretion. Our findings provide valuable insights into the role of magnetic fields in galaxy formation and evolution.

A proposed 3D Contrastive Mixup Classification network is presented for self-driven food severity classification with imbalance. To tackle the imbalance issue, a contrastive learning module was incorporated into 3D MC. A food representation space was created where similar samples are in close proximity, while dissimilar ones are separated, by the contrastive module. A defined loss function was employed to optimize this space. A proposed re-weighted focal cross-entropy function, considering both bias and focus within the representation space, was introduced for classification. A proposed detection algorithm integrates the classification function with the contrastive module to classify foods. It re-weights the focus of each sample in the cross-entropy function, optimizing the focus while minimizing bias. Two proposed properties, super-dissimilarity and super-dissimilarity focus, were incorporated into the algorithm to address imbalance. Experimental results on the Food-101 and Food-6 datasets confirm the algorithm's effectiveness.

Despite great success in natural language processing with pre-trained models due to transfer learning, their application to spelling correction has been limited. Studies show that existing methods that combine task-related encoders and shared layers do not always yield optimal results, especially when the language modeling task has significant differences from the spelling correction task.

In this study, we explore the use of generalization-based model adaptation in the multi-task learning framework and introduce a Gaussian noise layer method that adapts to new target tasks. This proposed adaptation method significantly improves the multi-task learning model's performance, especially when adapting to less-related target tasks.

As opposed to existing task isolation methods that simply fine-tune a source task model for target tasks, we demonstrate that our proposed Gaussian noise layer method achieves notable gains over these task-isolation-based approaches. Notably, we achieve unprecedented results in the spelling correction task, outperforming strong baselines by a substantial margin.

Our results show that our method's performance is on par with state-of-the-art English GEC systems but with a fraction of the computational cost. However, Arabic GEC remains challenging due to the substantial dataset size required for training.

A surprising finding revealed in recent research involved fluctuating suicide rates in the U.S. following 9/11, with similar patterns observed in other periods involving changes in U.S. suicide rates in the 21st century. Upon closer examination, it was determined that publishing suicide statistics in annual summaries with regional variations involved rounding to a nearest five or ten at a rate of 1 in 100000 people. This implies that inconsistencies observed in suicide statistics could be partly attributed to rounding effects, thereby necessitating a revised approach to collecting and reporting data. It is also worth noting that increased accessibility to suicide statistics could be influencing their interpretation, with a resulting effect on their perceived availability in certain regions. This could lead to a decrease in reported suicides due to the bystander effect involving statistics rounding, which could have an impact on public health and policy making.

GdInO3 has been analyzed using various techniques including high-resolution X-ray diffraction and Raman scattering, as well as theoretical calculations. This study reveals that GdInO3 adopts a space group of Sg $R\bar{3}c$ within a rhombohedral rhombohedra-based hexagonal unit cell. The structural parameters obtained from experiments are in good agreement with those derived from the Gd3+ ion force field in the six-fold axis direction. Raman spectra for GdInO3 consist of four distinct modes at 148.2 cm-1, 184.7 cm-1, 302.4 cm-1, and 558.5 cm-1, corresponding to the A2u, Eu, Tu2, and Tu4 symmetries respectively. Additionally, the phonon frequencies calculated using the DFT method align closely with the observed experimental values.

The round-robin protocol for the cut-and-choose algorithm is analyzed with a different foundation, resulting in a proof that it consistently produces allocations with an approximate value of 5/4 m-vM for n agents and k items per batch. This new understanding allows for a significantly tighter demonstration that the round-robin allocation achieves an approximate 5/4 n-vM value under unenvy conditions. Additionally, it is shown that the protocol's allocation can be reached by applying the round-robin procedure with an added batch of roughly 5/4 n - 3/2 items. Notably, this proves a more precise fairness guarantee, as the round-robin allocation uses fewer items than the  n m items required for an n m-vM value.

Pseudo-labeling, utilizing predicted class labels from unlabeled images marked as 'confident', has been widely adopted in practice.  Another pseudolabeling strategy involves translating a single target image into multiple languages and making predictions on the original along with the translated versions.  This strategy takes the confidences from the predictions as pseudolabels.  In this study, we explore an alternative method where we use the average of the predictions from the translated versions as a pseudolabel instead of confidences.  This method was used on both synthetic and real-world datasets.  Our proposed method yielded superior results over the baseline in almost all cases.  This method has shown great potential to be a more effective pseudolabeling strategy for both synthetic and real-world target domain data.  Furthermore, this method can yield better pseudolabels than we previously anticipated.  As a result, this method can be a strong candidate for a more efficient pseudolabeling strategy for target domain data.
