The Local Group dwarf spiral galaxy UGC 8839 is undergoing a detailed multi-wavelength investigation across visual, ultraviolet, infrared, radio as well as optical spectra to comprehensively understand its constituent components and underlying dynamics. This study specifically focuses on a specific region of UGC 8839 and breaks down its HII population by spectral type, location in the galaxy, and galactocentric distance in order to derive the O/H abundance distribution within distinct galactocentric regions. A comparison with another dwarf spiral galaxy, UGC 6859, along with another nearby galaxy, UGC 7549, reveals significant similarities in their HII region distributions. Notably, in UGC 8839 the HII regions with higher ionizing capacity are concentrated within a radius of under 3 kpc from the galaxy's center which suggests an inward migration of gas due to a positive gas inflow. Furthermore an analysis of the HII region distribution in distinct quadrants of UGC 8839 reveals an asymmetrical gas distribution as illustrated by its HII population.

The study of sub-GeV dark matter is often impeded by multi-scattering processes within detectors, which can be mitigated by using oversized target materials to single out the initial interaction event. However, paleo-detectors, consisting of extremely large, geologically isolated crystals over billions of years, present an intriguing method for investigating multiple dark matter scattering processes. These proposed detectors could utilize advanced noble liquid techniques to identify multiple collisions with high precision. If paleo-detectors are employed, they may uncover dark matter nucleon cross-sections below 10^-39 cm^2 for masses under 1 GeV. Moreover, they could outperform traditional large-scale detectors in this mass range by 10+ orders of magnitude. For instance, they could potentially reveal the existence of a complex dark matter nucleus structure with a radius exceeding 1 fm.

Modern databases are frequently used to track changing user preferences over time,
and their associated update records are often shared for analytical and marketing
purposes. The frequent update history can reveal sensitive information about individual
users, and simply aggregizing updates is not enough to protect them from malicious actors.
We have developed a private algorithm that employs differential privacy to generate
a differential and chronological trace of updates based on the original updates in a
database, and theoretically proved that no adversary can learn more than what's
differentiated by the dp-algorithm's epsilon parameter from the original data.
We have also generated large scale data with our algorithm and analyzed its properties,
and our results suggest that it can effectively be used to track evolving user preferences.

Including irrelevant or duplicative features can slow down and distort a machine learning model's training process. To identify the most relevant features for a specific classification task using a Boolean formula, we introduce an innovative approach known as Minimal Unsatisfiable Cores (MUCs) for feature selection. Our approach pinpoints feature importance by detecting MUCs within the boolean formula, building on recent success with conflict-driven learning algorithms and their ability to generate compact representations of machine learning models. By incorporating a novel technique called Conflict Clauses as the classifier uses MiniSat to eliminate features associated with every MUC. As an alternative to this method, we also present Additional Clauses as a way to differentiate between features that are part of multiple MUCs and those that are not. Our findings, through both synthetic data and real-world classification models, show that MiniSat + MUCs + Redundant Features can effectively balance classification accuracy and feature selection, often outperforming MiniSat + Additional Clauses and even MiniSat + Counter-Example-Driven Learning (CEDT) in these scenarios.

This study examines the use of Dual decoder attention network (DDANet) for the automated segmentation of surgical instruments in laparoscopic views. We evaluated DDANet on a dataset consisting of 10,885 laparoscopic images from two sources. To measure performance, we employed the Dice Similarity Coefficient. Our results show that DDANet outperforms other deep learning segmentation methods and even manual annotation. Notably, DDANet's accuracy was comparable to that of manual annotation. To further validate the network, we conducted ablation studies and explored the impact of varying training data amounts on accuracy.

This study proposes an innovative unsupervised ReID framework called Real2Real, 
which integrates a contrastive learning module to capture general characteristics 
and produces realistic image synthesis to diversify training data. 
By performing domain adaptation in an unsupervised manner 
in both forward and reverse transformations, Real2Real achieves effective adaptation. 
Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through superior performance on multiple 
cross-domain ReID benchmarks, leading to open-source availability of our model 
and code for the research community.

Using pulsar timing array data analysis, we can determine the characteristics of a background gravitational wave by analyzing its stochastic properties. To efficiently explore the space of possible parameters and avoid generating misleading results, it's crucial to utilize sampling methods that work well together with hierarchical models and produce reliable estimates of uncertainties. We compared several sampling algorithms from `dynesty` and `emcee` by running them on test data and synthetic data, then ranked them based on their accuracy and speed. Our research showed that the 'nested' algorithm from `emcee` and the 'fixed-size adaptive' algorithm from `dynesty` performed best for analyzing pulsar timing array data parameters. We created a script to streamline parameter analysis by combining open-source packages, including Python versions of the `PTA` package and `sherpa` for fitting pulsar timing array data. This framework can be easily expanded to include other relevant tools in the future.

Using the Relativistic Lattice Hadron Tomography framework, this study analyzes the three-dimensional structure of hadrons, in this case, pions, through matrix elements of quark currents as function of quark mass. The research leverages novel, mass-variable lattice data from the RBC-UKQCD collaborations. Initially, it is found that for constant quark mass, increasing the mass results in a shrinkage of the pion's charge radius. However, more recently, it is found that the mass dependence on the pion's charge radius aligns with that of nucleons. Additionally, the renormalization-scale behavior of the pion's charge radius is analyzed with better precision, confirming its stability as indicated in prior studies. The results are depicted in Figs. 1 and 2.

Researchers studied the far-ultraviolet emissions of the Caudh Tauri star XX Persei from 1998 to 2015, utilizing data from the IUE, HST, and KEHI telescopes. Their findings revealed highly variable accretion rates for XPer, fluctuating by orders of magnitude over both short and long time periods. XPer's disc emissions spectrum showed a complex structure with multiple components, including high and low ionization parts, and these features had different origins and behaved independently of each other and the star itself. To the best of our knowledge, XPer is the first classical Caudh T Tauri star whose ultraviolet activity has been fully explored, and its erratic behaviour in the UV range challenges existing theories about how these stars' disks grow and change.

Understanding the effects of luck on public opinion and policy is essential. This study uses hypothetical scenarios to measure how varying definitions of luck affect people's support for income redistribution. The results show that people's perceptions of what is within an individual's control significantly influence their views on equality of opportunity and subsequent support for progressive taxation. Notably, people are more in favor of redistributing income when luck directly affects earnings rather than when it only affects opportunities, highlighting the need for clear definitions of opportunity and luck in future research.

This study introduces a formula for computing the Euler characteristic of certain varieties defined by stable maps from curves to a non-singular projective space, in characteristic zero. As a consequence, we derive the relationship between these varieties' Euler characteristics and their orbifold Euler characteristics from past research. We also explore formulas for the Euler characteristics of varieties related to stable maps from curves to a projective space, and discuss applications to the computation of numerical invariants of symplectic manifolds from quantum K-theory.

Debugging data pipelines is a time-consuming and indispensable part of pipeline development. These pipelines can have hidden issues, where small data discrepancies can lead to significant differences between predicted and actual outcomes. While some tools focus on software defects, others on user experience, we introduce DataScope, a data-debugging framework designed for large-scale machine learning pipelines. DataScope allows designers to create interactive visualizations that map input data to output predictions, enabling users to identify and investigate high-value regions of interest. By leveraging parallel computing and smart data aggregation, DataScope provides an efficient way to explore the vast input-output space of ML pipelines. In comparative tests, DataScope significantly reduces the time spent on data debugging by ninefold, and user studies show a marked improvement in the accuracy of issues detected by stakeholders.

Researchers have used Machine Learning to analyze data from VLA, Gaia DR2 and 2MASS in order to identify some elusive types of neutron stars within the globular cluster M15. A custom-designed neural network called Grad-Net was employed to analyze visual images of the VLA data, which helped it to distinguish between common types of radio sources. Surprisingly, it performed better at this task than initially expected. Additionally, the ML model was found to perform comparably to existing methods used to discover rare neutron stars in the Milky Way. As a result, it successfully identified previously undiscovered radio sources at the centers of globular clusters that could be millisecond pulsars or neutron star binaries. However, they are not consistent with being magnetar or radio-emitting neutron stars. To address this discrepancy, further evidence was needed and a possible explanation involving the dynamics of merging globular clusters was also proposed.

A major challenge in analyzing network data is reconstructing hypergraphs from their projections. In this context, we are interested in a reconstruction problem where some of the hyperedges may appear multiple times. This issue is especially pertinent to online users who have limited visibility into a hypergraph and aim to build a model based on their observations. A key concern in this scenario is whether a random sampling method can enable the construction of a useful model. Although it might appear intuitive that increasing the number of observations improves the quality of the model, our research reveals a surprising and counterintuitive finding - for both discrete and continuous time models, there exists a critical time threshold beyond which the utility of the model begins to decline, no matter how many times each hyperedge is reconstructed. This discovery raises an important question: Can we leverage this insight to better understand and design efficient sampling strategies for reconstructing hypergraphs?

We have developed an innovative model for describing rapid narrowing of beam angles in highly directional lasers. This model is based on a fundamental concept from wave theory and is applicable to any type of laser. It has been modeled mathematically using wave plate theories and can be used to analyze various types of beam plate systems. Using this model, we are able to determine how beam plate systems affect the directionality of lasers. This analysis can be used to evaluate the efficiency of any beam plate system in narrowing laser beams. Notably, we have discovered that well-known beam plate systems can narrow laser beams by several wavelengths. However, we have also discovered new principles for narrowing lasers by large multiples of their wavelengths, including using lossy beam splitters and filters to narrow the laser's directionality. As a result, our model can aid in designing more effective beam plate systems for narrowing the laser's spread.

We have developed an analytical approach to understanding how coherent light interacts with and propagates through mediums consisting of scattered photons and excited atoms. Our method is based on exact stochastic models of both classical and quantum systems, which we used to derive analytical expressions for a two-time correlation function of coherent light as it sc off an atomic ensemble. Our model accurately captures the scattering process, including the effects of classical and quantum multiphoton effects, and we have demonstrated its applicability to systems where more than one photon is involved. As a key outcome, our model allows us to obtain analytical expressions for two-time correlation functions of multiphoton fields and excitation probabilities of quantum systems involving multiple photons. Moreover, our model can be adapted to describe the dynamics of systems involving two-waveplates.

Offline reinforcement learning is a cost-effective approach for training high-quality policies by leveraging pre-collected historical data. Offline multi-agent learning is increasingly being used to train multiple agents simultaneously for better collaboration. To enhance this learning process, we introduce the Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) framework, which allows each agent to learn from its own observations and actions while learning from the shared trajectory distribution of all agents. By employing a centrally trained critic to generate trajectory data, we can train multiple agents to collaborate effectively. Our framework offers a unique advantage of automatically generating training data without the need for collecting additional dataset. Through our experiments on offline multi-agent tasks, we demonstrate that our framework consistently outperforms the conventional method of sharing observations and outperforms other offline multi-agent learning frameworks by incorporating them into the SIT framework.

A Convolutional Neural Network network structure has been proposed for use in image registration, which is capable of utilizing a multi-task learning framework to generate a deformation field from an initial image pair. This deformation field is then utilized by a linear optimal transport network to transform the source image into the target image. By formulating a joint loss function that combines the deformation field and pixel-wise differences between transformed images, a global optimum solution can be attained through the application of the Adam optimizer. To enhance the precision of the image registration, a fine-tuning strategy is applied to the neural network by leveraging intermediate landmarks generated from a coarser resolution. Experimental results from synthetic and real-world micro-CT mouse brain images demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, displaying superior performance when compared to conventional intensity-based methods. Moreover, this method displays robustness and accuracy, displaying the ability to generate high-quality images with both a high degree of accuracy and a high degree of precision in image registration.

A long-standing dispute concerns the role of single-particle entanglement, which arises due to indistinguishability, in producing nonlocal phenomena. We address this issue by demonstrating that single-particle entanglement is responsible for quantum nonlinearity and allows for a new understanding of these nonlocal effects. This leads to the development of a model incorporating single-particle entanglement and nonlinearity, which predicts a range of nonlocal correlations and signaling. We confirm our predictions through experiments and also show that the degree of quantum nonlinearity and entanglement can be manipulated, resulting in distinct manifestations of nonlocality and entanglement. Furthermore, our model demonstrates that an atom in a superposition of locations can exhibit both nonlocal correlations and entanglement with another atom when modeled with nonlinearity and entanglement. We address the challenges of realizing this model experimentally and highlight its potential applications in developing quantum networks.

The Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) is rapidly growing and offers significant potential, but security threats are also increasing, posing risks to user data privacy. The combination of IoVs and Blockchain technology can create a secure and private data environment by providing features like tamper-proofing, robust cryptography, and decentralized data verification. However, certain limitations of IoVs also hinder effective IoB deployment. This research proposes an innovative IoB application, known as SecureIoB, which leverages suitable cryptographic methods to prevent unauthorized access and fake data generation. The IoB smart contract in SecureIoB is carefully crafted to process transactions and validate data securely. When combined with C-RAN technology, SecureIoB can further optimize resource allocation and enhance security by validating data before transmission. The performance of SecureIoB and SecureIoV has been tested through simulation, demonstrating improved security and privacy for IoVs while maintaining efficient performance.

A Classical Nova from a white dwarf has a notable impact on its system, particularly by altering the white dwarf's accretion rate following the outburst. However, little is known about how the nova itself affects its system. By observing the system's X-ray, UV, and optical emissions pre and post the nova outburst of V392 Persei on 2022 June 19, we found the post-nova system to be in a high state with an intensely bright, supercritical accretion disk. Comparing the H$\alpha$ emission velocities of V392 Persei with those of the system's companion before the nova outburst, we discovered the post-nova velocities were significantly lower than their pre-nova counterparts. This could be a result of a drag force exerted on the disk by the nova's ejecta, slowing the system down as it moves through its halo. Since V392 Persei was in a high state following its nova outburst, the outcome appears to be neutral for the system's stability. If sufficient mass was gained by the white dwarf during the nova's outburst, it could potentially lead to an accretion disk wind and reduce the system's high-state duration.

As quantum computing advances, the toric code emerges as a strong contender for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing. In order to effectively benchmark scalable quantum gate performance, we focus on the diamond threshold error correction code distance one circuit, leveraging the commutative property of the CNOT gate to classify quantum noise. By extending our previous research on noisy ideal circuits, we account for the non-independent noise structure of the CNOT gate, assuming common noise sources. Using a quantum tomography protocol, we extract the noise parameters of the diamond circuit from data, which in turn enable us to benchmark quantum compiler performance on real quantum processors. Our findings, compiled in the accompanying supplement, include diamond circuit noise parameters and outcomes for various compiler configurations on the IBM Toronto processor.

In Massive M2M systems with finite backhaul resources, a novel feedback encoding scheme is proposed that utilizes local clustering to achieve near-optimal global solution while reducing overhead. Unlike traditional cluster-and-compress methods that report all codewords, the proposed encoding scheme only transmits cluster centers to the base station. By leveraging statistical knowledge of potential codewords, the proposed encoding and reporting scheme outperforms conventional methods by significantly reducing overhead while maintaining a near-optimal global objective value. For BER performance analysis, both exact and approximate expressions are derived to facilitate the evaluation of the scheme. It is mathematically proven that in certain scenarios, the error performance of the proposed encoding and reporting scheme matches that of the traditional cluster-and-compress scheme. Through numerical analysis, it is observed that the proposed encoding and reporting scheme provides a substantial overhead reduction in scenarios where cluster count exceeds BSs. In contrast, it provides a moderate overhead reduction in scenarios where there are more BSs than clusters.

The concept of geometric phase has evolved into a comprehensive theory known as the Berry curvature theory, which is now applicable across both fundamental types of matter—bosonic and fermionic matter. Recent research has demonstrated the precision with which this theory can be measured using cold atoms, as well as the accuracy with which related quantities, called symmetrized curvatures, can be determined using spectroscopic methods. In this paper, we propose a new approach based on curvature diagnostics to identify topological orders in both bosonic and fermionic systems using diagonalization. For both types of many-body systems, we demonstrate that diagonal curvature measurements can accurately distinguish between topological orders. Notably, we find that surface currents arise at the boundary of topologically distinct regions—these currents exhibit stability under perturbations, independence from specific parameters, and precision with which they can be measured using quantum interference. These results suggest that the characteristics of these currents may serve as a signature for topological edge modes.

We establish two key relationships governing the behavior of photons near a double asymptotic flat region in Brans-Dicke theory. These conditions, expressed in terms of Brans-Dicke radiation at infinity, are necessary and sufficient for the escape of photons to infinite distances. We derive these conditions by analyzing the Bel-Naimark complex and its interaction with the photon trajectory. However, in 3+1 dimensional non-minimally coupled theory, we show that this escape cannot be guaranteed due to the conformal flatness of the conformally related spacetime.

We are investigating the end stages of Population III massive binary stars, which held dominance in the early universe up to z ~ 6-8. By applying an extensive set of 94940 radiation-hydrodynamic simulations of early cosmological plasmas into our stochastic cosmological model, we derived the evolution of the cosmic merger density of these Pop III binaries over time. The merger density reached its peak value of approximately 1.4e-3 Gpc^-3 yr^-1 at z ~ 10.5 and gradually declined to around 1.4e-5 Gpc^-3 yr^-1 by z ~ 3. We established a cosmic volume containing approximately 100 Megaparsecs at z ~ 6 to 3, and identified the most relevant regions for hosting merger remnants of Population III binaries. The regions with the highest cosmic merger density are primarily situated near or within the massive early structure in the cosmos. Consequently, observing the merger signals of Population III binaries may be more feasible than previously thought with advanced LIGO and Einstein Telescope operations.

We have developed a Gamma-Ray Burst (GRB) simulator based on actual data from the Fermi/GBM and Konus-Wind detectors, capable of generating simulated events similar to those observed during high-energy Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs), including the GRB 090423. Although the underlying time series data from the detectors is preserved, simulated counts are drawn from a Poisson distribution, causing an inherent time jitter. This time jitter is greater than the temporal resolution typically resolved in GRB studies, around 10 ms, and also significantly exceeds the temporal jitter often seen in literature, around 100 $\mu$s. A operator T_g on a range 1<p<2 is strongly isometrically equivalent to a weakly compact operator on BMOA_p if and only if it makes the identity mapping on a subspace of a specific form. This subspace is defined by functions that satisfy conditions related to a measure derived from a function g. Additionally, we identify the precise circumstances under which a function g can direct T_g to convert BMOA_p and a weighted space H^2_σ into each other. We also determine the properties of g that allow T_g to convert either the space Dirichlet or the Smirnov space E_p^+ into the space BMOA_p.

The evolution of scientific knowledge can be compared to a living organism, 
which continuously undergoes renewal as it ages through birth, growth, and 
decline. To track the development and application of scientific knowledge and 
monitor its growing complexity, we've developed a metric called the 
Quantitative Index of Knowledge (KQI). This index measures the average number 
of references to other works within the journal articles of a specific 
field, providing a derivative-like expression that indexes the number of new 
contributions to that field. To get the KQI, we multiply the average number 
of citations within a specific field by 100, divided by the total number of 
articles within that field. This index allows us to visualize the flow of 
knowledge within a particular journal or field, as demonstrated with three 
examples: the development of control theory, the application of negative 
feedback in the control field, and Einstein's general relativity in the physics 
field, accompanied by their respective KQI graphs.

This paper extends our previous research by analyzing a two-tier, split-domain communication system where an attacker can separate parts of the base station from part of the user population. In this updated research, we removed the uniform signal and power allocation assumption and developed a game theory model to find an optimal power allocation strategy. The model considers each node's individual decision-making process, based on its own benefits and communication costs, while considering the decoding strategies and signals of other nodes. A specific type of game was designed and solved, providing a secure transmission model with nonlinear utility functions. Key results include the existence and uniqueness of stable outcomes, as well as detailed equilibrium analysis for a two-player version of the problem.

To achieve non-classical entanglement between distant points, we propose using a topological laser edge as a platform. By integrating this edge with artificial quantum emitters, we can achieve non-local photon correlations when the emitters interact with edge modes. Using a photonic Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain edge integrated with a semiconductor chip, we emulated this system with emitters created by femtosecond laser writing. These emitters, when placed beneath a narrow waveguide, were found to strongly couple with the one-dimensional mode. The result was enhanced and blue-shifted, while emitters that did not interact with the mode could be designed by adjusting the writing angle. Furthermore, we found that by emulating a photon loss model, we could achieve non-local photon correlations when the emitters' loss rates were below a critical threshold. By increasing this threshold with the waveguide's width, we took advantage of the topological protection of the edge mode to reduce emitters' loss rates and achieve non-local photon correlations when the emitters' loss rates were below this threshold. By integrating the emitters with the photonic SSH chain edge and the semiconductor chip, we could benefit from this protection to create non-local entanglement between the emitters.

This paper addresses the challenge of creating smooth paths for automated vehicles navigating through busy city crossings by examining how traffic lights impact vehicle movement. We focus on using traffic light phases - specifically yellow and red periods - to prioritize efficiency and safety when designing paths. Our proposed solution involves an optimization method that takes into account the position of the vehicle, the presence of a pedestrian crossing, and the efficiency of the traffic lights. We developed a solution to quickly find suitable processing times that allow the vehicle to stop before the crossing during a red light. Through simulation, we showed the effectiveness of our proposed method in providing smooth and safe paths for automated vehicles.

Interactive learning techniques, like text-based learning games for skill acquisition and text-based simulations for world modeling, have been developed.
However, the time-consuming nature of these tasks with native language processors limits their practical applications.
To overcome this limitation, we introduce TextWorldExpress - a family of ultra-fast (up to 10^6 times faster) pre-trained text world models using efficient neural machine translation world engines.
These models maintain strong execution capabilities (10^4 times faster) compared to their original counterparts.
We demonstrate that TWExpress can achieve similar performance to text-based reinforcement learning agents but at a significantly reduced training time.

Recent studies focused on tensor-oriented hardware designs have showcased significant potential for optimizing linear algebra operations through custom tensor hardware frameworks. However, these approaches often sacrifice high-level programming ease and flexibility in favor of performance gains, leaving a gap in creating tensor hardware that balances both factors. Addressing this limitation, we introduce a novel hardware architecture named FDHT-LSTM, which reimagines linear algebra operations using a combination of tensor decomposition and recurrent neural networks. Leveraging the properties of associative functions in TDLSTMs, FDHT-LSTM L-shift registers enable efficient processing of multiple tensor operations while accommodating various data types and precisions through modular design modules. Evaluations using the TensorStream benchmark demonstrate that our proposed hardware outperforms traditional tensor decomposed models and even standard GPU models in both operational throughput and energy efficiency, all while maintaining high program flexibility.

Current cutting-edge NLP models rely heavily on vast corpora of NLP data. This is particularly true for tasks requiring significant data, such as semantic role labeling. Our work explores a range of data augmentation techniques across various NLP settings and aims to rectify previous shortcomings by investigating their effectiveness in low-resource NLP scenarios. In our comprehensive study, we examine textual substitution, synonym replacement, synthesis-based, and translation-based augmentation methods. Our experiments on textual and synthesis-based strategies show promising results, particularly when using the ROVER and RANSAC post-processing techniques for handling introduction sentences generated in paraphrasing. As a result, we identify optimal strategies for multiple data augmentation methods and provide a basis for further research in resource-constrained NLP applications.

derived from four different, yet compatible perspectives: first from the viewpoint of vacuum

and finally from the effect of a U(1) gauge field on black holes in AdS. The resulting

A new proposal is introduced for using the path-integral quantum Monte Carlo method to calculate multiple electronic states of a molecular system within a coordinated framework. In this approach, the reference space for the quantum propagator is broken down into discrete vertical segments, with each segment representing a different quantum state. The key to determining the energy and orbital properties of a selected state lies in analyzing how the population of that segment evolves over time. Now, the reweighting of wavefunction segments can be redefined with consideration for both inter-state and intra-state factors. One major advantage of this framework is its natural handling of near-degenerate quantum levels - there's no need to assign arbitrary labeling to quantum states since they are instead described continuously across the model space. Using phosphine and nitrogen dioxide as examples, the approach effectively estimates both intrastate and interstate quantities for multiple states of these molecules. When applied to the $N_2O$ system, the methodSuccessfully models five lowest-lying quantum states using ab initionestimation parameters.

Let's consider a one-dimensional equicharacteristic local ring, R, that is excellent and equidimensional within a characteristic p > 0 environment. Assume H^0_(m)(R) has a finite zero submodule, and let's denote its elements as $\Gamma(x)$. For any ideal, I, we define $\Gamma_I(x)$ as the set of all elements in H^0_(m)(RExt_R^1(R/I), x) that map to zero under the local multiplication map. Furthermore, let's introduce $\tau_I$ as the set of elements in I that don't belong to any proper minimal reduction of I. It's crucial to note that $\tau_I$ can also be characterized as the union of all $\Gamma_I(x)$ for x belonging to H^0_(m)(R). Finally, let's introduce $\tau$ as the set of elements in R that don't belong to any minimal reduction of $ \bar{e}\x^+ (I) $ for any proper ideal, I, and let's show that this can be expressed as the union of all $\tau_I$ for I ranging over the set of $\frak m$-primary ideals in R.

We develop a game model for participants in a non-convex redispatch market, 
where we analyze the impact of an all-or-none ordering strategy on market 
dynamics. Our model enables us to demonstrate that this ordering design 
significantly influences grid operator's procurement decisions, potentially 
resulting in suboptimal solutions that grid operators would otherwise avoid. In 
contrast, GSO's procurement decisions have a negligible effect on the game's 
outcome. We further explore social welfare implications and propose efficient 
algorithms to resolve the game under different design scenarios. Numerical 
experiments validate our findings and illustrate the advantages of all-or-none 
design over gradual adjustment strategies.

This study determines Galois groups within the context of polynomial splitting fields in a p-adic function field Fq(t), under specific conditions, including a condition where all possible splitting types are compatible, as outlined by Fr\"olicher and Raynaud. Additionally, it makes progress on a conjecture regarding Galois groups in p-adic function fields, as proposed by S. Liao and provides the first non-maximal examples for such cases. S. Liao's findings also relate to S. Wolfram's work, as they show that certain compatible splitting types imply a specific transitive Galois group, while demonstrating that this implication does not always hold, and provide a formula for a compatible set of splitting types that leads to the symmetric group Sn, and parametric families for both Sn and proper subgroups of Sn.

My analysis focuses on identifying a rare decay of the Higgs boson into two photons in the high mass range, specifically between 250 and 800 GeV. To accurately pinpoint any potential new heavy resonance in the four-lepton final state, I utilized a shape analysis based on the invariant mass of the lepton system. To account for background events, I employed an exponential function in the 500-800 GeV range and a Gaussian distribution in the 200-500 GeV range. Given the difficulty in distinguishing signal from background in the four-lepton channel due to the presence of top quark pair production, I added a top quark quark pair contribution to the main background model. Considering the difficulty in measuring the four lepton centroid precisely with the detector, I incorporated a shift parameter in the mass variable in the likelihood function to account for this uncertainty. Making use of both the zero-tag and one-tag jet categories detected by the ATLAS detector, I utilized a combined set of data and simulated background events to conduct this analysis. Using 20.3 inverse femtobarns of Run 2 data at center-of-mass energies of 13 and 8 TeV, I found no evidence of a four lepton resonance beyond the Standard Model expectation. Based on these findings, I established 95% confidence level exclusion limits on the couplings of the Higgs boson to two photons in this

In models with additional scalar sectors, such as two-Higgs-doublet models, we investigate how precise, combined analyses of the Standard Model Higgs boson's properties can pinpoint new, heavy color-adjoint scalar particles that affect the diphoton decay channel. These findings suggest that even with current data, experiments can set confidence levels for such particles within a few hundred GeV to 1 TeV, and future colliders can determine their exact mass ranges. Additionally, we demonstrate that the Higgsstrahlung process and gamma-gamma decay channels are highly sensitive to such scalars, potentially making them easier to detect than other processes like HH production or HH-tbar, which typically have smaller constraints due to their smaller rates. As a result, HH-tbar might become the most productive area for discovering such scalars at the High-Luminosity LHC. Nevertheless, we also observed a potential loophole where such scalars could significantly increase the HH-tbar rate without affecting the HH ratio, and we found that current data can already provide confidence levels for these particles within a few hundred GeV to over 1 TeV.

A long-lasting cold period at Saturn's south pole summer stratosphere has led to unique atmospheric phenomena unlike those seen at Earth's north pole. A permanent cold air mass at Saturn's south pole has resulted in a continuously evolving northward boundary, in contrast to the rotating high-altitude cold ring observed at Earth's north pole. Additionally, there are differences in polar stratospheric temperatures and temperatures at the 100 mbar level in the southern polar regions during the winter, which reflect variations in atmospheric circulation strength. This has led to a developing polar night jet and distinct vortex structure, which eventually caused the disappearance of the southern polar night jet in late spring. This all occurred before Saturn's upcoming north pole winter, which has already seen the development of a persistent north pole stratospheric cold air mass with unique atmospheric ice clouds.

We investigate solutions to the Schrödinger equation in space with a boundary, 
examining conditions under which solution amplitude grows without limit in a short time. 
In confined spaces, specific, tighter constraints are required compared to open spaces. 
Our work demonstrates that the Morrey space criteria developed by Gidas and Sideris are still relevant in confined spaces. 
We also establish an alternative, more relevant version of the Sideris method based on potential behavior near the boundary, 
requiring less stringent conditions on solution decay at large distances.

This study introduces a fresh perspective from commutative algebra to examine the characteristics of commutative algebra over fields with different mathematical properties. It further establishes relationships between various aspects of negative and positive characteristic mathematics. Additionally, the Computation Museum website is created to demonstrate computation results from both characteristic-zero and positive-characteristic settings.

New time-dependent many-body perturbation theory has been applied to model metal-insulator transitions in strongly correlated systems. This research extends the Brueckner-Green diagonal expansion to second order for a semi-occupied spectrum and first order for a fully occupied绝缘体 spectrum. However, combining these approaches yields incorrect results due to violations of the 'sum rules of spectral weight'. These findings indicate that the breakdown of spectral weight sum rules is caused by divergent perturbation theory, rather than nonadiabatic effects. To resolve this issue, it is necessary for diagonal expansion terms to include a consistent set of self-energy inverse propagators. As an illustration, we analyzed a 1D Hubbard model metal and ultracold atom Bose-Hubbard insulator, finding that both insulating and metallic phases share the same spectral weight in their ground states. Nonetheless, metallic and insulating phases exhibit distinct spectral weights in their excited states. A perturbation to the Hamiltonian can induce a metal-insulator transition by shifting insulating excited states into the metallic spectrum.

Building on previous work, a quantum double dark-soliton state in one-dimensional Bose gases has been examined. We observe that, for a small interaction strength, this state can be characterized by a precise analytical density distribution. Furthermore, general features of the quasi-localized double-soliton structure are demonstrated to hold for any interaction strength. A sudden perturbation to the system's external potential is also analyzed, revealing that the nonadiabatic process can efficiently produce a multiple coexisting soliton state, with potential applications in creating complex solitary wave structures in laboratory settings.

The paper defines and examines symplectic double vector bundles in the context of their associated 2-symplectic structures on the corresponding double bundles. It establishes that not all symplectic double vector bundles possess a compatible second structure. Furthermore, the concept of a symplectic triple vector bundle is developed and related to the anti-autoequivalences of symplectic double vector bundles. Finally, the work builds upon prior research on symmetric multiple vector bundles by exploring their 2-symplectic counterparts.

A recent study reinterprets the connection between Kirillov's measure and geometric measure in Lie algebras and semisimple algebras. This new framework provides methods to compute the Plancherel and Harish-Chandra measures for orbits within linear algebraic sets defined by invariants, extending previous work to include these new implications. Moreover, this framework can be applied to compute the Plancherel and Harish-Chandra measures for a range of non-equivalent irreducible representations of $Sp(4,\mathbb{R})$.

At the synchrotron facilities, combining x-ray spectroscopy and scintroscopy is not common. Nonetheless, there are some areas of research across multiple fields that demand the use of x-ray double-dispersion spectroscopy or sticroscopy in order to analyze heavy elements in their complex many-body states. This study proposes an algorithm based on phase-reconstruction technology that is capable of utilizing data from both monochromators to isolate the relevant data within a comprehensive two-dimensional data set. As evidenced by both computer simulations and actual x-ray experiment results, this algorithm significantly enhances the efficiency of extracting energy spectra from energy projections, reducing the energy loss that typically occurs with traditional retrieval methods, and with single-shot experiments, it demonstrates the feasibility of capturing multiple energy spectra simultaneously with multiple central energies.

A key feature of the quantum code 1D parity check is its ability to protect against errors in a manner similar to how the Ising model with random bonds displays strong statistical correlations when looking at the spin-spin correlation in an external magnetic field. This code's effectiveness in measuring quantum logical operator stability can be enhanced by analyzing the effects of a time-independent disorder on the spin-spin correlation, which in turn resembles the behavior of a classical Ising model in a specific external field. As a result, the stability of the quantum logical operator can be more accurately assessed, which is a significant improvement over previous methods that involved studying the dynamics of a noisy quantum system and led to a more manageable relationship between the stability of the quantum logical operator and the classical spin-correlation length.

Using Tellurene and Tellurene-germanium quantum-well structures, we investigate the impact of tellurene layer strain and thickness on spectral properties, driven by an external chemical potential. Findings reveal that strain and tellurene thickness significantly impact spectral characteristics, allowing for a non-trivial gap of up to 1.5eV, deters Raman scattering above 2eV for high Raman gaps, and enables manipulation of a coexistence region between trivial and non-trivial gaps. Additionally, we examine the influence of a Tellurene layer's position in the quantum well, discovering it deters large gaps of over 2eV in Germanium and increases a coexistence region, resulting in multiple gap openings. Our work offers valuable insights for the development of Tellurene-based topological quantum-well and tellurene topological photonics applications.

A recent model has been modified to model the flow within a fractured porous medium by incorporating a single Dirac-$\beta$-function to block the pores of a matrix. The resulting system was analyzed to determine if blocking the flow through the fractures was a gradual process. The model's parameters include a dimensionless time, $t$, and two distinct flow velocities: $u_1$ and $u_2$. The model demonstrates that blocking the fractures is not a smooth process but rather involves two distinct regions separated by a sharp boundary that moves over time. In one region, the $\beta$ function remains constant at zero, while in the other region, it increases with time and is directly proportional to the square root of time. This boundary between the two regions is where $\beta$ jumps from zero to a constant value and moves at a constant velocity. As time progresses, the region where the $\beta$ function increases with time expands, and the model also indicates that there is a minimum value for this region. Furthermore, it has been shown that this minimum region is where the $\beta$ function is equal to three halves.

A new variant of a spin valve has been created which can switch between para- and ferromagnetic states depending on the presence of a low magnetic field. It is possible to switch between these states at exchange fields as low as several hundred oersteds and the spin valve exhibits distinct magnetic behavior in both states. The transition between the two states of magnetization can be achieved using an extremely low exchange field, and the change in magnetic properties results in a noticeable change in the spin valve's spin-valence effect. The magnetic configuration of this spin valve can also be altered by a coil-mounted electromagnet, and the magnetic state can be reversed without the need for a high exchange field. The spin valve's design uses two layers of materials with different magnetic anisotropies, and it is possible to create a new type of magnetic state called "compensated antiferromagnetic state" in which the net magnetization is low. This state of magnetization can be used to increase the sensitivity of magnetic sensors and make them more resistant to interference. The spin valve's design can also be used to create a controllable type of magnetic state that is similar to compensated antiferromagnetic state, and it is possible to achieve this in a wide range of exchange fields. This type of magnetization can be used to create a more sensitive and accurate type of spin valve sensor that is resistant to magnetic interference.

In formal decision-making scenarios, choosing a course of action is determined by a
predefined set of options and evaluation function that reflects the goal.
However in a related zero-sum game situation where history influences future possibilities for action and goal achievement is assessed based on action history rather than a single action choice. Simply plugging evaluation function into action option would result in ignoring the connection between actions and goals. To address this challenge we suggest a more intuitive goal representation method that can be used to calculate a more informed action recommendation that considers the relationship between actions and goals. This new method can be used to guide action selection for certain goal representation methods that make it easier to find the optimal action. Additionally we show how this method can be applied to a specific goal representation method and demonstrate its advantage over a more common approach through an example and further support through theoretical and empirical analysis.

The presence of complex semantic relationships in written and spoken language, 
mediated by discourse markers, significantly influences how we perceive and 
interpret our surroundings and each other. Nevertheless, annotating these subtle 
nuances in text remains a challenging task. To facilitate this, I have created a 
new, comprehensive dataset called DiscSense, which consists of over 13,000 
annotated instances of discourse markers and the subtle semantic relationships 
they convey within Wikipedia articles. DiscSense is uniquely valuable as it 
offers a detailed classification of discourse markers based on the semantic 
relationships they encode, making it an essential resource for a wide array of 
tasks, including the detection and detection+classification of these subtle 
semantic relationships in text.

A distinct energy gap separates nonradiative decay and bandgap energy in certain insulators doped with transition metal ions. According to the Mott-Seitz model, this difference arises from a decay process where a d-electron is excited from a doubly occupied orbital, transferring energy to the lattice and resulting in a charge transfer. This model can be explained by considering the difference in confinement between the holes in the host crystal and the dopant ion. A similar mechanism may apply to group III ions like Cr3+, but a more complex excitation is required, involving the simultaneous excitation of multiple phonons to absorb the large energy gap. This is because charge transfer in this case is accompanied by an increase in lattice energy, rather than a decrease.

A new algorithm for training multilayer perceptrons is outlined in this paper, which directly solves the error surface equation of the network. Unlike traditional methods that rely on linearized error approximations, our algorithm identifies an exact error equation for any given network configuration, enabling a precise computation of error signals. These signals are used to update network weights in a manner proportional to them. Our approach eliminates the need for a training algorithm by accurately calculating error propagation and utilizing a stochastic weight update method. We demonstrate our algorithm's performance on the XOR problem and the Iris dataset with promising results.

A specific homeomorphism-homotopy model is examined, where the domain and target spaces are defined by a spherical surface and a solid ball respectively. The energy calculation is modified to account for a deformation of the spherical surface within the ball's interior. Due to the non-trivial homotopy properties of the space, energy-favorable configurations for certain topological twists are identified. These twists correspond to magnetic skyrmions. It's discovered that not all magnetic skyrmions belong to a single topological class; rather, they are divided into distinct classes based on their homotopy properties. A more detailed analysis shows that these properties are determined by a specific homotopy group and influence both the topological class and energy of the magnetic skyrmions. All aspects, including the total energy, per-unit-length potential energy, and balance between these energies are explained through a breakdown into two components. One component represents the energy of a magnetic skyrmion in a 3D ball's interior, while the other is derived from the surface integral of this component's difference from its equilibrium state. The model's predictions are supported by experimental data and can be applied to design magnetic skyrmions with specific topological properties for their practical applications.

Using a minimal basis set of s and p Gaussian functions centered on nuclei, a comprehensive set of ~10^6 test functions was created to evaluate the accuracy of Hartree-Fock and density functional theory (DFT) with Gaussian-type functions for both diatomic molecules and atomic systems up to Krash. When normalized to a maximum nuclear separation of R=2.0 bohr, the all-electron basis set required to achieve a 10^-4 energy precision via HF-Fock transformation for CO2 was reduced from the conventional 50 Gaussian functions per function to just 12 functions. In contrast, for H2 at R=8.0 bohr, convergence to the exact HF energy within 10^-4 was only achievable with 50 Gaussian functions per function. Similarly, for Kr, a 50-Gaussian-function-basis-set yielded a HF energy of -391.9866, deviating by 0.0146 from the exact value, indicating a need for an augmented basis set to achieve the desired precision. Notably, both HF and DFT exhibit similar convergence patterns. To address this, a revised, basis-set-independent definition of screening is advocated to accurately assess Coulomb correlation within the HF framework.

A sudden transition to synchronization in systems that experience a structural change has been observed in various fields. We present a comprehensive theory to explain explosive synchronization transitions in networks with both dynamic and static properties. Our derived condition for hysteresis in such systems agrees well with simulation results. Notably, we find that structural and dynamic disruptions often co-occur and that their interaction significantly impacts the synchronization behavior of the system. We also explore the implications of this co-occurrence on the hysteresis effect and provide a case where our model yields an enhanced understanding of the dynamics at play.

In low-rong approximation problems, we often encounter intricate geometries that pose significant challenges to optimization. To address this, we propose a method for computing local geodesic convexity and strong convexity/smoothness properties under the assumption of restricted strong convexity and smoothness. By leveraging these characteristics, we develop efficient bounds for the factorized objective's geometry, which are then applied to identify basins of linear and superlinear convergence for a range of problems, including kernelized logistic regression, PCA, and semi-supervised learning. Our findings also reveal distinct patterns of convergence for locally unique and non-uniquely identifiable solutions.

The edge chromatic number of a graph $G$, denoted $\chi_e(G)$, refers to partitioning the edges of $G$ into sets where no two adjacent edges are in the same set. A coloring meeting this criterion is termed proper edge-coloring. Additionally, a coloring is considered strong if not only adjacent edges but also those with a short path between their endpoints have different colors. Specifically, every edge must share a color with all other edges in the same color set, with a short path between them not present in $G$. In 1990, Gyárfás proposed a hypothesis that the minimum number of colors needed for strong edge-coloring does not exceed $(2\Delta-1)(\Delta+1)$, with equality achievable only when $\Delta=3$. This hypothesis was disproven by Faudree, Schelp, and others in 2004 who found a bipartite graph with maximum degree 3 for which the minimum number of colors needed for strong edge-coloring does not exceed $(2\Delta-1)(\Delta+1)-1$. This study further investigates whether additional colors are required for bipartite graphs with a maximum degree higher than 3, with a focus on bipartite graphs where $\Delta=4$. It is shown that the hypothesis does not hold for $\Delta=4$ and the upper bound can be reduced to $2\Delta^2-5\Delta+4$. This study

Traditional approaches to calculating gravitational-wave backgrounds typically assume random phase relationships, which may break down in scenarios involving coherent gravitational waves. The presence of heavy particles in the universe's early stages could slow down phase de-correlation, increasing the GW signal's amplitude and altering its spectral features. This effect becomes significant for particles with masses between $10^{-7}$eV and $10^{-4}$eV and could provide an observational means to determine the properties of these particles, such as their mass and how many species they comprise. One such particle candidate is the axion, and we have identified the most sensitive current experiments for GWs, including the B-mode polarization of the cosmic microwave background and atomic clock measurements of the sum of axion-like particle masses. We have also identified the SAGE antenna as the GW detector with the greatest potential to detect the coherent GW signal generated by the axion, and we have outlined the future antenna designs required to achieve this goal.

Recent research has shown that swarms of microswimmers can show collective behavior known as the snowman-like effect. To better understand this phenomenon, a theoretical model based on active helical dynamics was developed. This model accounts for individual swimmers moving in a helical pattern, including those that rotate in opposite directions. By creating a statistical snapshot of swimmers in a confined space, researchers found that swimmers typically align in clusters but can form two distinct groups if they rotate in opposite directions. Furthermore, they identified a key feature of microswimmer movement called the snowman-like effect, or streamer effect, which creates a forward flow that aids the swarms' collective behavior. This model provides insight into the active helical dynamics of swarms and paves the way for more advanced studies of microswimmers in various environments.

This study employs a genetic algorithm through the Co-alternative Reactions Model, to tackle the issue of avoiding a "Finger Game" equivalent in a matrix game with multiple options. It reveals that in a slow learning process, the anticipated distance from Nash Equilibrium is comparable whether learning is individual or collective. Conversely, in a fast learning process, the anticipated distance is greater in the latter case. Furthermore, this study examines dynamic learning processes in large populations and determines the anticipated distance from Nash Equilibrium based on a specific strategy's long-term frequency.

To protect personal data from illegal access, another party, or even unintentionally, extracting useful information from text is crucial. Thanks to advancements in natural language processing, we can now use existing tools to identify security concepts within text. However, we still lack a comprehensive system that utilizes the full potential of current NLP advancements for the security extraction process. We propose an innovative approach that combines a bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory network with a security-aware dataset and a flexible, security-focused ensemble method. We evaluate our approach using the CyberGuard Dataset and outperform other commonly used NLP models, demonstrating the effectiveness of our method. All experiments and codes associated with this research are available on GitHub.

We've developed a new model that integrates the choice of extreme opinions and coexistence of conflicting views observed in societal conflicts. Combining mean field theories from this model yields equations that are directly comparable to their Ising model counterparts, allowing us to treat opinion dynamics and extreme behaviors through a unified spin model framework. Despite this, we've developed a mixed model that better captures key characteristics of extreme opinions and conflict dynamics, which we can now investigate using established statistical physics methods. Analyzing a variant of this model with stochastic update rules reveals that, on average, we see the expected level of magnetization but unexpected variability in fluctuations. Similarly, we find that magnetic susceptibility displays an expected average level but unexpectedly varied fluctuations. Subsequently, we've established that the curvature of the free energy landscape determines not just the average levels of magnetization and coexistence but also extreme variability in these values.

The COVID-19 virus can be transmitted through respiratory droplets expelled by infected individuals, with droplet sizes significantly influencing infection spread. Although some research has modeled airborne disease transmission, many studies lack experimental validation, especially in environments where people are in close proximity. We developed a method to track multiple colored droplets released into a room using high-speed video, then used this technique to test how droplets behave under various conditions relevant to COVID-19 infection spread. Our experiments revealed a new pattern of suspended droplet settling, which we used to verify and extend the validity of an existing model. The outcomes demonstrate that in certain environments, larger populations of smaller droplets may remain suspended longer than smaller droplets. Our method provides valuable insights into understanding the spread of viruses with shorter transmission lifespans.

Inverse and ill-posed problems are complex challenges prevalent in a wide range of applications, including remote sensing, spectroscopy, and source reconstruction. Their solutions typically rely on statistical approaches utilizing Bayesian inference, optimal control, or compressive sensing techniques. A novel method employing learning approximations through neural networks has recently gained significant interest due to its capacity to handle high-dimensional problems, its application-specific generalizability, and its inherent stability. Deep learning's universality theorem has been proven, and recent studies have explored optimizing loss functions to reconstruct signals from incomplete measurements or spectral data. Additionally, transfer learning has been proposed to create reusable neural network stabilizers for tomographic reconstruction from sparse data. Furthermore, neural networks have been employed in optimal control to solve the inverse Stokes problem and reconstruct complex geometries from partial flow field measurements.

This study focuses on computing both ordinary and symbolic power coverages of the ideal edges in oriented graphs, considering their weight system. If the graph remains cycle-free, we determine a criterion for when the ordinary and symbolic powers become equivalent. Additionally, we propose and partially solve the problem for another key edge ideal without cycles. This solution also addresses and resolves a related question from previous research.

Modern neural networks are vulnerable to silent data corruptions, which can be triggered by carefully crafted input gradients that exploit floating-point operations' limited precision. These operations cause some data updates to be lost during training, and although researchers have developed various training restriction methods to mitigate this issue, most of them rely on assumptions of uniform data clip points that are not present in real systems. This paper introduces a new approach called non-uniform range restriction that realistically models data loss and allows for the efficient generation of non-uniform clip points. This method's effectiveness has been demonstrated by utilizing it in two practical applications: training and inference. Specifically, using non-uniform range restriction during training significantly improves the ability of neural networks to generalize, while applying it during inference makes the network's predictions more robust and efficient to compute.

Decentralized ledger technology, with its inherent security features like graph algorithms, can be effectively utilized to optimize netting in the financial sector. In this study, we offer a netting framework that offers a unified solution for financial institutions to manage their payment obligations, providing a more cost-effective and efficient method to minimize costs by netting payments across multiple institutions. This model provides flexibility by providing separate solutions for different types of payments, including bilateral agreements, foreign exchange triangles, and open market transactions. Our framework can also provide network-based solutions for different scenarios. Notably, our netting strategy can be further enhanced by incorporating a selective default mechanism, which allows for the prioritization of more critical financial institutions during times of economic instability. With this approach, we can develop a protocol to prevent systemic risks and financial instability even in cases where total debt exceeds the combined value of all assets.

We investigate the Jordanian twist both in its basic form and a broader variation. Our analysis reveals that a broader twist not only inherits properties from the simpler twist but also ensures compatibility with a classical Jordanian twist.

A new approach is proposed that combines character-level and word-level features using an insertion-based convolutional neural network interface for name tagging in low-resource languages. This approach, referred to as the Coarse-to-Fine (C2F) approach, refines character-level labels by incorporating word-level information. To enhance performance further, an extended version called the C2F+ approach adds character-level features derived from BC54 pre-trained word vectors. Notably, the proposed methods achieve a 2x improvement in performance over a baseline for name tagging in languages with limited data. Furthermore, the proposed approaches are successfully applied to annotate open-domain person name data in German, which serves as a foundation for developing machine-readable disambiguation corpora in various languages.

Researchers have examined how particles produced in the collisions of various particles at a high energy level compare to each other. They found that as the collision scale increases from smaller particles like protons to heavier ions like lead, the ratios of different particles change in a similar manner to heavy ions colliding at a lower energy level. This observation across different collisions suggests that quantum chromodynamics matter, influenced by a phenomenon known as color glass condensate, may also occur in the collisions of heavy ions at even higher energy levels.

This study investigates dialogue state tracking models trained on datasets with misclassified labels, a common issue in real-world data. We assess the robustness of various model architectures by training and testing them on the golden Dataspace and a newly created erasure Dataspace, where names have been intentionally mislabeled. Our findings show that most model designs are susceptible to noisy labels, with recurrent neural network-based models being particularly vulnerable. Surprisingly, the dense vector representation model achieved better results than the other transformer-based models. We also conducted further experiments to understand how label noise affects model performance and identified potential improvements, such as using filter layers and carefully selecting loss functions. Our results offer valuable insights into developing dialogue state tracking systems that can be relied upon in real-world applications.

We investigate how the structure of cities impacts civil disturbances in environments governed by social forces. To study this, we incorporate spatial characteristics of various cities into a simulation and measure time-dependent fluctuations in agitation levels. By analyzing both temporal variability and spatial patterns of unrest, we reveal that the topological features of a city follow a universal principle that holds true across different urban landscapes. This topological structure becomes embedded in the dynamics of unrest, exhibiting a specific scaling behavior. Furthermore, we observe that specific aspects of urban design, like compactness and the distribution of open spaces, play a role in shaping the spread of unrest. To support our findings, we present a theoretical model using a stochastic process, which can predict these behaviors and is backed by real-world data.

To assess a key measurement related to star formation, specifically the Br$\beta$ luminosity, we expanded upon the capabilities of the star formation rate framework developed with Prospector. By incorporating the $\log \lambda$ luminosity for various spectral regions, we were able to verify the accuracy of the derived star formation rates and $\lambda 4350$ emission line luminosies for a range of simulated galaxies. We used the $\chi^2$ values for two specific wavelength intervals as luminosity constraints, utilizing both wide and narrow filters centered around $\lambda 4350$. We found that, in most cases, Prospector derived accurate measurements for both H$\beta$ and Br$\beta$ luminosities, even in scenarios where the abundance of ionized oxygen was low, which is typical for massive galaxies. However, we also identified scenarios where Prospector could struggle to derive accurate Br$\beta$ luminosities. These scenarios included situations where the abundance of Br$\beta$ was significantly lower than H$\beta$ due to variations in ionized gas excitation conditions or topological effects within the HII regions. We found that, in these instances, adding observational Br$\beta$ data into the analysis could serve as a prior constraint to counteract this tendency. This work examines a summary of key findings related to the connection between
positive polynomials and the geometry of Gram matrices. Specifically, we will
discuss how the number of components in a positive polynomial's sum of squares
decomposition is influenced by the rank of matrices within the Gram spectrahedron.
Our discussion will also cover recent studies that analyze the Gram spectrahedron's
rank and geometry using combinatorial methods, as well as the connection between
Gram matrix rank and control theory realizations. Finally, we will summarize open
problems that require further investigation at the conclusion.

This report summarizes key findings from the FASERν experiment's first operational dataset, acquired during the run at FSRun30 with the Large Hadron Collider in 2022. Despite the experimental setup being live for only 16.5 days, a total of 65 neutrino interactions were detected, consistent with theoretical predictions. Utilizing this dataset in conjunction with prior constraints from the FASER collaboration, a more precise limit was imposed on the neutrino non-unitarity matrix, which is now more restrictive than the existing constraints on the lepton unitarity derived from the quark sector by a factor of four. Notably, this limit is not influenced by neutrino mass. To fully exploit the detection capabilities of the FASERν experiment, an upgrade known as FASERν2 has been proposed, featuring a more sensitive detector and the ability to distinguish between different neutrino types through charge identification, which would significantly enhance the experiment's sensitivity over the next decade. Upgrades such as these would be utilized during runs at the High Luminosity LHC.

We have developed a symbolic decision procedure to check language containment between regular expressions. This procedure builds on a previous work by A. Kuich at https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.04291, which used a regular expression-based simplification based on Brzozowski's operator for a specific language property. Our approach extends this framework a factor by incorporating automata-based operations on labeled products, allowing a more accurate checking of containment for regular expressions.

Disabling the VIO system can quickly deplete navigation estimates, 
necessitating VIO models capable of learning from video input alone. 
To achieve this, we transform conventional Tightly Coupled VIO (TC-VIO) 
systems into VIO deep learning (VIO-DL) models, leveraging VIO ground truth 
data to train VIO-DL models. Leveraging a VIO-DL model enables a VIO system 
to recover from failures, such as VIO/GPS/degradation, utilizing VIO 
data to refine the robot's navigation estimate. Furthermore, VIO system 
failures are no longer a cause for concern, as VIO data is used to 
refine the robot's navigation estimate even when VIO fails. 
However, VIO-DL models typically rely on VIO ground truth data for training, 
which is not always feasible in real-world scenarios. Thus, we introduce 
VIO-DL models trained without VIO ground truth (VIO-DL NVG), utilizing 
VIO sensor outputs and existing navigation estimates to train the model. 
These VIO-DL models learn to replace VIO algorithms and leverage their 
machine learning-based VIO solution to integrate VIO data into the 
navigation estimator. The proposed VIO-DL NVG framework is evaluated on VIO 
and GPS degradation data from two mobile robots in diverse outdoor and
