We establish a generalized version of an existing constraint on the edge-coloring required to ensure every monochromatic subgraph contains a specific type of shape. For the case of a triangle, our finding matches the existing formula. However, for shapes that are not triangles, a generalized version of our formula can be applied. Additionally, we prove several specific examples, including a lower bound that is unbreakable and both exact upper bounds that are reversible.

We investigated the three-dimensional density distribution in the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) using a anisotropic power model, which was applied to a vast dataset of over two million GCIs from a 1.3km/s bandwidth density map. The results demonstrated significant anisotropy in the density structure, particularly within 100pc scales. The anisotropy decreased with increasing scale and was not present beyond 300pc scale. The anisotropic structure aligns with the CMZ's geometry, where long bars and short arcs are oriented perpendicular to each other. Notably, Swartzchild's $1/r^4$ law was found to hold within 100pc scale but broke down beyond this scale. A similar pattern was observed in the velocity dispersion of GCI's gas velocities, which also transitioned from an anisotropic to an isotropic structure beyond 300pc scale. A similar scale was observed for the transition from Newtonian to non-Newtonian gravitational potential. The CMZ's 300pc scale may mark the boundary of a bound structure, which is consistent with the 200-500pc size of the Galactic bulge's bar.

Human-computer interactions using face recognition have a significant advantage
over methods requiring the entire face, as users only need to direct their gaze
towards the screen. Building on this concept, a novel face detection system has been
developed that only requires a part of the face, focusing on the eye region. This
new system utilizes a eye-centric deep learning framework that processes a part of the
face with a CNN to detect the user's attention. To improve performance and focus on
accurate gaze detection, a CNN-based classifier called EF-Net was proposed. By
employing data augmentation techniques and transferring knowledge from pre-trained
models, EF-Net achieved exceptional results with a 93.55% accuracy on the proposed
eye-focused detection dataset. These enhancements led to a 5.8% increase in
accuracy compared to the baseline method. The improved system has been successfully
prototyped and exhibits a 93.55% accuracy, representing a response time of 217ms.

This study compares the robustness of determining masses in both single and multiple qubit systems, while also single and feshing qutrit systems against two types of noise. While two types of coherent noises were considered, only dephasing and bit-flip noises were considered. It is found that single and three-level qutrit systems are more tolerant to bit-flip noise than both single and two-level qubit systems. Conversely, systems are more tolerant to dephasing noise when there is less than 50% probability of a bit-flip. It's also found that double qubit single and three-level qutrit systems are more tolerant to dephasing and bit-flip noises, respectively. Furthermore, this study provides optimal single and double unitary dynamics for both single and two-level systems.

Our recent discoveries indicate that the minimum energy required for annihilation radiation at 5.11 MeV can be surpassed by over 30% polarized positrons, which in turn may have implications in cosmology and a deeper comprehension of the universe's nature. Given this finding, it becomes essential to increase the positron polarization levels even further. In light of this requirement, we have identified a suitable mechanism - the interaction of a polarized photon with a copper target - which generates highly spin-dependent, spin-dependent negative electrons that can be converted into highly polarized positrons through process of positronization, thereby meeting the necessary criteria.

We've developed a new approach to Olshanskii's 2-sphere construction in polynomial diameter, making it possible to add an entire class of non-amenable, torsion-free nilpotent subgroups of any given polynomial order to the constructed groups. Through this modification, we can preserve the polynomial diameter property while increasing the number of conjugacy classes within a specific nilpotent subgroup to match that of the original construction.

This research focuses on detecting temperature changes as small as 0.1 degrees Celsius using a new circuit. The invention uses three different ways of storing electrical charges in a single component that is very sensitive to temperature but unaffected by other factors like voltage. By using a special mathematical method and a look-up table, the circuit can precisely measure the temperature based on the data from the three storage areas. The proposed design is so sensitive that it can detect even the smallest temperature changes, which is impressive considering it is based on simple and well-tested principles. Furthermore, a new way of combining existing storage methods results in a new kind of sensor with excellent temperature detection capabilities but complete immunity to interference from other factors. As a result, this new approach outperforms many other types of sensors of its kind.

Three-dimensional mean-field models featuring a self-sustaining mutual interaction between magnetic field components and flow have been studied for over a decade. However, previous models lacked a key feature found in actual magnetic field components: the mutual stabilization provided by a twisted torus geometry. Our research employed a specific twisted torus configuration in a spherical zone, where we calculated the stability limits through a linear stability analysis in a time-independent scenario. Our findings revealed that the range of magnetic field configurations sustained by this arrangement was significantly larger than that of non-interacting configurations, indicating that twisted torus geometries could better represent the range of magnetic field configurations maintained by self-sustaining stellar dynamo processes. Furthermore, we found that this mutual stabilization effect was also present in more complex scenarios including rotation and convection.

When moving from strong to weak coupling, AdS/CFT correspondence allows us to employ a hydrodynamic description of a conformal fluid with high viscosity. Using a higher-derivative extension of AdS gravity, we can establish a direct connection between renormalization group equations and the dynamics of an irreversibly evolving fluid. This connection enables us to utilize domain wall solutions as a type of "relaxation time approximation" and non-linear domain wall solutions as a "two-fluid approximation." These approximations lead to modified non-linear differential equations and linearized hyperbolic PDEs, respectively, both of which incorporate a non-linear dilaton potential. This connection provides a framework to address specific renormalization group flows, such as those from non-supersymmetric type IIB supergravity and the corresponding type IIA theory, by describing them as evolving fluid solutions. By introducing effective pressures and densities, we can derive the equation of state for these flows and find that they are characterized by a specific, finite viscosity-to-density ratio. This ratio is approximately $1.84$ for type IIB and approximately $1.74$ for type IIA, with both values being universal across different initial conditions. These findings provide a framework to address the issue of irreversible renormalization group flow and the resolution of the RG paradox, with both issues being fundamentally linked to the irreversibility of thermodynamic flow and the loss of unitarity.

When searching for music lyrics or audio, a music search engine proves more efficient than standard web searches. To create such a engine for general audiences, we need accessible music lyrics data. After analyzing various music lyrics sources, we processed and compiled a comprehensive music lyrics dataset containing nearly 200 million annotations from multiple languages on Weibo. Named CDRC-200, this dataset was designed around user feedback and includes an annotation tool to encourage community contributions.

If the topological groupoid $G$ has a product structure, a non-trivial topological groupoid extension of $G$ exists, forming a short exact sequence in topological groupoids. This product structure topological groupoid extension corresponds to a specific mathematical object - a gerbe over a topological stack. In a general topological setting, a significant relationship is revealed between topological groupoid extensions and a topological stack object known as a 'stacky' or 'stacky' bundle.

Observations of submillimeter lines from three massive stars forming in T Monocerotis indicate a shared timing of core collapse across the region, suggesting a common origin. To understand the core growth over time, a model is developed using data from the ALMA observations of SMM 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8 as well as AtMon 1a,b in Monoceros Star Forming Region. Core masses are calculated and analyzed in relation to their corresponding stellar masses. The study finds core masses range from $0.04-0.64 M_{\odot}$ and at 4.1Myr, core masses proportionally match the formed stellar masses. However, not all core precursors lead to the same type of stars. Some cores associated with less massive stars may have undergone secondary mass accumulation or could have been initially more massive. This research provides a framework for core growth analysis and supports the idea of core mass determining the final stellar mass under equal physical conditions.

The paper establishes a dynamic Godel algebra under a Clopen operator based on a finite structure known as a forest. Conversely, every finite algebra of this type can be linked to a finite forest through duality. The paper explores key properties of these algebras and reveals that subalgebras of the algebra in question are isomorphic to direct products of finite algebras, each derived from a specific forest. Moreover, the subalgebras whose duals are transitively closed within the forest's order provide sufficient conditions. Finally, the paper defines the spectrum of a finite Godel algebra and characterizes it using the forest structure.

A 3D point cloud LiDAR classification task is performed without assigning class labels to individual points, instead only labeling local regions known as patches.

To evaluate various label assignment strategies, we experimented with different methods including patch-level labeling, object-based labeling and a new hierarchy-based labeling strategy.

We also evaluated the impact of labeling different objects with the same class and objects with distinct class labels in the same patch.

Our results show that context from neighboring points significantly influences classification performance and that our proposed hierarchy-based labeling method strategy outperforms other methods.

To demonstrate practical applications, we used our hierarchy-based labeling strategy to evaluate LiDAR classes in large-scale scenes and a self-driving car's interior.

This study explores the impact of differentiation and integration on the definiteness of zonal functions defined on the n-dimensional sphere. It retains key properties, referencing computations from lower-dimensional spheres. Moreover, it derives formulas for differentiated and integrated zonal functions from the n-dimensional sphere.

Recent studies have suggested a connection between the ultra-high-energy cosmic rays and the highest-energy neutrinos that the Earth has detected. Using our established theoretical framework, we have re-evaluated this link in light of new data from various cosmic ray observatories, including IceCube and ANTARES. By combining our model's predictions with actual observations from seven GrB events detected by the LHCd collaboration, we have found the best fit parameters and calculated a 95% confidence interval. In doing so, we have found evidence suggesting the correlation posited by Abraham et al. is unlikely, as it contradicts our model's predictions and is rejected with statistical significance. Consequently, this correlation is now considered excluded within a certain confidence level.

We have developed a quantitative assessment method for evaluating the surface roughness
quantified by the 'roughness factor' $\gamma$ within the context of Euclidean space.
This measurement is factorized into two components - $\gamma = \rho \times \eta$.
Here, $\rho$ quantifies the frequency of non-short edges, while $\eta$ measures the
average length of these edges.
To obtain $\gamma$ we first calculate $\rho$ and $\eta$ separately using distinct
approaches and then multiply them.
The calculation of $\rho$ is based on the definition of a 'short edge' and involves
statistical analysis of edge distribution.
The calculation of $\eta$ is determined by comparing the minimal distances between
opposite plate bubbles in a liquid foam to the total path length of these distances.
The proposed quantification method of $\gamma$ has been tested on 3D printed models
and 3D reconstructed data from micro-CT scans of deactivated foams.
It is established that $\gamma$ can effectively differentiate between various types
of non-rigid surface deformations in foams.

Deep learning-based convolutional neural networks have surpassed traditional methods in classification tasks due to their impressive feature extraction capabilities. However, these capabilities are further enhanced when combined with ensemble techniques, which create multiple classifiers to minimize classification difficulties. This study proposes a novel pyramid ensemble classification framework using unified backpropagation learning for unified implementation and optimization of all ensemble members. Additionally, we introduce an adaptive fusion strategy that dynamically adjusts feature weights from each classifier based on their individual difficulties. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the superiority of our pyramid ensemble framework over other ensemble methods and state-of-the-art classification framerworks across three distinct datasets.

In a rotating gap-filling scenario known as the rotating Hele-Shaw problem, there are multiple possible configurations: a singular ray, a smooth curve, a filled area, and a gap extending to the corner. Research by Saffman and Taylor in 1984, as well as Hales in 2005, have demonstrated that for low rotation rates, a singular ray remains stable, whereas moderate to high rates result in curve formation. A study by S. G. Khruslov and A. V. Mel'nikov in 2013, revealed that a curve can transform into a filled area through a Snail-to-Blob instability. The membrane tension introduces additional dynamics, causing the Khruslov-Mel'nikov instability to give way to an instability of the filled state and results in a time when a gap appears. The threshold tension beyond which the singular ray starts to break up is determined. The dynamics near this threshold have been modeled and the resulting time-dependent angle has been shown to follow a power law.

A new interpretation of dissipated work in nonequilibrium thermodynamics has been proposed through a rigorous derivation based on a master equation approach. This derivation provides a clear definition of internal work at a nonequilibrium steady state, defining it as a change in a microstate's energy resulting from modifications to the Hamiltonian, minus any energy changes caused by a shift in the microstate probability distribution. When averaged, this internal work yields the traditional nonequilibrium dissipated work. However, at an individual system instance level, measured work performed on a system does not necessarily equal internal work due to a fluctuation term originating from the probability distribution's change. This derived definition of internal work is general and can be applied to various scenarios, including sudden changes in Hamiltonians, linear nonequilibrium thermodynamics applications, and switch-based information processing.

We used high-resolution ALMA data to measure the abundance ratios of two complex hydrocarbons, finding a ratio of 0.25 for cyclopentadiene and 1.4 for isoprene between their respective molecular forms. In contrast, for benzene, the CCH to CN ratio is 1.0. These findings imply that both stable and less stable hydrocarbon formations coexist in the region surrounding V883 Ceti.

In recent years Look-Ahead Attention has seen significant success in enhancing neural machine translation performance. Despite its apparent effectiveness, its underlying theory of attention remains unclear. By examining cyclically generated look-ahead data, we've discovered that look-ahead information is largely redundant and that attention weights assigned to it tend to be minimal. To further investigate this phenomenon, we've created the Uniform Look-Ahead attention variant and found that models using it achieve similar performance to those employing Look-Ahead Attention. This investigation into the look-ahead theory has yielded valuable insights that have performance implications for CACT and cross-lingual domain adaptation.

The rising complexity and cost of computers have made it necessary to use multiple machines in concert to handle tasks that grid computing technology can provide. This approach has significant implications for both technology and society, which calls for a user-centered and society-aware approach to its advancement. This is best achieved through open-source, nonproprietary methodologies that promote innovation, freedom, and inclusivity in the field. A key aspect of open-source grid computing technologies is incorporating features from grand-challenge-oriented architectures like Flocker. These architectures, designed for collaborative research projects, can serve as effective starting points for developing grid computing features, including those related to account management and authorization. This can also be done through a federated approach using accounts and authorizations that are compatible with existing Internet standards. As an example, a federated authorization system has been created using Linux MANTRA's ZDRAFTA framework in collaboration with CERN's grid computing infrastructure, showcasing the potential for successful implementation of grid computing features through the use of authorizations across multiple sites. This case study showcases how a translational approach, in combination with a federated approach, can lead to a deeper understanding and more effective application of grid computing features. This implies that the development and promotion of grid computing technologies should embrace and facilitate the creation of decentralized applications (P2P apps) to ensure their long-term success.

A new class of holographic models addresses these issues and provides solutions for dark matter's nature and the universe's evolution. A suitable match between theoretical predictions and observational data from the Euclid mission is predicted by an original model formulation. Using a variation of the Jercic-Mota parameter space, a dual relation is predicted between the model's characteristics and a measurable parameter. Key findings include a slowly declining equation of state parameter over time, with an optimal value aligning closely with observed data at present, and the model's presence in the power spectrum being under a minimal threshold. Furthermore, with appropriate parameters, an excellent match is achieved between model predictions and $\sigma_8$ observations, matchingly reflecting the universe's clumpiness.

A deep learning tool's predictive capabilities are showcased in comparison to multiple existing models, highlighting complexity variations and a match with Baryon Acoustic Oscillations data. The model's predictions are validated against future redshift data available to the Euclid mission.

It has been suggested that curiosity can be influenced by peers, but current understanding of its core drivers remains limited. To address this gap, we present a novel approach based on a variation of the effort-based utility model which allows us to derive a new, intuitive metric for peer impact based on shared interests and exposure. Using large-scale data from nearly one million users on nearly ten million programming challenges, we tested this approach and found strong evidence that peers significantly impact curiosity, also discovering variations in this effect across different contexts and scales. Additionally, our model helps us better grasp the dynamics of curiosity itself.

When scaling beyond two-dimensional spatial data, graph Matérn processes enable
efficient scaling of covariance calculations while maintaining smoothness. By
extending to graph modifications, various matricial forms are produced that
realize the graph Matérn process and allow efficient implementation in non-
conjugate learning settings using mini-batch techniques. These implementations
support parallelization and storage-efficient computation of posterior
distributions. By contrast to other graph Matérn implementations, our approach
is suitable for use with standard stochastic gradient methods.

As cities expand, effectively monitoring urban environments becomes increasingly difficult. The prevalence of ridesourcing vehicles offers a potential solution, as their widespread use on city streets enables them to gather valuable sensory data. However, determining the most efficient way to deploy this data for effective environmental monitoring remains an unresolved challenge. Our research aims to identify the optimal ridesourcing fleet size and develop a novel communication protocol to enhance and reliably collect data for sensing coverage and monitoring performance. Through numerical analysis, we analyze different approaches to coverage collection, comparing their effectiveness in real-world scenarios. Our results demonstrate that our protocol achieves reliable coverage collection with a significantly smaller fleet than previously assumed. Furthermore, our approach enables efficient data collection for cities of moderate to large scale, highlighting the potential of using mobile sensors to environmentally monitor urban areas.

Our study investigates the implications of limits set by $J/\psi \to \text{invisible}$ decays on dark matter interactions with nucleons, specifically examining cases where J/psi decays result in J/psi resonances production via t-channel scattering mediated by dark photons. By combining theoretical amplitudes with experimental constraints from proton-scattering experiments and $e^+e^-$-collisions, our research demonstrates that certain dark matter parameters can be ruled out which were previously thought to be consistent with current data and could potentially explain the excess observed in the $\gamma\gamma$ spectrum from the Galactic Center. Furthermore, theories that facilitate nucleon-scattering mediated by dark photons can facilitate regions of the parameter space that could be detected by next-generation dark matter detectors and potentially explain the excess observed in spin-independent electron scattering experiments.

Recent research has shown that state space models, specifically Variational Autoencoders and State Space Linear Models, can effectively capture the essence of signal processing and linear time-invariant filters. These models utilize the discretization of first-order differential equations or their continuous equivalents to provide a flexible and interpretable approach to signal analysis. Building on this foundation, our work extends the capabilities of explicit variable stepsize state space GRLMs, allowing for an efficient approximation of nonuniformly sampled data by nonuniformly spaced Lagrange interpolating polynomials. Through a series of analyses and visualizations, we show that this approach can significantly outperform uniform stepsize models and other commonly used interpolation techniques, making it a promising direction for future signal processing applications.

The Minimum MFSSA Co-variance method extends the minimum covariance matrix quantity approach by considering a set of shifted signals. Initially, we determined suitable lags for these shifted signals to calculate the covariance matrix rank. MFSSA's MF-kernel parameter was determined using an iterative optimization approach. We assessed MFSSA's accuracy and computational efficiency across multiple test scenarios, finding it to be 3-4 dB more accurate than MF-kaMFSA for clean and noisy data. While the choice of a distance metric in MF-kernels affects performance, we found the Euclidean distance to be effective. MFSSA's novelty lies in its ability to incorporate domain knowledge from various fields, making it adaptable to diverse applications, including temperature curve analysis, image classification in remote sensing, and financial time series forecasting.

The growing availability of machine-human collaboration data highlights a concerning phenomenon where algorithms exhibit behaviors reminiscent of human flaws, namely over sensitivity and over stability. This issue poses significant challenges for leveraging such collaborations to enhance performance. To better understand these tendencies in artificial systems, we investigated the behavior of deep-learning-based automatic essay-scoring models, notably BART. Our research revealed that these models display over sensitivity and over stability, deriving extra points for excessive writing and penalizing references to common objects, despite providing irrelevant accuracy information. This behavior is reinforced by human collaborators who rely on models' feedback for minor nuances but are unwilling to rely on their judgments on core concepts. We discovered that simple adjustments to the models can reduce over sensitivity and over stability issues. Ultimately, our findings suggest that deep-learning-based automatic evaluation tools exhibit these tendencies across various applications beyond automatic essay scoring.

For independently distributed increments with a mean of zero and standard deviation one, a random walk $S_n$ is examined where the variance of the sum of $n$ increments is equal to $n$. As $n$ grows larger, Berman identified two critical points in the behavior of the maximum of the random walk when examining the probability that $S_n$ is positive and the average value of $S_n$ is greater than or equal to $x$ for $x$ in the interval $[0,x_0]$, with $x_0$ being a fixed constant greater than or or equal to zero. These points determine whether the asymptotic behavior follows that of $n^{-1/2}$ for large $n$, or $n^{-1}$ for independently distributed increments. The parameter 'b' also plays a role in affecting the behavior of the probability, with 'b' being equal to $bx_0$ for a constant 'b'. Furthermore, we derive the behavior of the probability for values of 'b' less than or equal to $-x_0$.

A continuous plasma generator has been designed and operated at University of Michigan's Department of Chemical Engineering. The plasma generator uses a low-power radio frequency source to maintain a plasma. By employing a visual observation method and a plasma parameter measurement system, the influence of electron temperature and gas density on the plasma's characteristics was analyzed. The research identified optimal plasma parameters, which resulted in the production of O- and N2 emission lines. The plasma's characteristics changed in response to variations in electron temperature and gas density, which provided valuable insights into the operation of plasma sources.

The success of biological control using nematodes depends on the level of infection and the speed of spreading, which in turn is influenced by how many nematodes are released. We aim to understand the dynamics of insect population growth after adding nematodes to the environment. Our research involves creating models that account for the movement of nematodes in the air and on the ground. We use computer simulations to evaluate the nematode distribution and its impact on insects. Our results show that introducing a vertical component to the model increases the number of insects infected with nematodes. We also compare our findings to a flat model and discuss the implications of nematode application on insect population growth rates at birth.

A widely adopted strategy for reducing the computational complexity of deep learning networks while preserving performance involves employing a W-shaped architecture. This design concept has been successfully applied to a range of supervised classification tasks and is presently being used in the development of W-shaped classification algorithms for nuclear armed missiles. However, no prior research has explored implementing a W-shaped network for the automatic detection of nuclei in histopathology images. Building upon this gap, a W-shaped network has been designed and implemented for more efficient and accurate automatic nucleus detection. This newly proposed network utilizes two streamlined encoder-decoder branches that efficiently extract relevant features from input images, effectively identifying and marking nucleus regions. As a result, it outperforms conventional single-network approaches in terms of both precision and speed, demonstrating exceptional accuracy and real-time processing capabilities.

This study focuses on certain mathematical structures known as number fields with specific characteristics related to quadratic and symplectic groups. We establish a connection between the rank of twist orders at critical points in a specific setting and the non-isomorphism of two complex representations. Additionally, we determine the central critical rank formula for a significant class of these structures. This result builds upon previous work by Zhang and contributes a theoretical foundation for the formula previously conjectured by Li and Luo.

A graph G is considered Hamiltonian if it contains a Hamiltonian path, a sequence of connected vertices that visits every vertex in the graph. Building on this concept, a hypergraph is defined as having a Hamiltonian path if such a path exists within its structure. We introduce a new concept, the Hamiltonian path index, which measures the minimum number of edges that need to be removed from a graph G in order to obtain a graph with a Hamiltonian path. A similar, novel concept, the Hamiltonian path index, is also proposed for hypergraphs. Notably, we investigate the relationship between a hypergraph's Hamiltonian path index and the number of its edges that need to be removed to achieve a hypergraph with a Hamiltonian path. In our research, we determine the Hamiltonian path index for specific types of uniform star hypergraphs and prove that a hypergraph is Hamiltonian if and only if its Hamiltonian path index is zero.

COVID-19 patients sometimes die due to a shift from controlled cell death to uncontrolled cell death.  It has been observed that certain anti-inflammatory drugs, which block controlled cell death pathways, also inadvertently obstruct uncontrolled cell death.  Consequently, cells accumulate and are released into the bloodstream, exacerbating the severe symptoms.  Recent research suggests a promising treatment option by combining two drugs with distinct mechanisms.  This approach may prevent accumulated cells from being released into the bloodstream.  However, there is still a lack of understanding regarding how to optimize the dosage and administration schedule for this combination to effectively manage both controlled and uncontrolled cell death.  This research aims to be a step in that direction by employing a mathematical model to describe both cell death pathways and developing optimal control strategies.  A numerical method is used to find local solutions, while parametric optimization and physician input are employed to locate feasible solutions.  These results provide a framework optimal control solutions can be used to inform clinical decision-making, including dosage and administration timing.  However, further clinical studies are necessary to validate these findings.

This paper outlines a methodical approach for developing efficient algorithms capable of identifying exogenous variables automatically, often overlooked in complex systems. By building on causal models and probabilistic algorithms, these methods can streamline the processing of complex data by pinpointing complex correlations. However, this strategy requires a precise causal model and can be computationally demanding. A simpler alternative method is also introduced, and its effectiveness demonstrated through an application to a complex weather simulation, outperforming traditional approaches in speed while maintaining or improving overall performance.

The Michelson programming language is being utilized for the development of Ethereum-based contracts, and the HELMHOLTZ static analysis tool aids in verifying Michelson programs. This study extends HELMHOLTZ to automatically generate a refined version of Michelson code, which is then subjected to formal property verification with the Idris programming language. We manually constructed an interpreter for Michelson in the F* language with assistance from the HELMHOLTZ tool, specifically the MIP2MORPHEN compiler-transformer. This collaboration has produced the MIPF* interpreter, and we demonstrate its effectiveness by showing how the analysis capabilities of HELMHOLTZ can enhance the formal verification of Michelson programs, with a case in point being the encoding of a secure auction contract on the Ethereum blockchain.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have significantly advanced CNNs and FC Neural Networks.  However, these models are now capable of encapsulating GCNs within their architecture.  By integrating components from both the FC and CNN models, we can construct a type of neural network that uses GCNs as its underlying framework.  This integration gives us access to the broad generality and high expressiveness of existing models while also providing them with the ability to account for the topological structure of input data.  As a result, this type of model is now capable of outperforming the competing algorithms on a variety of real-world datasets used for transductive and inducible node classification.  Moreover, it does so while also maintaining a high level of computational efficiency.  This efficiency is mainly due to the sparse adjacency matrices and diagonal weight matrices commonly associated with GCNs.  This efficiency can be further increased by an order of magnitude with the introduction of a sparse mask into the model, with only a negligible decrease in performance.  This modified version of the model is called S-GCN.  It is mainly designed to overcome the two common limitations associated with existing GCN models.  Firstly, it overcomes their tendency to suffer from over-smoothing.  This problem commonly arises when deep networks are employed.  This issue is further exacerbated when a single induced feature dimension is used for all nodes in a graph.  This limitation is often observed when high-dimensional tabular data is integrated into graph data.

We investigate a hairy black hole in four-dimensional spacetime, governed by a Heisenberg ferromagnetic interaction, and characterize its properties within a cosmological context. Calculations of entropy and temperature reveal intricate dependencies on rotation and cosmological constants, both alone and in combination. Notably, we find that at a fixed cosmological constant, the entropy of these black holes scales quadratically with the number of degrees of freedom and is equivalent to the entropy of standard Chern-Simons black holes derived from pure gravity. Conversely, the temperature of CS black holes exhibits a linear relationship with the number of degrees of freedom. Furthermore, we explore the possibility of a holographic duality between a holographic model and general linearized gravity on a spin-2 field and analyze the conditions under which the black hole is stable.

A novel approach is presented for working with exact symmetries in theoretical physics. This framework focuses on symmetries that preserve a theory's defects and is applied to theories with affine Lie algebra symmetries. By utilizing this method, we are able to derive the fusion rules for certain high-level algebraic structures, such as the $su(2)$ algebra, which has a well-known application in theoretical physics. This work also demonstrates the value of considering global symmetry groups, which may overlook fundamental algebraic structures by treating broken symmetry generators as equivalent. This is particularly relevant for theories experiencing spontaneous symmetry breaking.

Elastography localization technique is hampered by the presence of acoustic speckle noise in ultrasound B-mode images. Lateral accuracy exceeds axial accuracy in ultrasound elastography localization technique due to the isotropic nature of ultrasound resolution. Regulatory authorities mandate high lateral resolution in elastography visualization due to its lower inherent resolution. A new proposed super-resolution technique utilizes trained deep learning networks to enhance elastography lateral resolution. Two specific configurations of the proposed approach were evaluated for their ability to improve lateral resolution in elastography visualization. Experimental results from computer simulations and real-world data sets proved that the proposed method outperforms existing lateral resolution enhancement techniques, producing high-resolution images free of artifacts. Furthermore, integrating the proposed approach with conventional elastography processing steps leads to more accurate lateral displacement estimation and high-resolution elastographic strain maps.

Pseudocode has long been used to verbally outline complex computational solutions, with recent interests in Pseudocode's capabilities to represent and verify sophisticated algorithms like page recommendations and retrieval methods. This concept of Pseudocoding, where Pseudocodes serve as written specifications for developing and testing systems from user perspectives, can be formally defined. A associated specification language based on Pseudogolfer is introduced, which uses logical pseudocodes to create Pseudocodes that are both correct and secure, aligning with their intended purposes. This language leverages first-order logic to describe and verify complex system behaviors, ensuring Pseudocodes are mathematically sound representations from user viewpoints.

Given a set $D$ consisting of 0-1 valued $k$-tuples, and a Boolean lattice $B_k$ of all such $k$-tuples, a coloring $\chi$ is considered a rainbow rainbow coloring if for every subset $A$ of $D$, there exists another subset $A'$ within $D$ where $\chi$ is constant on $A'$ and a superset of $A$. This paper explores the number of elements required in $D$ for a rainbow Ramsey property to be satisfied, specifically denoted as $crb(N, N, N, k) = N$ if for any coloring $\chi$ of $B_k$ using $N$ colors, a rainbow subset of size $N$ is guaranteed to exist for every subset of $D$ with size $N$. Building on previous research, new upper bounds are established for $crb(N, N, N, k)$, with specific focus on small values of $k$. Moreover, a lower bound is also determined for $crb(N, N, N, 2) = \Omega(\sqrt{N}\cdot 2^{\sqrt{N}})$.

We developed an initial method to create a coarser approximation for the $k$-means clustering problem using just one pass through the data. Our algorithm is suitable for both online and batch settings and can also be applied to useful distance functions like $ℓ_0$, $ℓ_1$, and $ℓ_2$. Specifically, we designed a general method based on reducing the problem to finding the median, and then using existing coarser approximations for the median to solve the $k$-means problem.

This paper addresses the challenge of modeling scenarios within complex environments, where an agent must navigate and avoid being caught by one or more pursuing agents. We focus on grid-based settings and propose a novel approach by dividing the environment into distinct regions of influence. By representing these regions as a simplified structure in a graph, we aim to capture the dynamic interactions between the evading agent and its pursuers more effectively. We introduce specific metrics to analyze these interactions and present real-world case studies to validate our method. Our results show a significant improvement in calculating future dynamics and demonstrate that our approach yields more accurate predictions of possible outcomes. Furthermore, our framework reveals patterns in complex scenarios, providing a more efficient solution to pursuit-evasion problems on grid-based settings.

A set of joint probability distributions over variables X_0, X_1, ... ,X_{n-1} is defined as a an n-tuple. This n-tuple can be represented as a hypergraph if the variables X_i are distinct. A concept called nontransitivity has been previously defined for probabilistic models and previously undefined concepts like cyclic symmetry and cyclic alignment have been formally defined in this work. A key finding in this paper is that a nontransitive model must be cyclically symmetric. Another significant conclusion is that causal Markov chains are inherently nontransitive. A model is classified as cyclically aligned if its cyclic permutations follow the same causal structure. Conversely, a model is classified as nonaligned if its cyclic permutations follow reversed causal structures. This paper also explores the possibility of combining aligned and nonaligned models in a cyclic manner. A class of cyclically symmetric Bayesian networks is discovered which allows for efficient computation of marginal probabilities through the use of a simplified sum-product algorithm. This is in contrast to general Bayesian networks, where computing marginal probabilities can be computationally expensive. Furthermore, this paper reveals that cyclically symmetric Bayesian networks may appear deceptively complicated but can often be understood through a remarkably simple lens.

Our research focuses on developing an unsupervised method to translate historical CCTV camera images from older technology to digital CCTV. We've adapted the cycleGAN framework for this purpose. To enhance AdaIN within the AdaIN architecture, we've made key modifications to achieve a more natural color and a smoother image output. Moreover, our AdaIN implementation allows the AdaIN style features to be learned from color images while preserving the content of grayscale images. Our proposed design has been successfully tested on actual surveillance images, demonstrating its effectiveness in upgrading black and white images from older CCTV technology to color and digital images.

In this research, we examine representations learned in open-domain dialog systems from multiple perspectives. A new score function is introduced to measure alignment across various views, which serves as the foundation for our approach. Our method employs teacher student algorithms to train representations that learn from each other's feedback. Experimental results from dialog training and evaluation show that our method significantly outperforms current techniques by achieving top rankings in various representation learning tasks. To facilitate further study of multi-view dialog representation learning, we make our source code publicly available.

In this research, we establish the geodesic nature of a potential vector field in a manifold where the manifold's geometry is governed by conformal $\eta$-Ricci-Yamabe soliton equations. This condition enables us to express the Laplace equation directly using the soliton's parameters. Additionally, we examine gradient conformal $\eta$-Ricci-Yamabe solitons with constant expansion and demonstrate that they reduce to conformal solitons with harmonic dilations. Furthermore, we derive the associated potential vector field as a Killing field under these conditions.

A new approach to understanding deformed halos is presented, where their structure varies based on their arrangement of rotational states.  We have developed a method to calculate these structures and found that statements about the placement of halos in deformation space are now predictable based on the arrangement of their states.  Furthermore, this method allows us to connect the structural features of halos to their single-particle spectra.  Using this method, we have calculated the structures of several deformed halos and several of them have been discovered experimentally.

One key limitation of BasicVSR is that its use of linear projections in self-attention restricts its capability to model complex relationships in video restoration tasks, leading to suboptimal performance. To address this issue, BasicVSR++ was developed by incorporating non-linear cross-correlation projectors and the use of CBDCA to efficiently integrate historical frames while maintaining computational efficiency. Our experiments demonstrate that BasicVSR++ significantly outperforms BasicVSR with a notable improvement of 0.522 dB in PSNR on the EDID dataset and achieves a substantial reduction of 65% in computational efficiency compared to BasicVSR, with a minimal decrease of only 0.125 dB in performance.

This study addresses the challenge of describing processes in which partons transform into W or Z bosons and subsequently participate in 2 → 1 reactions. We develop corrections to leading order in the electroweak sector and confirm that these corrections do not interfere with conventional parton distribution functions (PDFs). The approach proposed can be applied to processes involving measurements of single bosons single top quarks or Higgs bosons produced via vector boson fusion or in association with a top quark.

Using multiple models in reinforcement learning is a common strategy to enhance sample efficiency through data reuse. However, combining several models into one can inadvertently introduce conflicting information, potentially degrading performance. We believe an alternative approach lies in avoiding a unified model combination, instead leveraging separate learning algorithms that learn distinct policies and knowledge representations. This method proves particularly effective in a critical problem of learning multiple skills from unrelated tasks, such as locomotion. By eschewing a unified dynamics model and instead learning separate policies and dynamics models in parallel, we allow each component to learn without being constrained by irrelevant data. Our algorithm, PARADOX, builds on this principle of parallel learning to efficiently learn multiple skills from seemingly unrelated tasks.

We establish a condition for a noncompact boundary to be considered compact at a specific point. Building on this, we derive a representation of the heat equation solution on a manifold with boundary, incorporating the fundamental solution of the interior and a boundary integral term. This representation leads to a new estimate for the heat equation solution in space-time domains with a compact boundary.

Godel's 1931 incompleteness theorem demonstrated that every consistent formal system capable of representing basic mathematics has statements that can neither be confirmed nor refuted within that system. This notion was significantly expanded in 1946 by Rosser, who developed a more comprehensive version of Godel's first incompleteness principle. Despite its theoretical significance, little has been explored into the applications of Godel's and Rosser's findings in computer science and related disciplines until very recent years. This article serves as an overview of Godel's and Rosser's discoveries, with a focus on their fundamental concepts and a detailed examination of a simple model representing shared knowledge and knowledge that eludes formalization. Additionally, it addresses various questions that arise from this model.
This study proposes an extension of Hadamard's three circles theorem to function elements centered at the origin with infinite radius of symmetry in $\mathbb{R}^n$ for $n \ge 2$.

When planning a survey, selecting an appropriate subset of a population is a critical step. The proposed paper presents a new method for choosing a balanced random sample based on a predefined weight. The author details an iterative procedure that continuously refines a weighting scheme for a given population. This procedure is shown to converge under specific conditions. The paper also provides multiple examples to illustrate the method and discusses its theoretical properties as well as practical applications in the context of survey design.

Traditional robot tasks that involve mapping and navigation typically assume calibrated sensors, but widely adopted approaches to task planning often neglect sensor calibration. A more effective pathway is direct regression to a task, which obviates the need for intermediate steps like sensor calibration. In this research, we explore a single-step method that utilizes an artificial neural network to map sensor data directly to task-execution actions. This model is trained through a combination of reinforcement learning and visual feedback. To accelerate training and execute tasks with greater sample efficiency, we incorporate a secondary policy that relies on simulated data. This approach is tailored to a non-calibrated camera calibration task and showcases the feasibility of direct sensor calibration for task execution through targeted experiments.

After receiving observed evidence, we often need to generate samples from a modified version of a previously defined distribution that takes into account this new information. Conditional generative adversarial networks (CGANs) can provide approximate posterior samples based on a reference black box that is itself replaced by a CGAN in a second-step procedure derived from the CGAN's minimax game. A proposed solution involves using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN (C-W2G) as the backend for Bayesian inference in high-dimensional problems. This paper demonstrates how a C-W2G can efficiently use a single evaluation of its game to produce approximate posterior samples after observing data. Specifically, this paper shows this method's effectiveness in inferring object poses from images.

This study aims to provide a comprehensive examination of linearity in fractional order systems. Key aspects such as determining the matrix structure, establishing invariant subspaces, and assessing controllability and observability in systems with fractional derivatives will be discussed and analyzed.

We propose a dynamic beam training method for multi-hop terahertz connections between Oculi's Oculix platforms. This method aims to maintain optimal system performance by continuously adapting to changes in the communication environment. A key innovation introduced is the concept of a training window that can be adaptively adjusted based on the optimal configuration. We developed a model to efficiently compute a near-optimal algorithm for this adaptive adjustment. Our model takes into consideration various system parameters and provides a efficient computation of a near-optimal algorithm for the adaptive adjustment of the training window size. We modeled the time required for a packet to travel from one end to the other, including the adaptability of the system. We also introduced an efficient computation of a near-optimal algorithm for the adaptive adjustment of the training window size. To validate our approach we performed simulations using realistic parameters. To illustrate the benefits of our dynamic beam training method we compared it to a static beam training method and a traditional coherent beam tracking system. To validate our approach we performed simulations using realistic parameters. To validate our model we conducted experiments with a 48 GHz connections using Oculix's Oculix platforms. To validate our approach we performed experiments with a 48 GHz connections using Oculix's Oculix platforms which demonstrated that our dynamic beam training method outperformed the static beam training method and the coherent beam tracking system. The pulsar radio source of B1133.6+16 is renowned for its intense scattering, 
which scatters the pulsar's radio waves, distorting its light curve and 
hindering precise timing measurements. To gain a clearer view, we combined 
telescope observations with theoretical calculations to analyze the scattering 
patterns. By examining individual scattering layers, we discovered five of them, 
with four lying approximately 1000 parsecs away from Earth. These results can be 
used to study the structure of the scattering medium and the scattering's effect 
on the propagation of radio waves.

In recent years, deep learning models with cascaded architectures have been widely employed in various tasks involving quasi-periodic signals, including speech recognition. These models consist of multiple front-end extractors followed by a back-end classifier. By treating each frame's feature vector as an instance within a circular manifold, a single universal transformation can be applied to extract frame-dependent features. Building on this concept, a simplified circular neural network variant, called the Simple Universal Circular Neural Network (SUCNN), was proposed with a single front-end and a simplified parameter-sharing mechanism. Experimental results demonstrated that SUCNN outperformed cascaded networks using frame-invariant transformations in speech recognition, achieving a 2% relative reduction in error with just one front-end compared to four. Furthermore, combining a simpler front-end with an explicit circular layer resulted in better feature representations than more complex cascaded networks, indicating that incorporating explicit quasi-periodic constraints can lead to more effective feature learning.

When working with substantial text documents for annotation tasks, the necessity for multiple rounds of processing highlights the potential for technology to enhance annotator efficiency. Annotators often need to execute several steps per section, including section division, identification of key parts, and creation of corresponding sections in a target document. To automate or streamline these steps, users often need to switch between multiple browser tabs, a process that can be significantly speed up by utilizing a single interface with two iframes. However, this basic solution falls short in providing crucial context from both documents. Our proposed solution involves a unified interface featuring two iframes, augmented with a shared area for section metadata, allowing for enhanced contextual understanding and faster, more user-friendly multi-document annotation sections.

We've developed a computational tool to simulate the atmospheres of planets located in the zone where conditions are right for liquid water, considering water vapor and the influence of chemical composition metallicity has on gases like carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, and ammonia. By utilizing retrieval analysis on real-world data from two planets - Terraformed Gliese-436b and Neptune-mass HD85512b - our model extracted key parameters including the concentration of CO2, metallicity, and the opacity scaling factor in a heterogeneous model. However, more cases are needed to refine this metallicity-sensitive atmospheric model and demonstrate its capability in identifying the presence of specific molecules with low abundance from satellite spectroscopy.

We examine the stability of a zero-energy peak in the spectral density of a one-dimensional topological superconductor. This peak arises from a Majorana mode isolated from the rest of the system. Its persistence is hindered by environmental interactions, including thermal effects, random impulses, and temperature-dependent fluctuations. By computing the majorana correlation in the context of master equation dynamics and by using the master approach, we demonstrate that the influence of finite temperatures, velocities greater than zero, and discrete spectra can be quantified and potentially managed.

Road inspections are crucial for maintaining infrastructure but can be slow and labor-intensive due to the vast amount of data involved. To address this challenge, we developed RoadAtlas, an intuitive dashboard that expedites inspections by leveraging pre-compiled summary statistics from our system to rapidly identify potential issues. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RoadAtlas by showing how it enabled a full dataset inspection in under a day, a task that would have taken months using traditional methods. Moreover, we designed an iterative user feedback loop within RoadAtlas to ensure the system continues to evolve based on user input, thereby enhancing its functionality and usability over time.

Lazarus and Maltsiniotis originally defined a functor from the bicategory of gorillas to the bicategory of gorillas, linking topological algebra K to its algebraic counterpart A through topological Hochschild homology (THH) at a specific value A. Building upon this work, we describe a universal THH functor denoted as $\unicode{212B}$, which serves as a universal object for the gorilla-bicategory, thereby replacing one structure with another within the context of gorillas-bicategory. This universal functor exhibits a direct relationship with the THH functor, which can be demonstrated through the observation that the natural transformation between the universal $\unicode{212B}$ and the THH functor is precise (an equivalence of gorillas). Additionally, we establish a connection between the universal $\unicode{212B}$ and the shadow of the bicategory of gorillas, proving that the universal $\unicode{212B}$ is equivalent to the pseudo-loxodromic shadow of the bicategory of gorillas. This article extends the work of Jacobson and Hillar on topic algebras by utilizing 2-categorical algebraic type theory.

Recently, significant progress has been made in the field of sound source classification, particularly with the emergence of deep learning techniques. Current research primarily focuses on identifying single sounds or distinguishing between mixed sounds in a limited frequency range. To advance the field of sound source classification, this work introduces the VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS) benchmark, which aims to evaluate the ability to identify multiple sounds with spatial information within the mixed spectrum. Using pre-recorded tracks and simulated propagation, we created a dataset consisting of 12 frequencies, 9 sound types, and additional real-world data. With the provision of annotation tracks and production details, this work presents a comprehensive benchmark for identifying mixed sound sources and demonstrates the potential of our method to achieve high accuracy with frequency aggregation.

Hyperslab Graph Convolutions (GS-GCN) is a novel approach that applies a lorentzian transformation to Euclidean space within a hyperbolic framework. 
Our analysis reveals that node embedding in GS-GCN preserves a literal linear interpretation, where a finite Euclidean ball becomes a hyperbolic slab. 
Contrary to previous hyperbolic graph convolutional networks (HGCNs) that encode node features using a diagonal Lorentzian transformation, 
our GS-GCN proposes a novel approach to node feature encoding that offers a literal linear interpretation. 
To evaluate the GS-GCN model's performance, we conducted experiments on four real-world datasets. 
Our findings demonstrate that GS-GCN surpasses state-of-the-art hyperbolic models in graph convolutional networks (GCNs), 
showing superior generalization capabilities and robustness when trained on a reduced dataset. 
Furthermore, GS-GCN achieves enhanced efficiency by offering a more compact representation of the data.

This study investigates the recoverability of a boundary condition within a linear second-order elliptic equation that has smoothly varying coefficients,受限于同类型系数边界条件限制。The domain is fixed, smooth and compact, and we're focused on a part of its boundary. Our main contribution is a visibility inequality that considers a single point, which leads to our primary stability finding. The approach involves an original use of the Tataru approach using a single function, along with a novel application of the geometric optics approach to prove controllable observability inequalities.

A new type of quantized phenomenon, known as a TSS, emerges from the nonreciprocal interaction between light and mechanical motion in a single-optical device. By developing a hybrid system with one optical cavity, a mechanical resonator and a pair of coupled microwave resonators, we show that the TSS can be observed through a significant asymmetry in the dynamics of light's spontaneous propagation. We derive a set of design principles for this system and demonstrate that it can be tailored to achieve the 50:50 split of photons in the microwave resonators, even after a pulsed injection. Furthermore, we find that the position of the mechanical resonator has a significant impact on the system's nonreciprocal behavior. By breaking the symmetry of coupling, we can control the propagation difference and design the system to realize a visualized TSS in the microwave resonators.

To understand the SCCF's limitations, we can view it as a modified version of the mu-calculus with additional features like uniqueness and atomic properties, which then allows it to be seen as a more basic form of System F. In its advanced variant, we can consider the SCCF with full quantification and classical logic as part of a specific type of a dependent system. In both scenarios, we can demonstrate that SCCF has a structural equivalent to a more complex logical system, while proper SCCF has a more restricted form and exhibits explosive behavior.

Social interactions are often explained using statistical physics concepts, yet their limitations are also recognized. This study proposes a new approach, based on the idea that an effective temperature can be used to describe social systems and, as a result, their non-equilibrium nature. This solution allows for a more straightforward derivation of the Tsallis distribution and offers a fresh perspective on the significance of this statistical model.

In linearized gravity, incorporating a mass term for the graviton in a general theory of gravity is not compatible with special relativity. This incompatibility arises specifically in the transverse and traceless components of the graviton, which are also affected by a violation of rotational symmetry due to a mass term. This issue is absent in AdS space due to the inherent mass term in AdS gravity required by unitarity. As a result, the number of propagating degrees of freedom in AdS gravity matches those in the DGP model's brane, where a massive graviton also appears. This unique property of the AdS gravity's unitary mode enables the realization of anti-de Sitter / conformal field theory with a half integer spin difference, despite the extra constraint from AdS symmetry.

For any signed graph $H$ and a group $\mathcal{G}$, an extended $\mathcal{G}$-double cover of $H$ is defined as a $\mathcal{G}$-labeling on the edges of a graph $\varGamma$ that adheres to specific adjacency rules based on the signs of the edges in $H$. This concept is referred to as a $\mathcal{G}$-extended double cover of $H$. In our research, we investigate the structural properties of extended double covers, focusing on planar characteristics and cyclicity. We verify a 2009 proposition by Dantus in detail, demonstrating that the extended $\mathbb{Z}_2$-double covers of a signed graph are cyclic if and only if the original graph is a tree or a complete graph with five vertices. We provide multiple examples to support this conjecture. In this work we break down the properties of Hamiltonian dynamics into four categories: those that preserve volume, those that are solvable, those that are chaotic, and mixed behaviors. We organize known results and state in terms of categories for equilibrium states under a given potential and temperature, summarizing various states of matter such as insulators, conductors, and more exotic phases like Weyl semimetals, from the perspective of quantum mechanics. We also provide a new characterization of quantum equilibrium states that unites these concepts. Additionally, we extend some of our statements to systems that lose coherence.

The concept of negative temperature can be effectively illustrated using a two-level system and becomes mathematically non-restrictive when generalized to any two distinct states.

A notable challenge arises in employing the standard Hamiltonian for a system with infinite possible outcomes, as it typically results in both energy eigenvalues being infinitely large.

However, adopting a relative energy scale resolves this issue.

To offer a more adaptable approach than utilizing a spin-1/2 system, we develop the two-level model using variables from the harmonic oscillator.

This model can be utilized to describe a system consisting of two different vibrational states.

We illustrate the negative temperature concept through this two-level harmonic oscillator system via precise analytical formulas.

Nevertheless, real-world applications of such a system encounter issues due to infinite displacement and momentum eigenvalues associated with harmonic oscillators.

To address this, we propose a modification where anharmonic potentials replace those of harmonic oscillators.

Specifically, we utilize the quartic anharmonic potential with two distinct equilibrium points, creating what we term the "double-well anharmonic oscillator" (DWAO).

DWAO enables a more realistic two-level model by incorporating equivalent energies, displacements, and momenta for its two states.

Utilizing DWAO, we demonstrate the negative temperature phenomenon through relevant observables such as average energy, quasi-energy gap, and probability distribution.

We've developed an approach to estimate the structure of restricted signed sumsets $A{-}A$ for finite sets $⊂Z_n$. This method focuses on identifying large integers that can be expressed as differences between elements of $Z_n$. Consequently, these integers can be excluded from further analysis. Determining $A{-}A$ primarily relies on identifying components within a related set consisting of smaller integers. These components can often be described using union and operation on sets. Furthermore, we can estimate $A{-}A$ based on the properties of these components. This approach provides sufficient conditions for $A{-}A$ to possess a specific structure and offers an alternative structure to existing results by Chebolu and Koh. Additionally, we have used this approach to derive structures for specific types of sets known as cyclic and arithmetic progressions.

Our research aims to explore the potential of using computer-aided diagnosis systems to reduce the labor required for colorectal polyp classification by trained medical professionals. We specifically used a pre-trained deep neural network to automatically classify and grade colorectal adenomas from optical images. Our results show that our proposed method significantly outperforms conventional techniques, achieving a 21 to 45 percent lower error rate. Furthermore, our system is so effective that it surpasses the accuracy of a board-certified surgeon in certain scenarios. To aid the development of this computer-aided diagnosis, we made our dataset and code publicly available for other researchers to review and build upon.

This study offers a novel wave number continuous finite element method for resolving high-frequency acoustic scattering issues with a mixed boundary condition. This approach efficiently manages time derivatives by employing the Helmholtz equation and effectively handles frequency-dependent elements through appropriate normalization. To analyze computational costs, we establish an inscription property for the related 1D element. This enables construction of a stable basis for any number of wave number values within a given range. Additionally, this property leads to the creation of an interpolation scheme for scalar and vector field approximations. These approximations retain inclusion in their respective Sobolev spaces and demonstrate countable stability. As a result, this scheme forms the basis for developing a number of stable finite element methods. This includes constant and linear finite element methods using the proposed 1D element. This approach effectively eliminates round-off errors related to high-frequency applications. It also offers alternatives to traditional orthogonalization methods for creating stable bases. This results in efficient computation of coefficients for linear finite element methods, scaling logarithmically with the number of degrees of freedom. This solution avoids expensive computations associated with factorizing large matrices related to finite element discretizations. This implies constant complexity in terms of frequency for such computations. This is achievable through re-formulating the discrete problem and applying suitable pre-conditioning techniques to related systems of equations.

We continue the work form 'Jets of correlations in the higher-spin XXZ chain' by providing additional details on the rapidity dependence of scalar products and form factors that underpin the jets of correlations function.

This study explores the challenges of speech translation with limited data, investigating few-shot and neural meta-learning approaches. We developed a few-shot speech translation method, leveraging pre-trained speaker-agnostic and speech representation models, trained via a neural linear layer. Our method achieves superior results in low-shot learning scenarios, notably enhancing speech translation performance by 5.4% on average. Additionally, we developed a neural meta-learning learning algorithm, focusing on adapting speaker agnostic representation and aligning speaker identity. This algorithm leads to improved performance in a speech separation task and provides better speech translation outcomes compared to prior methods.

A new approach to describing a particle's electric and magnetic multipoles is presented, based on the irreducible tensors of SO(3), to overcome issues with conventional definitions. This new definition addresses problems with orthogonality and normalization, and yields unique multipoles that directly relate to a particle's radius and scattering behavior. These multipoles are used to analyze a dielectric sphere, revealing that they provide a clearer understanding of scattering and can be applied to enhance optical measurements of particles.

We demonstrate that Schur elements are essentially Harish-Chandra images of certain bimodules which correspond to a specific subset of $U(\mathfrak{gl}_n)$ that is known as the diagonal centralizer algebra. Additionally, we propose a concrete basis for these Schur elements and establish their connection to shifted Schur polynomials through the Harish-Chandra isomorphism.

We apply a small dark sector and parity symmetry to type-II seesaw mechanism theory to study its robustness. By adding two singlet scalar fields and a vector-like fermion doublet to the scalar sector, we modify the potential to ensure a stable vacuum, preserve dark parity symmetry, and enable neutral lepton condensation for generating mass. With these changes, we can achieve dark matter abundance, scale-separation dark matter stability, and consistency between dark and visible sector scales for neutrino mass generation. Our analysis shows that the dark matter relic abundance can be met for parameters within $10$ TeV, and dark matter can be thermally produced when the dark sector scale is between $10^4$ and $10^7$ GeV. Additionally, this multi-scale type-II seesaw model can naturally occur and be tested at the LHC and dark matter detectors.

In transition metal oxides, strong spin-orbit coupling gives rise to intricate phenomena, potentially offering a pathway for dynamic manipulation of spin-orbit parameters through controlled light pulses. However, a key challenge lies in accurately determining the spin-orbit coupling strength and addressing theoretical discrepancies. We address this by incorporating a configuration interaction model that accounts for strong electron interactions and crystal field splitting, and we demonstrate that the effective spin-orbit coupling strength is not merely a atomic property but is significantly influenced by these factors. This approach enables us to derive a Hermitian Hamiltonian that incorporates strong correlation effects and field splitting, and we apply it to CeO2 as an example, revealing that the effective spin-orbit coupling strength differs from its atomic counterpart due to these external influences.

We determine the relationship between the I-functions of toric complete intersections and their slices defined by additional boundary divisors. By comparing these I-functions, we derive a formula that relates them and use this derivation to transform the J-function identities associated with toric complete intersections into one another.

Using artificial intelligence for medical image analysis is increasingly common, but these systems' reliability can be compromised due to flaws in their underlying convolutional neural network designs. Current research on improving such representations has primarily focused on natural images, which limits its applicability to accurate and reliable medical image predictions. To address this shortcoming, our work investigates a new code space generated by a variational autoencoder that encodes artificial medical images, which accurately reflects actual physiological changes caused by certain pathologies. We demonstrate that by leveraging this code space and injecting relevant knowledge into the neural network, we can enhance medical image predictions and treat adverse effects as variational problems with well-defined solutions. Our proposed approach yields significant improvements over existing methods while enabling more robust encodings, as demonstrated through real-world experiments and ablation studies on MRI brain images affected by Alzheimer's disease.

Multidimensional data presentation can be challenging for non-experts. To tackle this, we've created a new design assistant named ViDaExpert for multivariate data visualization. This AI assistant, based on reinforcement learning, combines multivariate data visualization knowledge with user preferences to generate diverse visualization designs. Users can provide feedback on generated designs, and ViDaExpert can learn and generate new designs based on this input. Our user study shows that a feedback-based design can achieve similar presentation effects to its non-expert counterpart with fewer elements. Moreover, a significant majority of participants found that multivariate data visualization knowledge aids in understanding complex data. Furthermore, users found the interactive interface and design options provided by ViDaExpert to be intuitive and beneficial in presenting complex multidimensional data. We have made ViDaExpert publicly available on GitHub for others to use.

This study utilizes a second derivative monomial approximation of high order to approximate a function defined over two dimensions, with a focus on a refined grid. To facilitate this approximation, a resolution grid is created by taking the Cartesian product of two one-dimensional grids. Each dimension's grid consists of equidistant points defined by a step size 'h', with the grids extending from -1 to 1.
